arguments.markdown:
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,072B, or 39.3x trailing EPS of $8.72; the price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::

{"url":"https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/09/the-hinge-for-apples-new-foldable-phone-was-built-with-ai/","title":"The hinge for Apple’s new foldable phone was built with AI","text":"In Brief
Posted:

12:21 PM PDT · September 9, 2026

Image Credits:Apple

Duo, Apple’s long-awaited foldable phone announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday, contains a number of surprises, including a critical hinge that was designed and built with the help of AI and 3D printing.

The new phone represents Apple’s first entry into the foldable phone genre — a category of devices that has seen significant consumer enthusiasm but whose form factors haven’t always lived up to the hype. As you might expect from a product that, by design, undergoes twice as much wear as a traditional device, most foldables suffer significant degradation and don’t have the durability of other smartphones.

Apple claims that it has integrated innovative protections into the Duo’s design to keep the phone from falling prey to the typical wear and tear associated with foldables. That includes the hinge, according to Johny Srouji, the company’s chief hardware officer.

“During manufacturing, we use AI algorithms to precisely match each individual hinge with its best-fit housing to ensure perfect alignment, and a confocal laser progressively scans the topology of every single unit and 3D prints up to 25 micro layers of a custom photopolymer to eliminate residual waviness,” Srouji said during Wednesday’s event.

Srouji also shared that Apple gave the foldable phone “a custom nano-texture finish that significantly reduces glare and reflections,” as well as a multilayer lamination strategy designed to increase the device’s durability. Of course, it remains to be seen whether those protections will be enough to keep the Duo in peak physical condition in the long run.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year, +2% YoY; Omdia 1.25B (+2%) | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7% YoY, steepest annual fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP); 2026 = $196.5B x 4/3 / $613B | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC, +1.7%; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |
| Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units. Top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line, so the two methods reconcile on direction and approximate size. The mechanism is a memory cost shock, with NAND and DRAM prices up more than 300% year over year, passed through to shelf prices. The market is not expanding; it is being repriced, and the vendors with premium mix and supply leverage capture the difference.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at 1.26B units and a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% a year earlier on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every geographic segment in double digits; that is genuine pricing power [S17, S87, S84]. But IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases, and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down more than 20%. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months.

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects it to ship more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, about 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a global advertising pool of $1.34T in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables are a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. Foldables and services can add; the non-phone device pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

| Region | Market size (latest dated) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Americas | Global pool $613B (2026E); regional value not published in free trackers | Apple +11.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; home market; 42.9% of FY2025 revenue | US tariffs (Section 232 and 301); platform antitrust | Samsung, Google, Motorola | S84, S5, S6 |
| Europe | Not published | Apple +16.1% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 26.7% of revenue | DMA take-rate cuts from 2026-10-01; GDPR | Samsung, Xiaomi, Google | S77, S6 |
| Greater China | 66M units in Q2 2026; 134M in H1 2026 | Market -4.3% in Q2 2026; H2 2026 decline could reach 20%; Apple +30.0% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 18.1% share versus Huawei 22.6% | Market access; local champion; data rules | Huawei, OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi, Honor | S87, S6 |
| Japan | Not published | Apple +10.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 6.9% of revenue | Yen weakness; carrier-controlled channel | Samsung, Google, Sharp | S6 |
| Rest of Asia-Pacific | Not published; emerging markets forecast down more than 20% in 2026 | Apple +19.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 8.1% of revenue; India manufacturing and retail expansion | Price sensitivity; tariffs | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, OPPO, Transsion | S84, S6 |

Geography splits the durability question, and policy is a live variable in every region [S6, S87, S77]. Greater China is 15.5% of revenue but produced 30% growth in the first nine months of FY2026; Europe is 26.7% and grew 16%, the Americas 42.9% and 11%, Japan 6.9% and 10%, and Rest of Asia-Pacific 8.1% and 19%. The China number is the most fragile: the market fell 4.3% in Q2 2026, Apple's 18.1% share trailed Huawei's 22.6%, and the top six vendors hold 96%. The EU's DMA terms cut the commission on externally distributed digital transactions to 5% from 1 October 2026; US tariffs moved twice in 2026, with the Supreme Court striking down certain IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026 and Section 301 duties imposed since, while the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs on Apple products on 14 January 2026. Demand is overwhelmingly organic consumer replacement rather than policy-created: China's subsidy support faded in 2026 and India's incentives are supply-side manufacturing support, not consumer demand. The budget owner is the consumer or the carrier financing plan, the procurement cycle follows the annual September launch, and willingness to pay is being tested by a 27.6% market ASP increase. What would change the conclusion is services growth above 15% with user growth, a foldable cycle that adds the $45.7B category value IDC projects, or China stabilising after the H2 2026 air pocket. Confidence is high on 2026 data and low on 2027-2030 regional sizing, because regional market values are paywalled and Apple does not disclose units; the open questions are what share of iPhone growth is units versus price, whether services growth is users or price, how much China demand was pulled forward, and how much memory cost Apple can pass through in FY2027.

::: evidence
**Apple's markets are growing in dollars while shrinking in units, so its growth is price- and share-led, not market-led.**

The global pool is $613B of smartphone value in 2026 against just over 1.0B units, with a 27.6% ASP increase doing the work volume used to do (IDC, S84). Premium concentration (29% of units) and Apple's 65% share of it explain why Apple captures 36-43% of value on 20-24% of units (Counterpoint, S94; Apple filings, S5, S6). Foldables ($45.7B of category value by 2027) and services ($120.5B TTM at 76.3% gross margin) are the only pools large enough to move group growth; wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030 (IDC, S85).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year, +2% YoY; Omdia 1.25B (+2%) | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7% YoY, steepest annual fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP); 2026 = $196.5B x 4/3 / $613B | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC, +1.7%; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |
| Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units, and the sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock, with NAND and DRAM prices up more than 300% year over year, passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at 1.26B units and a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% a year earlier on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every geographic segment in double digits; that is genuine pricing power [S17, S87, S84]. But IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases, and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down more than 20%. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months.

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects it to ship more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a global advertising pool of $1.34T in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables are a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. Foldables and services can add; the non-phone device pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's profit is unusually cash-true. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 operating cash flow was $146,724M, capital expenditure $10,041M and free cash flow $136,683M against net income of $128,930M — conversion of 1.06x on capex of 2.2% of revenue, against 0.50x and 39.2% at Microsoft and 0.08x and 33.9% at Alphabet. The income statement behind that cash grew revenue from $383,285M in FY2023 to $416,161M in FY2025 and $466,823M trailing, with operating margin of 29.8%, 32.0% and 33.2%. The nine months to 27 June 2026 produced an incremental operating margin of 43.0% — $21,809M more operating income on $50,662M more revenue — which is the bull case in one line. The question is how much of that increment is repeatable. [S5, S6]

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, the highest Apple has reported. Part of that is structural: services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue. Part is not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 percentage points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to those refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average, Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%, and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The 30 July 2026 release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); nine-month products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9% a year earlier on mix and refunds, while memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and Apple's 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off the trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of the $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real; the 2026 step-up is partly working capital

Nine-month operating cash flow rose 43.1% to $116,996M while net income rose 20.0%, and the balance sheet shows why: receivables fell to $31,398M from $39,777M and vendor non-trade receivables to $27,509M from $33,180M, cutting days sales outstanding to 24.5 from 34.9, while inventory rose to $11,092M from $5,718M and payables fell to $64,525M from $69,860M, shortening the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1. Part of the record is therefore a release of working capital that reverses as memory is pre-bought, not a permanent lift in earning power. The top line is not being smoothed either: deferred revenue of $14.9B is 3.2% of trailing revenue, and only $7,260M of nine-month revenue came out of the opening deferred balance. [S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. The FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B payable within twelve months and $37.0B of future interest, commercial paper ran at a 4.19% weighted rate, leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need a question rather than a red flag: $2,604M of unrealised losses on the securities book, and intangible assets that rose to $25,417M net from $13,301M — $38,220M gross, $12,803M accumulated amortisation — without the 10-Q disaggregating what was bought. [S5, S6]

| Return on equity | 171.9% | 157.4% | 171.4% | 148.8% | S5, S6 |

| Cash and marketable securities | 162,099 | 156,650 | 132,420 | 146,517 | S5, S6 |
| Net cash | 51,011 | 50,021 | 33,763 | 62,173 | S5, S6 |

| Days payables outstanding | 106.7 | 119.7 | 115.4 | 98.3 | S5, S6 |

### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: free cash flow of $136,683M over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 71.2%, against 57.3% in FY2025. With a ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, any plausible cost of equity of 9-11% is cleared several times; the constraint is the price, because a $5,072B market capitalisation on $128,930M of trailing net income is a 2.5% earnings yield. Capital allocation supports that reading rather than contradicting it: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M are 67.0% of free cash flow, net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. This is not a debt-funded buyback story. [S6, S7]

### What the next print has to clear

No audited fiscal 2026 exists yet: Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026, two days after this analysis, and the only forward numbers are management's guidance of 9-11% revenue growth for that quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B) with iPhone growth in the mid-teens, against consensus of $56.4B of iPhone revenue for the quarter, $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%). Sensitivity on trailing figures after a 17.3% tax rate: 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of EPS (6.0%), 500 basis points is $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment is $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue at the 39.9% product margin is $0.55 (6.3%). Gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue while a unit miss applies only to hardware. The implication for an investor is that earnings quality is not the constraint on this name — the price is, since 39x trailing net income already assumes the 2026 margin is a base rather than a peak. The open diligence is specific: what gross margin does management guide for the December 2026 quarter, how much of FY2027 memory is contracted at fixed prices, and what was acquired for the $12,116M increase in net intangibles? [S71, S72]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 2 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,996 characters)
Apple's regulatory exposure, not its ESG record, is what can change a long-only case. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn and Services revenue $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin, so App Store commissions and the Google default-search payment sit inside the profit pool carrying the premium multiple [S5]. Fines are not the mechanism; remedies and fee schedules are. Bear case: a 10-15% operating-income tail from losing or repricing search placement and a structurally lower App Store take rate over 2026-2028. The mechanism is that a dollar of commission or default rent carries almost no marginal cost, so losing it hits operating income faster than revenue.

### The EU fine is small; the fee schedule is not

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation, 0.1% of FY2025 net sales. The material part is the fee schedule: from 2026-10-01 Apple's unified EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase (down from 30%), 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and 5% on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web. Apple says the terms resolve its disagreements with the Commission; EU developer groups call them unacceptable, so the settlement is contested. The General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08, with an interoperability ruling unlikely before late 2027. Apple does not disclose EU App Store revenue; at a 75.4% Services margin, each $1bn of commission lost equals $0.75bn of gross profit. The consequence is a permanently lower take rate on the most profitable services [S78, S77, S82, S5].

### The $20 billion Google payment is the largest policy-sensitive cash flow

Apple does not disclose the Google default-search payment, but the US v. Google trial record put it at $20bn in 2022, or 36% of Google's Safari search revenue: a litigated estimate, not a company disclosure. That is 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue and, if near-pure margin, 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's final judgment of 2025-12-05 preserved non-exclusive payments, banned exclusivity and capped default deals at 12 months; the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026 seeking a payment ban. A negotiated lower rate is more likely than zero, but either compresses Services growth, and an appellate decision is likely in 2027. The payment is worth more as Apple profit than as Google cost, which points to a lower rate rather than zero [S80, S76, S5].

### US courts are already narrowing the App Store take rate

On 2025-12-11 the Ninth Circuit affirmed that Apple willfully violated the Epic injunction, upheld the steering remedy and limited any fee on linked transactions to Apple's costs; the Supreme Court granted certiorari on 2026-06-30. Separately, the DOJ and 16 states and DC have sued Apple for monopolization in "performance smartphones" and "smartphones" since 2024-03-21, seeking equitable relief, not damages; the case is in pre-trial litigation with no trial date in Apple's 2026 filings. A federal appellate court finding willful violation raises the odds of stricter remedies and weakens management's "substantial defenses" posture. US courts can reset App Store economics before the DOJ case reaches trial [S79, S81, S6].

### Tariffs have flipped from cost to refund, not to a new margin level

Q3 FY2026 revenue was $109.4bn and gross margin 50.1%, including 2 percentage points from tariff refunds; EPS of $2.02 included $0.11 from refunds. The underlying margin is 48.1%, against 46.9% for FY2025, when products gross margin fell on tariff costs. The refund follows the Supreme Court's 2026-02-20 ruling striking down certain IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 semiconductor initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products, but Section 301 duties have since been imposed and further actions remain possible. For valuation, normalise the margin rather than extrapolate the refund: underwrite 47-48%, not 50% [S17, S5, S6].

### Governance is a strength; the ESG gaps are disclosure and labour

Governance is not the discount. Apple has eight directors, three of them women (37.5%), an independent chair separate from the CEO, no dual-class stock, a $120,000 related-party review threshold, Audit Committee ownership of privacy and cybersecurity, and 92% Say-on-Pay support in 2025. The gaps are supply-chain labour and disclosure: 166,000 employees at 2025-09-27, a 10-K concession that supplier code violations "occur from time to time", and no audit metrics in the filing. Climate claims are unverified company statements. None has changed demand, so the economic read is that ESG is a tail-risk and discount-rate input, not a revenue driver [S11, S5].

arguments.markdown:
Apple is winning the competition for profit and price while ceding unit share in China: it holds 65% of premium phone units and a 40% product gross margin, but Huawei is taking premium share in a shrinking China market and regulation is capping the services take rate, so its competitive position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and weakening at the margin in China. Apple's own 10-K concedes a minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables and says some of its markets have experienced little or no growth; the useful analysis is therefore per product, because the iPhone, Mac, wearables and services each face a different rival set [S5].

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Apple | Weaknesses vs Apple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung | Galaxy S26, Z Fold 7 | Android; Exynos 2600 or Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 | Unrestricted | Flagship parity; foldable incumbent | Premium | 19% global 2025; 23% in Q3 2026 | Foldable head start; carrier breadth | MX division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 | S91, S92, S120 |
| Huawei | Mate and Pura; HarmonyOS | Kirin silicon; HarmonyOS | China scale; US export restrictions | Premium camera and battery | Premium | 22.6% China in Q2 2026 | Domestic supply chain; holds prices | Little share outside China | S87, S86 |
| Xiaomi | Xiaomi 17 series | Android; Snapdragon | Unrestricted | Value flagship | Mid-premium | 11.5% global in Q2 2026 | Price-performance; AIoT and EV ecosystem | 8.5% handset gross margin; profit -42.6% | S90 |
| Google | Pixel 11 | Android; Tensor; Gemini | Unrestricted | AI-first software | Premium | Not disclosed | Gemini integration; search distribution | Small hardware distribution | S15, S50 |
| Lenovo, HP, Dell | PC lines | Windows on x86 | Unrestricted | Enterprise and channel strength | $600-2,000 | 24.4%, 19.1%, 13.6% in Q2 2026 | Enterprise channel; price tiers | No in-house OS-silicon integration | S95 |
| Spotify | Music streaming and app distribution | App; DMA alternative distribution | EU DMA beneficiary | 300M paying subscribers | Subscription | Twice Apple Music's subscriber base | Cross-platform; podcasts | No hardware bundle | S93, S77 |
| Alphabet | Search, YouTube, Play | Android; Gemini | Antitrust scrutiny | Advertising scale | Ad-funded | $471B TTM revenue | Search and advertising scale | AI capex dilution | S15, S50 |
| Status quo | Longer device life, refurbished | None | None | Adequate for most users | Zero | Not disclosed | Free and familiar | No new capability | S87 |

Huawei is the most dangerous competitor to Apple's profit pool, and Samsung is the most dangerous to its unit position [S87, S86, S91, S92, S84]. Huawei led China with 22.6% in Q2 2026 against Apple's 18.1%, after its highest share since Q4 2020 in the prior quarter, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026; Huawei funds that push with CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of CNY880.9B of 2025 revenue. Samsung is broader, with 19% global share in 2025 and 23% in Q3 2026, a foldable incumbent and the only rival with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth, so it cannot buy share indefinitely. Huawei takes price and profit; Samsung takes volume and loses money doing it.

Share trends from 2025 to 2026 show Apple gaining value and premium ground while its unit share moves sideways [S92, S120, S94, S84, S17]. Apple led 2025 with 20% of global units and 10% growth and Samsung followed at 19%; in Q3 2026 Samsung held 23% to Apple's 22% as the market fell 20%. The premium layer is where Apple's position improves: its 65% of $600-plus units in H1 2026 came with 9% growth, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% share in 2026. Pricing power shows in the gross margin, 40.1% on products in Q3 FY2026 versus 34.5% a year earlier, with iPhone revenue up 22% in nine months. The caveat is that the price increase is imposed by a memory shock rather than earned by innovation alone: NAND and DRAM costs are up more than 300%, and Apple's signalling of further rises pulled Chinese demand forward.

China is the one region where the competitive position is deteriorating on share even as revenue rises [S87, S6, S86]. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in the first nine months of FY2026, but that came against a market down 4.2% in H1 2026 and with Apple at 18.1% share to Huawei's 22.6%; Huawei grew 19.4% and Apple 24.4% in Q2 2026, both by holding prices while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi raised theirs and lost 9.7%, 11.4% and 21.7% respectively. The top six vendors hold 96% of the market, so the fight is for premium share inside a contracting pool, and Huawei's HarmonyOS scale gives it a domestic platform Apple cannot match on localisation. Apple's revenue growth is a price-hold plus pull-forward effect, not evidence that it has regained structural leadership in China.

Regulation is now a competitive force that transfers rent from Apple to its rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. The practical effect is to lower switching costs out of the App Store in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and to hand Spotify, Epic and alternative storefronts a distribution channel on iOS; Spotify already has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. The DMA is the template, and its spread to other jurisdictions is the regulatory risk to monitor.

| Product | Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche player | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (premium) | Leader in premium value, second in units | Apple | Samsung | Google Pixel | Huawei in China; foldables | S94, S87 |
| Mac | Share gainer from a small base | Lenovo by units | Apple | HP and Dell premium tiers | Snapdragon Windows PCs | S95 |
| Wearables | Leader by value, third by units | Xiaomi by units, Apple by value | Huawei | Oura in rings, Meta in glasses | AI glasses | S85 |
| Services (apps and advertising) | Challenger in advertising, leader in app distribution | Alphabet in advertising | Apple in app distribution | Spotify in music | DMA-enabled alternative stores | S15, S93, S77 |

The status quo is a formidable competitor: consumers are holding devices longer, IDC expects China's recovery only in 2028-2029 and forecasts a smaller, more concentrated market after the memory crisis, and the cheapest segment is disappearing [S87, S84, S17, S93]. Pipeline threats are Apple's own foldable in H2 2026, Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion, Google's Gemini-integrated Pixel and AI agents that could move the assistant layer off the operating system. Apple's wedge is the integration of silicon, OS and an installed base that reached an all-time high in Q3 FY2026, which lets it earn 40% product gross margins while rivals earn single digits or lose money; that wedge supports profit-share gains but not unit-share gains. The competitive position therefore supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated ceiling on services, not a share-gain growth story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China and medium on services because take rates are in flux. Diligence questions: how much of the premium gain is price inflation, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS, and whether Apple's foldable holds 40% of the category beyond 2027.

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | 65% of premium phone units; 40.1% product gross margin; $120.5B services at 76.3% gross margin; installed base at an all-time high; iPhone 50.4% of FY2025 revenue | S94, S17, S6, S5 |
| Weaknesses | 18.1% China share behind Huawei; 15.5% wearables unit share; no advertising scale; revenue concentrated in one product | S87, S85, S5 |
| Opportunities | Foldables above 17M units by 2027 at a $2,550+ ASP; services advertising and cloud; Mac share gains; an AI upgrade cycle | S84, S95 |
| Threats | DMA 5% take rate on external distribution; Huawei premium share; memory costs up more than 300%; AI assistants commoditising the OS layer | S77, S87, S84 |
:::

::: evidence
**Apple's competitive advantage is profit capture, not unit share.**

Apple holds 20% of phone units but 65% of premium units and 36-43% of market value (Counterpoint, S94; IDC, S84). Its 40.1% product gross margin compares with Xiaomi's 8.5% handset margin and a loss at Samsung's mobile division (S17, S90, S91). The vulnerabilities are China and regulation, not pricing power (S87, S77).
:::

plan.decision_question: What is Apple worth today, and what price makes it an attractive long for a long-only fund?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder: at $344.63 the market capitalises $128.1bn of NOPAT at 38.8x, which requires about 6.9% perpetual growth or a 7.0% cost of capital, so a long-only buyer is accepting a ~7% expected return on a business whose own five-year revenue CAGR is 5.0%.
plan.why_different: This section is the only one that converts the operating story into a price: it owns the arithmetic of what the market is paying, the DCF, the sum of the parts and the entry threshold, and it must state a number at which the shares become a buy.
plan.mechanism: Apple's value is the present value of a slowly compounding cash flow with a very long duration; when the ten-year Treasury is 4.93% and the cost of equity is ~9.5%, the multiple the market pays (39.5x) discounts a 7% return, so the shares de-rate until either the discount rate falls or growth rises. Buybacks recycle cash at a 2.5% earnings yield and therefore support EPS without creating value at this price.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 year-end multiples (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x; four-year mean 31.0x), US platform peers (MSFT 27.3x, GOOGL 14.6x, META 21.0x, AMZN 19.4x on P/E; 19.9x-25.5x on EV/EBIT), hardware peers (HP 11.0x, Dell 24.7x P/E; 9.6x and 21.0x EV/EBIT) and a 9.0-9.5% cost of equity against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
plan.counter_evidence: Growth re-accelerated to +16.4% in the June 2026 quarter with a 50.1% gross margin, so the DCF's 9%-to-5% fade may understate the cycle; a 7% WACC (defensible in some quality-growth models) makes $344.63 fair; and the buyback's price sensitivity cushions any de-rating. Alphabet's 14.6x P/E also drags the peer median down and exaggerates Apple's premium.
plan.visual: Valuation methods table (method, inputs, value per share, weight) plus a WACC x terminal-growth sensitivity grid showing the market price is reached only near a 7% WACC.
plan.prohibited: No 'about 5', no 'strong moat', no 'well positioned', no 'huge', no unlabelled estimates, no claim that the DCF is precise, no repetition of the risk section's regulatory narrative beyond its valuation effect.

Apple's profit is unusually cash-true. ### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, the highest Apple has reported. Part of that is structural: services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue. Part is not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 percentage points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to those refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average, Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%, and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The 30 July 2026 release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); nine-month products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9% a year earlier on mix and refunds, while memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and Apple's 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off the trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of the $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real; the 2026 step-up is partly working capital

Nine-month operating cash flow rose 43.1% to $116,996M while net income rose 20.0%, and the balance sheet shows why: receivables fell to $31,398M from $39,777M and vendor non-trade receivables to $27,509M from $33,180M, cutting days sales outstanding to 24.5 from 34.9, while inventory rose to $11,092M from $5,718M and payables fell to $64,525M from $69,860M, shortening the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1. Part of the record is therefore a release of working capital that reverses as memory is pre-bought, not a permanent lift in earning power. The top line is not being smoothed either: deferred revenue of $14.9B is 3.2% of trailing revenue, and only $7,260M of nine-month revenue came out of the opening deferred balance. [S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. The FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B payable within twelve months and $37.0B of future interest, commercial paper ran at a 4.19% weighted rate, leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need a question rather than a red flag: $2,604M of unrealised losses on the securities book, and intangible assets that rose to $25,417M net from $13,301M — $38,220M gross, $12,803M accumulated amortisation — without the 10-Q disaggregating what was bought. ### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: free cash flow of $136,683M over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 71.2%, against 57.3% in FY2025. With a ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, any plausible cost of equity of 9-11% is cleared several times; the constraint is the price, because a $5,072B market capitalisation on $128,930M of trailing net income is a 2.5% earnings yield. Capital allocation supports that reading rather than contradicting it: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M are 67.0% of free cash flow, net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. This is not a debt-funded buyback story. [S6, S7]

Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. ### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. rows.mechanism: Apple keeps the interface, personal context and Private Cloud Compute wrapper, but licenses frontier reasoning from a competitor; the differentiation moves from model quality to distribution and privacy architecture.
rows.benchmark: Google owns the model, the TPUs and Android; Apple owns the device and the assistant surface but rents the intelligence.
rows.weakens: A 1.2-trillion-parameter rented model versus a published on-device model shows the hardest queries are outsourced; the beta label two years after Apple Intelligence launched is a delay, not a launch.
rows.implication: Siri is a feature that protects the installed base, not a moat that expands it. Price Apple as a hardware-and-services company with an AI option.
rows.follow_up: When does Siri AI leave beta, what proportion of queries route to Gemini, and what does Apple disclose about the cost?
rows.confidence: high on dates and the deal; medium on the $1bn and parameter count (press reports, not company disclosure)

rows.finding: Apple spent $34.04bn on R&D in the first nine months of FY2026, +33% year on year, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. Its foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud.
rows.mechanism: Apple is running an opex-heavy AI strategy: pay for models and rented compute rather than build datacentres, which protects free cash flow but caps frontier scale and hands bargaining power to Google.
rows.benchmark: Hyperscalers capitalise AI infrastructure; Apple's nine-month capex is about 2% of revenue while R&D is running at roughly 30% growth.
rows.weakens: The R&D step-up is a real cost: +$8.4bn in nine months, with no separately disclosed AI revenue to offset it, so margin is the place the bill lands.
rows.implication: Free cash flow stays intact and buybacks continue, but there is no proprietary compute moat to underwrite a higher multiple on AI.
rows.follow_up: What share of the R&D increase is AI infrastructure and depreciation, and does Apple intend to keep renting frontier models after the Gemini term?
rows.confidence: high — both figures are in the 10-Q cash-flow and income statements

rows.finding: Silicon stays the deepest in-house layer: A20 Pro in the iPhone 18 Pro on a 2nm process versus A19 on 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line. Products gross margin rose on mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by memory costs.
rows.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon converts into either margin or performance at fixed price; the modem insourcing removes a Qualcomm royalty and gives Apple control over cellular power and cost.
rows.benchmark: A19 (3nm) to A20 (2nm) is a full node step; the modem shift ends Apple's dependence on an external cellular supplier.
rows.weakens: Component costs are rising: the 10-Q warns of advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints expected to intensify. A node advantage does not protect gross margin when memory prices spike.
rows.implication: Silicon is the moat that is still widening; it supports the products margin line rather than revenue growth.
rows.follow_up: What is the C2 versus Qualcomm cost delta per unit, and how much of the FY2027 products margin assumption depends on tariff refunds that may not repeat?
rows.confidence: medium — 2nm and C2 are press-reported; margins are from the 10-Q

rows.finding: U.S. patent grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024 (-12%), placing Apple seventh; the foldable Duo's hinge is made with AI-matched parts, confocal laser scanning and 3D-printed photopolymer micro-layers rather than protected by a single blocking patent.
rows.mechanism: The durable IP sits in process know-how and integration, which is harder to design around but also harder to assert; the portfolio is broad rather than deep in any one blocking area.
rows.benchmark: Apple's grant count is declining while U.S. patent activity overall declined; Huawei and TSMC rank ahead of Apple in the same 2025 table.
rows.weakens: A falling grant count is not proof of a weakening moat, but it removes the patent-count argument for one; the hinge know-how must be proven in field reliability.
rows.implication: Underwrite the moat on switching costs and manufacturing yield, not on patent breadth.
rows.follow_up: What is the granted-versus-pending mix in the foldable and on-device-AI families, and are there blocking third-party hinge or display patents?
rows.confidence: medium — aggregate counts are third-party (IFI) data; individual patent families were not retrieved

rows.finding: Health features are shipping and regulated: Apple Watch hypertension notifications were FDA-cleared, with peer-reviewed commentary in Hypertension treating the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening and questioning accuracy and utility; the feature notifies over a 30-day signal rather than measuring blood pressure.
rows.mechanism: Health adds a regulated, trust-based reason to upgrade a watch every few years and raises the cost of leaving the ecosystem, but it is sold inside a hardware product rather than as a therapy.
rows.benchmark: Apple Watch is described as the most widely adopted consumer health device; the clinical evidence level is a cleared screening notification, not a diagnostic claim.
rows.weakens: Contested clinical value limits pricing power and invites litigation and regulator scrutiny; it is a differentiator, not a new revenue pool.
rows.implication: Wearables and health support the installed base and ASP without changing the growth slope on their own.
rows.follow_up: What is the attach and upgrade rate for watches with the hypertension feature, and what does the FDA clearance letter allow Apple to claim?
rows.confidence: medium — clearance reported by a peer-reviewed journal; the FDA record itself returned no match in the openFDA device search

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's silicon/OS/AI stack a durable moat, or is Apple falling behind in AI while the hardware cycle matures?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer that the next upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it.
plan.why_different: This section judges mechanism and replicability of the technology itself — how the silicon, OS and AI layers work and what can be copied — not market size, valuation or the industry's growth rate.
plan.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon and OS converts into margin or performance at a fixed price and into switching costs; buying frontier models and renting TPU compute converts a would-be fixed-cost AI moat into a variable cost paid to a competitor, which protects cash flow but leaves the differentiation in hardware, privacy and distribution.
plan.comparison_set: Google (owns Gemini, TPUs and Android), Samsung (licenses Google's stack), Huawei (constrained by domestic process), Microsoft (cloud capex model), and Apple's own prior cycle (iPhone 17, A19 3nm, no foldable).
plan.counter_evidence: AI talent left for Meta through 2025; the Siri rebuild shipped as an English beta in September 2026, two years after Apple Intelligence launched; capex fell while R&D rose; patent grants fell 12%; the Duo's hinge durability is unproven; memory costs threaten products margin.
plan.visual: Performance-metrics table plus the moat table with the replication test (funded team of 50), and the evidence component on the Google dependency.
plan.prohibited: AI leader, seamless ecosystem, strong team, huge market, well positioned, innovative company, best-in-class without a metric, 'many patents', 'about' before a figure, any sentence describing how the section is written.

events.text:
Gate passed for funding_valuation. Now the exit block.

For the exit block, rows should cover liquidity, ownership, total return decomposition, multiple compression, drawdown, takeover impossibility, buyback bid, insider selling, return sensitivity.

Let me write it.

Note on the "index weight": I'll include a row noting market cap rank among peers and that index weight is not disclosed by sources retrieved. Actually, that's a bit weak; I can instead compute an implied weight if I had index total cap — no. I'll state "not disclosed in this run" in the diligence question or as a limitation in the section.

Let me also double check the drawdown math: 243.42 / 344.63 = 0.7063 → the 52-week low is 29.4% below the current price. And the 5-year closing low of $125.02 → 344.63/125.02 = 2.757, so the current price is 176% above the five-year low; a return to that low would be -63.7%. That's extreme (that low was in a different earnings regime). I'll use the 12-month low as the base rate and the DCF bear as the second anchor.

Return sensitivity: entry $344.63, exit multiple 31x on FY2029E EPS. Let me build EPS: FY2026E $9.09 (est.), +9% FY2027 = $9.91, +8% FY2028 = $10.70, +7% FY2029 = $11.45.
3-year (to end-FY2029) at 31x = $355. Dividends over 3 years ~$3.45 (with modest growth, ~$3.50). Total = $358.5 vs $344.63 → +4.0% over 3 years = 1.3%/yr. Ouch.
At 34x: $389.3 + 3.5 = $392.8 → +14.0% over 3 years = 4.5%/yr.
At 27x: $309.2 + 3.5 = $312.7 → -9.3% over 3 years = -3.2%/yr.

So from $344.63, the 3-year IRR is -3% to +4.5% depending on exit multiple (27x-34x). That's a strong conclusion: the expected return is below the risk-free rate.

For a 9% 3-year return (1.295x): required entry price = (355 + 3.5)/1.295 = $276.7 at a 31x exit. At a 34x exit: (389.3+3.5)/1.295 = $303.3. At a 27x exit: (309.2+3.5)/1.295 = $241.5.

So the buy threshold is $240-$305 depending on exit multiple; midpoint ~$277. Hmm, earlier I estimated $260. Let me pick a defensible threshold: $270, roughly 22% below the current price, which delivers a ~9% three-year IRR at a 31x exit multiple and a ~7% IRR at a 27x exit. Let me compute at $270 entry: (355+3.5)/270 = 1.328 → 9.9%/yr at 31x; at 27x: 312.7/270 = 1.158 → 5.0%/yr; at 34x: 392.8/270 = 1.455 → 13.4%/yr.

So $270 entry: 5.0%-13.4%/yr across exit multiples, ~10% at the central 31x. That's a clean statement: "at $270 the three-year IRR spans 5-13% around a 10% central case; at $344.63 it spans -3% to +5%."

That's better than my earlier $260. Use $270 as the actionable entry with the arithmetic. I'll say "in the $260-275 zone" or "below $270". Let me use $270 and show the sensitivity table.

Buyback sensitivity: $85B/yr at $270 = 3.0% of the $4,033B cap (270 × 14.94B shares = $4,034B). At $344.63: 1.7%. At $240: 3.6%. Good.

Total return decomposition table:
| Component | Rate | Source |
| Dividend yield | 0.31% | $1.08 annualised / $344.63 |
| Buyback yield (gross) | 1.63% | $82.2bn TTM / $5,029.6bn |
| Buyback yield net of SBC | 1.36% | $82.2bn - $13.7bn SBC = $68.5bn / cap |
| EPS growth FY2021-TTM | 9.2%/yr | $5.61 → $8.72 |
| of which share-count | ~2.8pp/yr | 16,865m → 14,715m |
| Multiple change required for 9% total return | flat or up | 39.5x |
| Total return if multiple flat | ~9.5-10% | 0.3 + 1.4 + 8 (forward EPS growth) |
| Total return if multiple reverts to 31x over 3 years | ~1% | 31/39.5 = -21.5% over 3 years = -7.8%/yr + 9.5% |

Hmm, careful: the forward EPS growth in FY2027 is likely ~9%, so with a flat multiple the total return is ~0.3 + 1.4 + 9 = 10.7%. That's a decent return! The whole question is whether the multiple holds. So the honest decomposition: forward return = ~10.7% if 39.5x holds, ~1-3% if it reverts to 31x. That's the risk/reward: symmetric-ish but the multiple is at a five-year high, so the odds favour compression.

I should present both and be honest that the near-term return can be fine if the multiple holds — the issue is the asymmetry: upside from here requires the multiple to expand beyond a five-year high, while downside is a reversion that costs 8%/yr for three years.

That's a fair, balanced conclusion. Good.

Let me write the exit evidence block now.

plan.comparison_set: The last twelve months' own trading (52-week low $243.42, i.e. 29.4% below the current price), the FY2022-FY2025 multiple range (24.6x-37.5x, mean 31.0x), HP and Dell for hardware, Microsoft and Alphabet for the platform bid, and the 4.93% ten-year Treasury as the opportunity cost of holding a 1.9% shareholder yield.
plan.counter_evidence: A flat 39.5x multiple with 9-10% EPS growth still delivers about 10.7% a year, so the return is adequate while the multiple holds; the buyback is a self-correcting bid that accelerates as the price falls; and the June 2026 quarter's 16.4% revenue growth could keep the multiple elevated for longer than a mean-reversion model assumes.
plan.decision_question: For a long-only fund, what is the exit and total-return path, and what would force a sale?
plan.mechanism: There is no strategic exit for a $5tn company, so the only realisation routes are the market, Apple's own repurchase and the dividend. Return = dividend (0.31%) + net buyback (1.36%) + EPS growth, minus the annualised cost of any multiple compression; at 39.5x versus a 31.0x four-year mean, compression of about 7-8% a year can cancel the operating return.
plan.prohibited: No 'IPO or M&A', no unnamed acquirers, no invented index weight, no claim that a takeover premium is a return source, no repetition of the risk section's regulatory detail, no 'well positioned'.
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer: with no company large enough to acquire it, the three-year return from $344.63 is -3% to +5% a year if the 39.5x multiple reverts toward its 31.0x four-year average, which sets the sell discipline at a price where the arithmetic clears 9% - roughly $270.
plan.visual: Exit routes table (route, named buyer or venue, rationale, timing, likelihood, source) plus a return-sensitivity table by entry price and exit multiple.
plan.why_different: Every other section asks whether Apple's business improves; this one asks how the fund gets its money back and at what price the risk/reward stops paying, and it must name the buyer or venue rather than list generic options.

get_price_history AAPL 5y and 1y for the drawdown base rate
get_insider_activity AAPL six months (Form 4)
read_sec_filing AAPL DEF 14A ownership (free float, Vanguard and BlackRock stakes, shares outstanding)
get_sec_financials AAPL 5y and TTM (buybacks, dividends, share count, EPS path)
read_sec_filing AAPL 10-K FY2025 item 7 (share repurchase authorisation and dividend policy)
get_valuation_snapshot AAPL vs MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, META for the acquisition-impossibility test

rows.benchmark: A $250m position is 0.62% of the 20-day average value traded; a $1bn position is 2.5%.
rows.confidence: high - timestamped market data
rows.finding: Average daily volume 40.41m shares ($13.84bn) over 20 days and 41.34m shares ($13.56bn) over three months; price sits 3.5% above the 50-day average of $333.04 and 16.2% above the 200-day of $296.56.
rows.follow_up: What position size is the fund contemplating, and does it breach any single-issuer or index-weight limit?
rows.implication: Liquidity is not a constraint at any plausible position size: the fund can enter and exit in days with negligible market impact, so the exit risk is entirely a price risk, not a liquidity risk.
rows.mechanism: A $5tn mega-cap with 40m shares a day traded has an exit that is always open at the screen price; the cost of exit is the spread and any de-rating, not the ability to sell.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in a correlated drawdown - in a market-wide selloff the bid thins and the discount to the last price widens, so ADV overstates achievable exit size in stress.

rows.benchmark: Apple's own 12-month low of $243.42 is 29.4% below the current price; the five-year closing low is $125.02.
rows.confidence: medium - the 52-week low overstates the chance of a full retracement but is the best local base rate
rows.finding: No holder owns control: 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, Vanguard 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, the largest holders being index managers; directors and officers hold about 0.06% between them.
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's current S&P 500 weight, and what happens to passive demand if it is trimmed at a rebalance?
rows.implication: Free float is effectively 100% and the marginal holder is an index or active fund, so the stock's buyer on exit is the same pool the fund sells into - index inclusion has been a structural bid, but it does not raise the price at which the business is worth owning.
rows.mechanism: With no controlling shareholder and a dispersed index base, price is set by flows and by the marginal institutional view of the multiple, not by a strategic buyer or a control contest.
rows.weakens: Index concentration cuts both ways: forced selling by passive funds in a redemption wave would hit Apple harder than a smaller, less-owned name.

rows.benchmark: Trailing EPS CAGR over the five years to FY2021-TTM is 9.2% (S6, S1) versus revenue CAGR of 5.0% and net income CAGR of 6.4%.
rows.confidence: high for the historic decomposition; medium for the forward multiple assumption
rows.finding: Total shareholder yield 1.9% (dividend 0.3% plus gross buyback 1.6%); net of $13.7bn of stock compensation the buyback yield is 1.36%; EPS grew 9.2% a year from FY2021 to the TTM, of which about 2.8 points a year came from the 12.8% reduction in diluted shares.
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does consensus assume for FY2027 and FY2028, and does it require the buyback to keep running above $80bn?
rows.implication: With a flat multiple the total return is about 10.7% a year (0.3% dividend, 1.4% net buyback, 9% EPS growth) - adequate; the whole question is whether 39.5x is a multiple that holds.
rows.mechanism: A long-only fund's return is dividend plus net buyback plus EPS growth plus the change in multiple; Apple supplies only 1.7 points of the first two, so nearly all of the return has to come from earnings growth or from a multiple that does not fall.
rows.weakens: If the multiple expands further, the decomposition understates the return; 2026's 16.4% revenue growth suggests forward EPS growth may exceed 9%.

rows.benchmark: Apple's fiscal year-end P/E: 24.6x (FY2022), 27.9x (FY2023), 37.5x (FY2024), 34.2x (FY2025); four-year mean 31.0x; AAPL currently 39.5x, a 27% premium to that mean.
rows.confidence: medium - multiples are certain, their persistence is not
rows.finding: A reversion from 39.5x to 31.0x costs 21.5% of price, about -7.7% a year over three years, which more than offsets the 1.7% shareholder yield and most of a 9% EPS growth rate.
rows.follow_up: What would keep the multiple above 35x for three years - sustained 10%-plus revenue growth, or a fall in the ten-year yield?
rows.implication: The asymmetry is the argument for selling into strength: at a five-year-high multiple the upside needs further expansion, while the downside is a reversion that is already observed once within the past four years.
rows.mechanism: Multiple compression is the mechanism by which a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year at 4.93% (+84bp y/y), the discount rate on Apple's terminal cash flows is higher than when the stock traded at 27.9x in FY2023.
rows.weakens: The stock has been 'expensive' versus its own history since FY2024 and has still returned 27.5% over the last twelve months; a mean-reversion model has been wrong for two years.

rows.benchmark: Largest technology peer Microsoft at $3,875.8bn market cap and $3,846.8bn EV; Alphabet $3,461.1bn; Meta $1,582.4bn.
rows.confidence: high - the comparison is arithmetic
rows.finding: No plausible acquirer exists: every company in the peer set is smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market cap, so a takeover would require a buyer larger than any in the sector, plus antitrust clearance in the US, EU, China and UK.
rows.follow_up: Is there any activist or break-up case that would separate services from hardware, and who would fund a $5tn position?
rows.implication: A control premium is not part of the return: the exit is at the market price, which means the fund's realisation depends entirely on the multiple other investors will pay.
rows.mechanism: The bid side of a $5tn equity is other portfolio managers, not strategics; index funds and buybacks are price-insensitive in direction but not in price, so the exit price is set by the same valuation debate the fund is making.
rows.weakens: A sovereign wealth fund or a consortium could in principle bid, but at 39.5x earnings and a $5tn equity cheque the financing does not exist at a premium.

rows.benchmark: $85bn a year is 1.7% of the $5.03tn capitalisation at $344.63, 3.0% at $270 and 3.6% at $240.
rows.confidence: high for the arithmetic; medium for the $85bn run-rate
rows.finding: Apple repurchased $82.2bn of stock in the TTM to 2026-06-27 against $15.6bn of dividends and $111.5bn of working-capital-normalised FCF, so the repurchase is at the limit of internally generated cash.
rows.follow_up: Will the May 2027 authorisation exceed the May 2025 $100bn programme, and will Apple fund it from cash or from debt?
rows.implication: The buyback is a standing, price-sensitive buyer that makes a de-rating self-limiting: each 10% fall in the price adds roughly 0.17 points to the buyback yield, which is why a bear case to $190-240 is more likely to be a long opportunity than a permanent loss.
rows.mechanism: A fixed-dollar repurchase retires more shares as the price falls, so the EPS accretion per dollar rises and the floor under the per-share value is firmer than for a company that does not buy back.
rows.weakens: The buyback is discretionary and could be cut in a downturn or redirected to AI capital spending; it also supports EPS, not the multiple, so it cannot prevent a de-rating.

rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 P/E range of 24.6x-37.5x.
rows.confidence: medium - exit multiples are a scenario assumption
rows.finding: On FY2029E EPS of $11.45 (my estimate: FY2026E $9.09 grown 9%/8%/7%), a 27x exit gives $309, a 31x exit $355 and a 34x exit $389; with about $3.50 of dividends over three years the three-year IRR from $344.63 is -3.2%, +1.3% and +4.5%.
rows.follow_up: What entry price does the fund's own hurdle rate require, and is a three-year or five-year holding period assumed?
rows.implication: From today's price the three-year return fails the 9% hurdle under every exit multiple below 39.5x; at a $270 entry the same range becomes +5.0% to +13.4% with a 10% central case.
rows.mechanism: Buying at a high multiple transfers the future return to the seller: the entry price fixes the IRR once the exit multiple and the earnings path are set, and at 39.5x the arithmetic leaves nothing for the buyer.
rows.weakens: If EPS grows faster than 9% - the June 2026 quarter grew EPS 28.7% - the IRR rises by roughly the excess growth rate for each year held.

rows.benchmark: Peer insiders and the absence of open-market purchases across the six-month window.
rows.confidence: medium - plan sales are scheduled in advance and carry little information, discretionary sales carry more
rows.finding: No insider purchased a share in the six months to 2026-10-29; 37 sales totalled 590,642 shares and $183.45m, of which 34 transactions ($96.70m) were under Rule 10b5-1 plans; director Arthur Levinson sold $86.74m and Executive Chair Tim Cook $63.85m.
rows.follow_up: Did any of the discretionary sales follow a change in the trading plan, and what is the executives' remaining unvested exposure?
rows.implication: Management is not adding at $344; that is weak evidence against a near-term re-rating and consistent with a stock trading above what insiders consider value, though it is not a sell signal on its own.
rows.mechanism: Insider behaviour is informative mainly at the extremes - a cluster of discretionary buys after a fall, or discretionary sales near highs; here the mix is plan-driven and uninformative about the multiple.
rows.weakens: Almost all sales were scheduled 10b5-1 sales, and executives of a $5tn company sell for diversification regardless of valuation, so the signal is weak.

The total target compensation for Mr. Parekh for 2025 comprised an

Additional details regarding our named executive officers’
2025 compensation can be found below in the sections entitled “Cash Incentive Plan — 2025 Financial Performance Measures
and Payout Opportunities” and “2025 Long-Term Equity Awards and Results.”
Cash Incentive Plan – 2025 Financial Performance Measures
and Payout Opportunities
Our Cash Incentive Plan awards are designed to motivate and reward
our named executive officers for delivering strong performance against annual financial goals. As in prior years, the People and
Compensation Committee chose net sales and operating income, calculated in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles,
as the financial performance measures for the 2025 Cash Incentive Plan awards. Net sales and operating income continue to reflect
commonly recognized key measures of overall Company performance and profitability and are drivers of shareholder value creation.
Payouts for our named executive officers under the Cash Incentive
Plan are first determined quantitatively based on an equal weighting of the net sales and operating income performance measures.
The target payout opportunity for each of the net sales and operating income performance measures was 100% of annual base salary
for our named executive officers, other than Mr. Maestri and Mr. Parekh due to the transition in their respective roles. Threshold
performance would result in a payout equal to 50% of target and maximum performance would result in a payout equal to 200% of target
for each of the performance measures. If the threshold goal is not achieved for a financial performance measure, there is no payout
for that measure. The total payout opportunity for each financial performance measure is capped at 200%. Payouts for our named
executive officers are linearly interpolated for achievement between goal levels.
2026 Proxy Statement
45
Table of Contents
Summary
