2025 Financial Performance Goals
The People and Compensation Committee considers factors relevant to the current fiscal year when it sets the net sales and
operating income goals for the annual Cash Incentive Plan awards because each year presents a unique set of challenges and
business conditions for our executives to navigate. Financial results from prior years are used as a reference point, but
the annual goals are set to align pay with performance that would reflect strong financial results commensurate with the projected
business and economic conditions for the current fiscal year. The goal-setting process for 2025 presented a unique set of
challenges due to an uncertain macroeconomic outlook, including trade policies and impacts and foreign currency fluctuations.
As part of its goal-setting process for 2025, the People and Compensation
Committee assessed a range of business scenarios that could impact net sales and operating income results for the year, considering
multiple factors and operational risks, and once again focusing on the underlying business performance rather than the absolute
growth rates. Acknowledging the risks, challenges, and uncertainties in the 2025 projections, as well as the exceptional efforts
that would be required of our executive team to continue to deliver results at a sustained level year-over-year, the People and
Compensation Committee set net sales and operating income goals at appropriately rigorous levels for the year. For net sales, the
threshold, target, and maximum goals were $380 billion, $391 billion, and $402 billion, respectively. For operating income, the
threshold, target, and maximum goals were $113 billion, $118.5 billion, and $124 billion, respectively. The threshold goals
represented the minimum level of achievement for a named executive officer to receive an annual cash incentive payout. The target
goals represented an underlying growth rate that, while challenging to achieve based on the considerations noted above, would also
represent strong financial performance on an underlying basis commensurate with the target payout opportunity. The maximum goals
represented exceptional financial performance for the year, based on the business scenarios considered.
2025 Financial Performance Results
Net Sales ($B)
Operating Income ($B)
For 2025, we reported net sales of $416.2 billion and operating income
of $133.1 billion, representing a year-over-year increase of six percent ($25.2 billion) and eight percent ($9.9 billion), respectively.
These achievements far exceeded expectations for the year and resulted in a maximum payout opportunity. In evaluating the
performance of the Company and the named executive officers in retrospect at the end of the year, the People and Compensation Committee
evaluated the results in the context of the approved goals, as well as alternate scenarios considered at the time the goals were
set. 2025 was an extraordinary year with an all-time revenue record of $416.2 billion, with growth in iPhone, Mac, iPad, and
Services, and all-time records in the vast majority of markets we track. These results reflect the tremendous customer enthusiasm
for Apple products and services, as well as our deep commitment to innovation. The net sales and operating income results
delivered for the year exceeded the maximum financial goals considered, resulting in a maximum payout opportunity for each named
executive officer. Accordingly, the People and Compensation Committee awarded maximum Cash Incentive Plan payouts to each of our
named executive officers.
46
2026 Proxy Statement
Table of Contents
Summary
Governance
Directors
Compensation
Proposals

Information
2025 Long-Term Equity Awards and Results
When setting the value of equity awards for our named executive officers, the People and Compensation Committee considers
the size and performance of Apple relative to peer companies and the scope of our named executive officers’ roles. Each
named executive officer, other than Mr. Cook, was granted a long-term equity award on September 29, 2024 of 50% performance-based
and 50% time-based RSUs. Mr. Maestri was also granted a time-based RSU award for his current role of Vice President, Corporate
Services. Mr. Cook was granted a long-term equity award on September 29, 2024 of 75% performance-based and 25% time-based
RSUs. The equity awards granted in 2025 were granted under, and subject to, the terms of the Apple Inc. 2022 Employee Stock
Plan (“2022 Plan”).
2025 Performance-Based RSUs
The People and Compensation Committee continued to use Relative TSR
as the metric for performance-based RSUs granted during 2025, with the S&P 500 as the comparative group because it continues
to be an objective and meaningful metric to evaluate our performance against the performance of other large companies and aligns
the interests of our named executive officers with the interests of our shareholders in creating long-term value.
Performance-based RSUs are a substantial, at-risk component of our
named executive officers’ compensation tied to Apple’s long-term performance. The number of performance-based RSUs
that vest, if any, depends entirely on Relative TSR for the applicable performance period. To earn the target number of performance-based
RSUs, Apple must achieve above-median performance at the 55th percentile of the S&P 500.
We measure Relative TSR based on the change in each company’s
stock price during the applicable performance period, taking into account any dividends paid during that period, which are assumed
to be reinvested in the stock. A 20-day trading averaging period is used to determine the beginning and ending stock price values
used to calculate the total shareholder return of Apple and the other companies in the S&P 500. The 20-day trading averaging
period mitigates the impact on the long-term Relative TSR results of one-day or short-term stock price fluctuations at the beginning
or end of the performance period. The change in stock price value from the beginning to the end of the period is divided by the
beginning stock price value to determine TSR.
The performance-based RSUs granted on September 29, 2024, have a
three-year performance period from the beginning of 2025 through the end of 2027. Subject to the terms of the award agreements,
between zero and 200% of the target number of performance-based RSUs will vest on October 1, 2027, depending on Apple’s Relative

Gate passed. Now strategy evidence block.

Strategy plan and rows.

plan.comparison_set: Microsoft and Alphabet (capitalise AI infrastructure), Samsung (follows Apple's price and form factor), Huawei (rebuilds a domestic stack), and Apple's own prior capital-return cycle (FY2025 buybacks $89.3bn).
plan.counter_evidence: R&D is funding rented intelligence rather than owned capability; capex fell; memory costs and tariffs pressure margin; India depends on expiring subsidies; DMA compliance consumes engineering time; Duo durability unproven.
plan.decision_question: Does Apple's strategy convert AI and services into growth without ceding platform control?
plan.mechanism: Apple funds the AI layer from the income statement (R&D and licensing) rather than the balance sheet (datacentres), keeps control of the interface, distribution and privacy layer, and returns the resulting cash through buybacks; platform control is preserved while the frontier-model layer is ceded.
plan.prohibited: AI leader, well positioned, strong execution, huge opportunity, seamless, 'about' before a figure, any sentence about how the section is written.
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model.
plan.visual: Milestone table with target dates and status, plus the partner table with signing dates.
plan.why_different: This section judges execution and allocation — dated milestones, partners and what must be true in twelve months — rather than the technology's mechanism or the market's size.

rows.benchmark: FY2025: $89.3bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends against $34.55bn of R&D.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple repurchased $62.1bn of stock, paid $0.27 a quarter in dividends, spent $34.04bn on R&D (+33%) and only $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn). In FY2025 it bought back $89.3bn under a $100bn authorisation and raised the dividend to $0.26.
rows.follow_up: Will Apple disclose AI-related depreciation or licensing cost separately, and does the buyback pace hold if margin compresses?
rows.implication: The strategy is shareholder-return first, AI as an operating expense. It supports EPS and limits downside, but it does not build an asset that a competitor cannot rent too.
rows.mechanism: Capital allocation reveals the bet: Apple funds AI from the income statement and returns the balance-sheet capacity to shareholders, treating frontier models as a purchased input rather than an owned platform.
rows.weakens: A 33% R&D increase with falling capex means the marginal AI dollar is opex; if AI features do not lift hardware ASP, that spending is a pure margin drag.

rows.benchmark: India assembled 36m iPhones in 2024; global iPhone output is 220-230m a year; all iPhone 17 models are now built in India.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.finding: Apple assembled about 55m iPhones in India in 2025, up 53% and roughly a quarter of global output, using Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron; Indian assembly and components still cost more than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expire on 2026-03-31.
rows.follow_up: Has the subsidy regime been renewed, and what is the landed-cost gap between Indian and Chinese assembly for U.S.-bound units?
rows.implication: The tariff hedge is working on volume but is not yet a margin tailwind, and it depends on policy that expires within the next twelve months.
rows.mechanism: Geographic diversification reduces tariff and concentration risk but trades a mature supply chain for a subsidised, higher-cost one; the strategy is insurance bought with gross margin.
rows.weakens: The shift is subsidy-dependent and costlier, so it does not improve unit economics; it also invites retaliation risk on the China side that the source does not quantify.

rows.benchmark: iPhone revenue grew 22% in the same quarter; services gross margin is roughly 1.5 times the company average.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Services reached $91.73bn in nine months of FY2026 (+14%) at a 76.3% gross margin, with advertising and cloud services cited as the growth drivers; the EU DMA generated 56 interoperability requests by 2026-03-22, of which 43 were closed and 27 confidentially.
rows.follow_up: What is the revenue at risk from DMA-driven sideloading and default-choice changes, and how much of advertising growth is search-revenue-share dependent?
rows.implication: Services is the profit engine and the part regulation can tax; the DMA is a recurring engineering and legal cost, not a one-off.
rows.mechanism: Services monetise the installed base at high incremental margin, but the DMA forces Apple to open interfaces and choice screens, which erodes the control that makes those services default.
rows.weakens: Growth is concentrated in advertising and cloud, the areas most exposed to platform regulation and to the Google search distribution deal.

rows.benchmark: Apple's own July 2024 paper disclosing 8,192 TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips, rented through Google Cloud.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.finding: Apple confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to use Google Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and about $1bn a year, while its own foundation models are trained on rented Google TPUs and its capex fell year on year.
rows.follow_up: Is the Gemini deal exclusive, what are its term and renewal date, and can Apple switch models without degrading Siri?
rows.implication: Partnering preserves cash and speed but cedes the frontier layer; the platform control that remains is the interface, the data boundary and the device.
rows.mechanism: Build-vs-buy resolved in favour of buy for the model and rent for the compute: Apple keeps capital light and ships sooner, at the cost of dependency on the company that also owns Android.
rows.weakens: Neither company confirmed the price or exclusivity, and the arrangement could be a bridge while Apple's own models improve — the 2026 Stepped MoE paper shows the research org still shipping efficiency work.

rows.benchmark: The Section 232 investigation opened in 2025; the Supreme Court ruling of 2026-02-20 struck down certain IEEPA tariffs.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: On 2026-01-14 the Commerce Department published initial Section 232 semiconductor findings that imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products; after the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, Apple applied for refunds and recognised them as a reduction of products cost of sales, while warning that memory and advanced-semiconductor supply constraints are expected to intensify.
rows.follow_up: How much of the products gross-margin improvement came from one-off tariff refunds, and what Section 301 measures now apply?
rows.implication: Tariff policy is now a swing factor in reported gross margin, which makes one quarter's margin a poor guide to the next.
rows.mechanism: Trade policy is being absorbed through the P&L rather than through supply-chain redesign alone; refunds flatter margin while the underlying cost of components rises.
rows.weakens: The refund is non-recurring and the 10-Q flags further Section 232, Section 301 or sector tariffs as possible, so the relief may reverse.

rows.benchmark: FY2025 fourth-quarter revenue was $102.5bn, up 8% year on year.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Apple reports fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results on 2026-11-02 having guided to 9-11% revenue growth, with iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo on sale from 2026-09-18 and the standard iPhone 18 deferred to spring 2027.
rows.follow_up: Do Duo units and Pro mix hold through the December quarter, and does services growth stay in double digits against DMA remedies?
rows.implication: The next twelve months are checkable quarter by quarter; the launch split means the March 2027 quarter carries a second iPhone cycle that the prior year did not have.
rows.mechanism: Splitting the launch moves revenue between quarters and lets Apple sell higher-priced Pro and foldable models into the holiday window while 2nm supply matures for the cheaper models in spring.
rows.weakens: Guidance of 9-11% is below the 16.4% growth of the June 2026 quarter, which implies deceleration into the launch quarter rather than acceleration.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year, +2% YoY; Omdia 1.25B (+2%) | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7% YoY, steepest annual fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP); 2026 = $196.5B x 4/3 / $613B | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC, +1.7%; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |
| Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units, and the sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at 1.26B units and a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% a year earlier on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every geographic segment in double digits; that is genuine pricing power [S17, S87, S84]. But IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases, and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down more than 20%. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months.

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects it to ship more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a global advertising pool of $1.34T in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables are a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. Foldables and services can add; the non-phone device pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

| Region | Market size (latest dated) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Americas | Regional value not published; global $613B (2026E) | Apple +11.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; home market; 42.9% of FY2025 revenue | US tariffs (Section 232 and 301); platform antitrust | Samsung, Google, Motorola | S84, S5, S6 |
| Europe | Not published | Apple +16.1% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 26.7% of revenue | DMA take-rate cuts from 2026-10-01; GDPR | Samsung, Xiaomi, Google | S77, S6 |
| Greater China | 66M units in Q2 2026; 134M in H1 2026 | Market -4.3% in Q2 2026; H2 2026 decline could reach 20%; Apple +30.0% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 18.1% handset share versus Huawei 22.6% | Market access; local champion; data rules | Huawei, OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi, Honor | S87, S6 |
| Japan | Not published | Apple +10.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 6.9% of revenue | Yen weakness; carrier-controlled channel | Samsung, Google, Sharp | S6 |
| Rest of Asia-Pacific | Not published; emerging markets forecast down more than 20% in 2026 | Apple +19.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 8.1% of revenue; India manufacturing and retail expansion | Price sensitivity; tariffs | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, OPPO, Transsion | S84, S6 |

Geography splits the durability question, and policy is a live variable in every region [S6, S87, S77]. Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue but produced 30% growth in the first nine months of FY2026; Europe is 26.7% and grew 16%, the Americas 42.9% and 11%, Japan 6.9% and 10%, and Rest of Asia-Pacific 8.1% and 19%. The China number is the most fragile: the market fell 4.3% in Q2 2026, Apple's 18.1% share trailed Huawei's 22.6%, and the top six vendors hold 96%. The EU's DMA terms cut the commission on externally distributed digital transactions to 5% from 1 October 2026. US tariffs moved twice in 2026: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026 and Section 301 duties were imposed since, while the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs on Apple products on 14 January 2026. Demand is organic consumer replacement, not policy-created: China's subsidies faded in 2026 and India's incentives are supply-side manufacturing support. The budget owner is the consumer or carrier financing plan; the procurement cycle follows the annual September launch; willingness to pay is being tested by the 27.6% ASP increase. What would change the conclusion: services growth above 15% with user growth, a foldable cycle adding IDC's $45.7B category value, or China stabilising after H2 2026. Confidence is high on 2026 data and low on 2027-2030 regional sizing, because regional market values are paywalled and Apple does not disclose units; the open questions are what share of iPhone growth is units versus price, whether services growth is users or price, how much China demand was pulled forward, and how much memory cost Apple can pass through in FY2027.

::: evidence
**Apple's markets are growing in dollars while shrinking in units, so its growth is price- and share-led, not market-led.**

The global pool is $613B of smartphone value in 2026 against just over 1.0B units, with a 27.6% ASP increase doing the work volume used to do (IDC, S84). Premium concentration (29% of units) and Apple's 65% share of it explain why Apple captures 36-43% of value on 20-24% of units (Counterpoint, S94; Apple filings, S5, S6). Foldables ($45.7B of category value by 2027) and services ($120.5B TTM at 76.0% gross margin) are the only pools large enough to move group growth; wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030 (IDC, S85).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple is winning the competition for profit and price while ceding unit share in China: it holds 65% of premium phone units and a 40% product gross margin, but Huawei is taking premium share in a shrinking China market and regulation is capping the services take rate, so its competitive position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and weakening at the margin in China. Apple's own 10-K concedes a minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables and says some of its markets have experienced little or no growth; the useful analysis is therefore per product, because the iPhone, Mac, wearables and services each face a different rival set [S5].

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Apple | Weaknesses vs Apple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung | Galaxy S26, Z Fold 7 | Android; Exynos 2600 or Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 | Unrestricted | Flagship parity; foldable incumbent | Premium | 19% global 2025; 23% in Q3 2026 | Foldable head start; carrier breadth | MX division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 | S91, S92, S120 |
| Huawei | Mate and Pura; HarmonyOS | Kirin silicon; HarmonyOS | China scale; US export restrictions | Premium camera and battery | Premium | 22.6% China in Q2 2026 | Domestic supply chain; holds prices | Little share outside China | S87, S86 |
| Xiaomi | Xiaomi 17 series | Android; Snapdragon | Unrestricted | Value flagship | Mid-premium | 11.5% global in Q2 2026 | Price-performance; AIoT and EV ecosystem | 8.5% handset gross margin; profit -42.6% | S90 |
| Google | Pixel 11 | Android; Tensor; Gemini | Unrestricted | AI-first software | Premium | Not disclosed | Gemini integration; search distribution | Small hardware distribution | S15, S50 |
| Lenovo, HP, Dell | PC lines | Windows on x86 | Unrestricted | Enterprise and channel strength | $600-2,000 | 24.4%, 19.1%, 13.6% in Q2 2026 | Enterprise channel; price tiers | No in-house OS-silicon integration | S95 |
| Spotify | Music streaming and app distribution | App; DMA alternative distribution | EU DMA beneficiary | 300M paying subscribers | Subscription | Twice Apple Music's subscriber base | Cross-platform; podcasts | No hardware bundle | S93, S77 |
| Alphabet | Search, YouTube, Play | Android; Gemini | Antitrust scrutiny | Advertising scale | Ad-funded | $471B TTM revenue | Search and advertising scale | AI capex dilution | S15, S50 |
| Status quo | Longer device life, refurbished | None | None | Adequate for most users | Zero | Not disclosed | Free and familiar | No new capability | S87 |

Huawei is the most dangerous competitor to Apple's profit pool, and Samsung is the most dangerous to its unit position [S87, S86, S91, S92, S84]. Huawei led China with 22.6% in Q2 2026 against Apple's 18.1%, after its highest share since Q4 2020 in the prior quarter, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026; Huawei funds that push with CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of CNY880.9B of 2025 revenue. Samsung is broader, with 19% global share in 2025 and 23% in Q3 2026, a foldable incumbent and the only rival with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth, so it cannot buy share indefinitely. Huawei takes price and profit; Samsung takes volume and loses money doing it.

Share trends from 2025 to 2026 show Apple gaining value and premium ground while its unit share moves sideways [S92, S120, S94, S84, S17]. Apple led 2025 with 20% of global units and 10% growth and Samsung followed at 19%; in Q3 2026 Samsung held 23% to Apple's 22% as the market fell 20%. The premium layer is where Apple's position improves: its 65% of $600-plus units in H1 2026 came with 9% growth, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% share in 2026. Pricing power shows in the gross margin, 40.1% on products in Q3 FY2026 versus 34.5% a year earlier, with iPhone revenue up 22% in nine months. The caveat is that the price increase is imposed by a memory shock rather than earned by innovation alone: NAND and DRAM costs are up more than 300% year over year, and Apple's signalling of further rises pulled Chinese demand forward.

China is the one region where the competitive position is deteriorating on share even as revenue rises [S87, S6, S86]. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in the first nine months of FY2026, but that came against a market down 4.2% in H1 2026 and with Apple at 18.1% share to Huawei's 22.6%; Huawei grew 19.4% and Apple 24.4% in Q2 2026, both by holding prices while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi raised theirs and lost 9.7%, 11.4% and 21.7% respectively. The top six vendors hold 96% of the market, so the fight is for premium share inside a contracting pool, and Huawei's HarmonyOS scale gives it a domestic platform Apple cannot match on localisation. Apple's revenue growth is a price-hold plus pull-forward effect, not evidence that it has regained structural leadership in China.

Regulation is now a competitive force that transfers rent from Apple to its rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. The practical effect is to lower switching costs out of the App Store in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and to hand Spotify, Epic and alternative storefronts a distribution channel on iOS; Spotify already has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. The DMA is the template, and its spread to other jurisdictions is the regulatory risk to monitor.

| Product | Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche player | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (premium) | Leader in premium value, second in units | Apple | Samsung | Google Pixel | Huawei in China; foldables | S94, S87 |
| Mac | Share gainer from a small base | Lenovo by units | Apple | HP and Dell premium tiers | Snapdragon Windows PCs | S95 |
| Wearables | Leader by value, third by units | Xiaomi by units, Apple by value | Huawei | Oura in rings, Meta in glasses | AI glasses | S85 |
| Services (apps and advertising) | Challenger in advertising, leader in app distribution | Alphabet in advertising | Apple in app distribution | Spotify in music | DMA-enabled alternative stores | S15, S93, S77 |

The status quo is a formidable competitor: consumers are holding devices longer, IDC expects China's recovery only in 2028-2029 and forecasts a smaller, more concentrated market after the memory crisis, and the cheapest segment is disappearing [S87, S84, S17, S93]. Pipeline threats are Apple's own foldable in H2 2026, Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion, Google's Gemini-integrated Pixel and AI agents that could move the assistant layer off the operating system. Apple's wedge is the integration of silicon, OS and an installed base that reached an all-time high in Q3 FY2026, which lets it earn 40% product gross margins while rivals earn single digits or lose money; that wedge supports profit-share gains but not unit-share gains. The competitive position therefore supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated ceiling on services, not a share-gain growth story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China and medium on services because take rates are in flux. Diligence questions: how much of the premium gain is price inflation, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS, and whether Apple's foldable holds 40% of the category beyond 2027.

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | 65% of premium phone units; 40.1% product gross margin; $120.5B services at 76.3% gross margin; installed base at an all-time high; iPhone 50.4% of FY2025 revenue | S94, S17, S6, S5 |
| Weaknesses | 18.1% China share behind Huawei; 15.5% wearables unit share; no advertising scale; revenue concentrated in one product | S87, S85, S5 |
| Opportunities | Foldables above 17M units by 2027 at a $2,550+ ASP; services advertising and cloud; Mac share gains; an AI upgrade cycle | S84, S95 |
| Threats | DMA 5% take rate on external distribution; Huawei premium share; memory costs up more than 300%; AI assistants commoditising the OS layer | S77, S87, S84 |
:::

::: evidence
**Apple's competitive advantage is profit capture, not unit share.**

Apple holds 20% of phone units but 65% of premium units and 36-43% of market value (Counterpoint, S94; IDC, S84). Its 40.1% product gross margin compares with Xiaomi's 8.5% handset margin and a loss at Samsung's mobile division (S17, S90, S91). The vulnerabilities are China and regulation, not pricing power (S87, S77).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales reached $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22% year on year, and R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months even as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. It turns one annual demand spike into two and lifts average selling price without claiming a new category of demand. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test of whether buyers follow. The Duo's hinge is machined with AI-matched parts, confocal laser scanning and 3D-printed photopolymer layers — real process know-how, but durability is unproven in the field. [S112, S114]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — roughly 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024 and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and about $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute, and its published foundation-model work continues, including a 2026 paper on stepped mixture-of-experts routing. Apple bought the part of the stack it could not ship in time. [S111, S122, S53]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at roughly $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

R&D of $34.04bn in nine months, up from $25.68bn, is attributed to AI infrastructure and headcount, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. This is a coherent capital-light strategy: free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and the company avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar is an operating expense with no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A 33% R&D increase with no separately disclosed AI revenue line is the number to watch for margin, not for technology. [S6]

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. Vertical integration pays twice: at a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory. The June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

The competitive comparison is less flattering than the silicon one. Google owns the model, the training chips and the Android distribution channel; Apple owns the device, the interface and the privacy architecture. Competitor cells below are qualitative and rest on the disclosed partnership facts; their silicon and cloud specifics were not independently verified in this run.

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |

| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin, domestic process | S113, S112 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Years of custom SoC design, 2nm allocation and modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity across devices, App Store, services at 76.3% margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | Duo hinge matched by AI, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google; no proprietary frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue; default positions under regulatory pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite** | **6.5/10** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | Minimum 3-4 years on hardware | — |

The replication test is unfriendly to the AI narrative and friendly to the hardware one. A funded team of 50 with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge in three to four years and an A-series-class system-on-chip in five, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant, by contrast, can be licensed in a quarter, which is precisely what Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which treats the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening while questioning whether the notifications are accurate and useful. It is a 30-day chronic-signal alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical and pricing claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor in the sources retrieved. These products deepen the installed base and create upgrade reasons, but they are sold as hardware features, not as platforms with their own economics. [S124]

| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Shipping | Announced 2026-09-09 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | First durability and return data | S114 |
| iPhone 18, 18e, Air 2 | Unlaunched, reported | Spring 2027 | — | — | Launch on 2nm | S112 |
| Services | Shipping | Ongoing | $91.73bn in nine months, +14% | 76.3% | DMA compliance | S6 |
| Wearables (Watch, AirPods) | Shipping | Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3 in FY2025 | Not separately disclosed | Not disclosed | Health-feature adoption | S5, S124 |
| Vision Pro | Shipping, niche | 2024 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | No successor confirmed | S5 |

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline that left Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking, and the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. Freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where individual grant numbers could not be verified against USPTO records in this run. [S117]

| Patent or portfolio | Area | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. utility grants, 2025 | Broad: silicon, RF, display, health | US | — | 2,722 grants | Granted, down 12% | Breadth without a blocking family | S117 |
| Foldable hinge and display assemblies | Hinge, crease, lamination | US, CN, EU (reported) | Multiple, dates not retrieved | Numbers not retrieved | Pending and granted, unverified | Duo durability and yield | S114 |
| On-device model compression and routing | Foundation models, MoE routing | Paper, not patent-specific | — | — | Published, held as know-how | Inference efficiency | S52, S53 |
| Health sensing (hypertension) | Optical chronic-signal detection | US | Not retrieved | Feature cleared; patent status unknown | FDA-cleared feature | Regulated differentiation | S124 |

Two things would change this judgement. If Siri AI leaves beta with usage and satisfaction data that show Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; the absence of such disclosure after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If Cupertino used the Gemini term to buy time for its own model and cut the licence at renewal, the dependency is a bridge rather than a structure. Until one of those is visible, the technology case for Apple rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on the machine facts, medium on the model economics, and low on patent depth, where a USPTO Patent Center search would settle what this run could not.

What would settle the open questions: the first full quarter of Duo warranty and return rates; the share of Siri queries served by Gemini and the licence's term; and the granted-versus-pending mix in the foldable and on-device-AI families.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales reached $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22% year on year, and R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. It turns one annual demand spike into two and lifts average selling price without claiming a new category of demand. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test of whether buyers follow. The Duo's hinge is machined with AI-matched parts, confocal laser scanning and 3D-printed photopolymer layers — real process know-how, with durability unproven in the field. [S112, S114]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — roughly 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and about $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute, and its published model research continues, including a 2026 paper on stepped mixture-of-experts routing. Apple bought the part of the stack it could not ship in time. [S111, S122, S53]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at roughly $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

R&D of $34.04bn in nine months, up from $25.68bn, is attributed to AI infrastructure and headcount, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. This is coherent: free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and the company avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar is an operating expense with no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A 33% R&D increase with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one. [S6]

| Capex, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $6.80bn (prior year $9.47bn) | 10-Q cash-flow statement | S6 |
| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

The comparison is less flattering than the silicon line. Google owns the model, the training chips and the Android channel; Apple owns the device, the interface and the privacy architecture. Competitor cells are qualitative and rest on the disclosed partnership facts, not independent verification.

| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Owns TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC design, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity across devices, App Store, 76.3% services margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, default positions under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite** | **6.5/10** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | 3-4 years on hardware | — |

The replication test is unfriendly to the AI narrative and friendly to the hardware one. A funded team of 50 with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge in three to four years and an A-series-class chip in five, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed in a quarter, which is what Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which treats the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening while questioning whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a 30-day chronic-signal alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical and pricing claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor in the sources retrieved. These products deepen the installed base and create upgrade reasons; they are sold as hardware features, not as platforms with their own economics. [S124]

| iPhone 18, 18e, Air 2 | Unlaunched, reported | Spring 2027 | — | — | Launch on 2nm | S112 |
| Services | Shipping | Ongoing | $91.73bn in nine months, +14% | 76.3% | DMA compliance | S6 |
| Wearables (Watch, AirPods) | Shipping | Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3 in FY2025 | Not separately disclosed | Not disclosed | Health-feature adoption | S5, S124 |
| Vision Pro | Shipping, niche | 2024 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | No successor confirmed | S5 |

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline that left Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking; the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. Freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where individual grant numbers could not be verified against USPTO records in this run. [S117]

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. utility grants, 2025 | Silicon, RF, display, health | US | — | 2,722 grants | Granted, down 12% | Breadth, no blocking family | S117 |
| Foldable hinge and display assemblies | Hinge, crease, lamination | US, CN, EU (reported) | Dates not retrieved | Numbers not retrieved | Pending and granted, unverified | Duo durability | S114 |
| On-device model compression | Routing, inference efficiency | Paper, not patent-specific | — | — | Published, held as know-how | Inference cost | S52, S53 |
| Health sensing (hypertension) | Optical chronic-signal detection | US | Not retrieved | Patent status unknown | FDA-cleared feature | Regulated differentiation | S124 |

Two things would change this judgement. If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If Apple used the Gemini term as a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on the machine facts, medium on the model economics and low on patent depth, which a USPTO Patent Center search would settle.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one demand spike into two and lifts average selling price without claiming a new category of demand. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test of whether buyers follow. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — roughly 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and about $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part of the stack it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at roughly $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

R&D of $34.04bn in nine months, up from $25.68bn, is attributed to AI infrastructure and headcount, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and the company avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar is an operating expense with no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A 33% R&D increase with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one. [S6]

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro process node | 2nm (A19: 3nm) | Apple launch specification | S113, S112 |
| Siri AI availability | Beta, English, from 2026-09-14 | Apple release | S113 |
| Assistant model scale | 1.2tn parameters, reported | Press reports, unconfirmed | S122 |
| R&D, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $34.04bn, +33% | 10-Q | S6 |
| Capex, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $6.80bn (prior year $9.47bn) | 10-Q cash-flow statement | S6 |
| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

Google owns the model, the training chips and the Android channel; Apple owns the device, the interface and the privacy architecture.

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |
| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Owns TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC design, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity, App Store, 76.3% services margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite** | **6.5/10** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | 3-4 years on hardware | — |

The replication test is unfriendly to the AI narrative and friendly to the hardware one. A funded team of 50 with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge in three to four years and an A-series-class chip in five, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed in a quarter, which is what Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which treats the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening while questioning whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a 30-day chronic-signal alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical and pricing claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor in the sources retrieved. These products deepen the installed base and create upgrade reasons; they are sold as hardware features, not as platforms with their own economics. [S124]

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Shipping | 2026-09-18 | iPhone $54.25bn in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by model | December 2026 mix | S113, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Shipping | Announced 2026-09-09 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Durability and returns | S114 |
| Services | Shipping | Ongoing | $91.73bn in nine months, +14% | 76.3% | DMA compliance | S6 |
| Wearables and Vision Pro | Shipping | Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3 in FY2025 | Not separately disclosed | Not disclosed | Health-feature adoption | S5, S124 |

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline that left Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking; the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. Freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where individual grant numbers could not be verified against USPTO records in this run. [S117]

| Patent or portfolio | Area | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. utility grants, 2025 | Silicon, RF, display, health | US | — | 2,722 grants | Granted, down 12% | Breadth, no blocking family | S117 |
| Foldable hinge and display assemblies | Hinge, crease, lamination | US, CN, EU (reported) | Dates not retrieved | Numbers not retrieved | Pending and granted, unverified | Duo durability | S114 |
| On-device model compression | Routing, inference efficiency | Paper, not patent-specific | — | — | Published know-how | Inference cost | S52, S53 |

If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If Apple used the Gemini term as a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patent depth.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) the equity is capitalised at $5,029.6bn and the enterprise at $4,967.4bn, which is 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn. Those multiples need either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021 to the last twelve months [S7, S6, S97].

| Metric | Value | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $344.63, 2026-10-30 20:00 UTC, NasdaqGS, USD | 2% below the 52-week high | S7 |
| Market cap / enterprise value | $5,029.6bn / $4,967.4bn | Largest in the peer set | S7 |
| 52-week range | $243.42-$351.73; price at the 93rd percentile | Uptrend intact | S7 |
| Returns | 1M +3.5%, 3M +11.6%, 12M +27.5%; vs S&P 500 +4.4, +10.4, +16.6 points; vs XLK +11.8, +9.2, +8.1 points | Leadership, and a haven inside a falling tech sector | S7, S12 |
| Moving averages | 50-day $333.04 (+3.5%); 200-day $296.56 (+16.2%) | Above both | S7 |
| Liquidity | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn a day (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | Any plausible position | S7 |
| Cash returned | Dividend 0.31% plus buyback 1.6% = 1.9% | Thin for a 39.5x stock | S6 |
| Multiples | 39.5x P/E trailing, 35.2x forward, 10.6x EV/Sales, 32.1x EV/EBIT | Top of the five-year range | S7, S97 |
| Forward earnings | A 35.21x forward P/E implies about $9.79 of EPS | Consensus proxy, not a disclosed estimate | S97 |
| Consensus revenue | iPhone $252.4bn FY2026 and $277.4bn FY2027 | 9.9% growth priced for FY2027 | S71 |

On forward earnings the shares are less stretched than the trailing figure suggests: 35.2x sits almost exactly on the twelve-month average of 35.7x, and earnings are growing. What has changed is the premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium that only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near; Alphabet, growing faster over the last year, trades at 14.6x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why it is a premium that the discount rate, rather than the operating story, controls [S7, S97, S14].

| Company | P/E (TTM) | EV/EBIT | EV/Sales | FCF yield | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple | 39.5x | 32.1x | 10.6x | 2.7% | S7 |
| Microsoft | 27.3x | 23.6x | 11.1x | 1.5% | S14 |

| HP | 11.0x | 9.6x | 0.5x | 15.0% | S104 |
| Peer median | 20.2x | 20.5x | 2.7x | 2.5% | — |

Samsung Electronics and Xiaomi, the two global handset peers, file no US GAAP statements and no market multiple for either was retrieved in this run; their comparison is therefore not disclosed here, and the hardware leg below leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and management guided the September quarter to 9-11% growth with iPhone in the mid-teens. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from about 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money in the same quarter for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is the number the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure flatters. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but nine-month operating cash flow rose $35.2bn year on year of which $25.2bn came from a swing in other current and non-current liabilities (+$10.0bn against -$15.2bn), not from profit. Normalising that swing leaves about $111.5bn, a 2.2% FCF yield and 45x P/FCF. Capital expenditure is rising from a low base at 0.77x depreciation, and research and development grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months, which caps the margin expansion the multiple assumes [S6].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The grid shows why the answer is contested: the market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%. That is the whole question, whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

| Market multiple cross-check | 27x / 31x / 35x FY2027 EPS of $9.79 | — | $264 / $303 / $343 | -23% / -12% / 0% | S7, S97 |

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of about $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap to $344.63 is what investors pay for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, estimated at about $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133, and a simple re-rating to 27x forward earnings is $264. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple grew earnings per share by more than a quarter in the June quarter, the shares have beaten the S&P 500 by a double-digit margin over twelve months, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years, and a valuation-led bear case has been premature for two years, as the twelve-month return in the trading table shows. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its five-year range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and FCF for FY2027-28 and a sell-side price target, none of which any source in this run disclosed.

Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one demand spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test of whether buyers follow. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) the equity is capitalised at $5,029.6bn and the enterprise at $4,967.4bn, which is 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn. Those multiples need either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021 [S7, S6, S97].

On forward earnings the shares are less stretched than the trailing figure suggests: 35.2x sits almost exactly on the twelve-month average of 35.7x, and earnings are growing. What has changed is the premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium that only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near; Alphabet, growing faster over the last year, trades at 14.6x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why it is a premium that the discount rate, rather than the operating story, controls [S7, S97, S14].

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and management guided the September quarter to 9-11% growth with iPhone in the mid-teens. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from about 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money in the same quarter for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is the number the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure flatters. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but nine-month operating cash flow rose $35.2bn year on year of which $25.2bn came from a swing in other current and non-current liabilities (+$10.0bn against -$15.2bn), not from profit. Capital expenditure is rising from a low base at 0.77x depreciation, and research and development grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months, which caps the margin expansion the multiple assumes [S6].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of about $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap to $344.63 is what investors pay for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, estimated at about $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133, and a simple re-rating to 27x forward earnings is $264. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple grew earnings per share by more than a quarter in the June quarter, the shares have beaten the S&P 500 by a double-digit margin over twelve months, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years, and a valuation-led bear case has been premature for two years, as the twelve-month return in the trading table shows. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its five-year range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. arguments.markdown:
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test of whether buyers follow. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part of the stack it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while payments for property, plant and equipment fell, as the metrics below show. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up of that size with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. Google owns the model, the training chips and the Android channel; Apple owns the device, the interface and the privacy architecture.

Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it.
