[S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]

Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) the equity is capitalised at $5,029.6bn and the enterprise at $4,967.4bn, which is 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; those multiples need either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021. On forward earnings the shares are less stretched than the trailing figure suggests, since 35.2x sits almost exactly on the twelve-month average of 35.7x; what has changed is the premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium that only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near, while Alphabet, growing faster over the last year, trades at 14.6x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls it [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Apple has raised no material equity in this period; the funding history is a capital-return history. Repurchases and dividends have been funded from cash flow while debt fell, and each dollar spent at 39.5x buys a 2.5% earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury.

Samsung Electronics and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements and no market multiple for either is publicly disclosed in the sources reviewed here, so that comparison is stated as not disclosed; the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell instead.

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and management guided the September quarter to 9-11% growth with iPhone in the mid-teens. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money in the same quarter for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure flatters. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but nine-month operating cash flow rose $35.2bn year on year of which $25.2bn came from a swing in other current and non-current liabilities (+$10.0bn against -$15.2bn), not from profit; normalising that swing leaves $111.5bn, a 2.2% FCF yield and 45x P/FCF. Research and development grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation, both capping the margin expansion the multiple assumes. Shareholders have received $438.6bn of repurchases and $75.0bn of dividends in the five fiscal years to FY2025, and a further $82.2bn and $15.6bn in the twelve months to June 2026, against a $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 [S6, S1, S5].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The grid shows why the answer is contested: the market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%. That is the whole question, whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

| Base | 9/8/7/6/5% | 33%, 9.0% | $212 | -38% | S6, S10, S72 |
| Bear: memory costs, services remedy | 4/3/2/2/2% | 30%, 9.5% | $133 | -61% | S6, S10, S72 |
| Market multiple cross-check | 27x / 31x / 35x FY2027 EPS of $9.79 | — | $264 / $303 / $343 | -23% / -12% / 0% | S7, S97 |

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap to $344.63 is what investors pay for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133, and a simple re-rating to 27x forward earnings is $264. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple's June quarter set a record for earnings per share, the shares have beaten the S&P 500 by a double-digit margin over twelve months, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years, and a valuation-led bear case has been premature for two years, as the twelve-month return in the trading table shows. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its five-year range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and FCF for FY2027-28 and a sell-side price target, none of which is publicly disclosed in the sources reviewed here.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while payments for property, plant and equipment fell, as the metrics show. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up of that size with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro process node | 2nm (A19: 3nm) | Apple launch specification | S113, S112 |
| Siri AI availability | Beta, English, from 2026-09-14 | Apple release | S113 |
| Assistant model scale | 1.2tn parameters, reported | Press reports, unconfirmed | S122 |
| R&D, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $34.04bn, +33% | 10-Q | S6 |
| Capex, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $6.80bn (prior year $9.47bn) | 10-Q cash-flow statement | S6 |
| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

Google owns the model, the training chips and the Android channel; Apple owns the device, the interface and the privacy architecture.

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |
| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Owns TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC design, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity, App Store, 76.3% services margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite moat** | **Strong hardware, weak AI** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | Years on hardware | S113, S6 |

The replication test is unfriendly to the AI narrative and friendly to the hardware one. A funded team of 50 with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge within a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed rather than built, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which treats the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening while questioning whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a 30-day chronic-signal alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical and pricing claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. These products deepen the installed base and create upgrade reasons; they are sold as hardware features, not as platforms with their own economics. [S124]

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Shipping | 2026-09-18 | iPhone $54.25bn in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by model | December 2026 mix | S113, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Shipping | Announced 2026-09-09 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Durability and returns | S114 |
| Services | Shipping | Ongoing | $91.73bn in nine months, +14% | 76.3% | DMA compliance | S6 |
| Wearables and Vision Pro | Shipping | Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3 in FY2025 | Not separately disclosed | Not disclosed | Health-feature adoption | S5, S124 |

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline, leaving Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking; the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. No individual patent number is cited here because none could be verified against a USPTO record; freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where that verification matters most. [S117]

| Patent or portfolio | Area | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. utility grants, 2025 | Silicon, RF, display, health | US | — | 2,722 grants | Granted, down 12% | Breadth, no blocking family | S117 |
| Foldable hinge and display assemblies | Hinge, crease, lamination | US, CN, EU (reported) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Pending and granted, unverified | Duo durability | S114 |
| On-device model compression | Routing, inference efficiency | Paper, not patent-specific | — | — | Published know-how | Inference cost | S52, S53 |

If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If Apple used the Gemini term as a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patents.

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap to $344.63 is what investors pay for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133, and a simple re-rating to 27x forward earnings is $264. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple's June quarter set a record for earnings per share, the shares have beaten the S&P 500 by a double-digit margin over twelve months, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years, and a valuation-led bear case has been premature for two years. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its five-year range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and FCF for FY2027-28 and a sell-side price target, none of which is publicly disclosed here.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while payments for property, plant and equipment fell, as the metrics show. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up of that size with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro process node | 2nm (A19: 3nm) | Apple launch specification | S113, S112 |
| Siri AI availability | Beta, English, from 2026-09-14 | Apple release | S113 |
| Assistant model scale | 1.2tn parameters, reported | Press reports, unconfirmed | S122 |
| R&D, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $34.04bn, +33% | 10-Q | S6 |
| Capex, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $6.80bn (prior year $9.47bn) | 10-Q cash-flow statement | S6 |
| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

Google owns the model, the training chips and the Android channel; Apple owns the device, the interface and the privacy architecture.

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |
| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Owns TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC design, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity, App Store, 76.3% services margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite moat** | **Strong hardware, weak AI** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | Years on hardware | S113, S6 |

The replication test is unfriendly to the AI narrative and friendly to the hardware one. A funded engineering team with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge within a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed rather than built, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which treats the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening while questioning whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a chronic-signal alert over a month, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical and pricing claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. These products deepen the installed base and create upgrade reasons; they are sold as hardware features, not as platforms with their own economics.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Shipping | 2026-09-18 | iPhone $54.25bn in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by model | December 2026 mix | S113, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Shipping | Announced 2026-09-09 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Durability and returns | S114 |
| Services | Shipping | Ongoing | $91.73bn in nine months, +14% | 76.3% | DMA compliance | S6 |
| Wearables and Vision Pro | Shipping | Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3 in FY2025 | Not separately disclosed | Not disclosed | Health-feature adoption | S5, S124 |

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline, leaving Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking; the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. No individual patent number is cited here because none could be verified against a USPTO record; freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where that verification matters most. [S117]

| Patent or portfolio | Area | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. utility grants, 2025 | Silicon, RF, display, health | US | — | 2,722 grants | Granted, down 12% | Breadth, no blocking family | S117 |
| Foldable hinge and display assemblies | Hinge, crease, lamination | US, CN, EU (reported) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Pending and granted, unverified | Duo durability | S114 |
| On-device model compression | Routing, inference efficiency | Paper, not patent-specific | — | — | Published know-how | Inference cost | S52, S53 |

If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If Apple used the Gemini term as a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patents.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) the market values the equity at $5,029.6bn and the enterprise at $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; those multiples need either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021. On forward earnings the shares look less stretched — 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x — but that is still a premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium that only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near, while Alphabet, growing faster over the last year, trades at 14.6x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls it [S7, S6, S97, S14].

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and management guided the September quarter to 9-11% growth with iPhone in the mid-teens. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money in the same quarter for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure flatters. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but nine-month operating cash flow rose $35.2bn year on year of which $25.2bn came from a swing in other current and non-current liabilities (+$10.0bn against -$15.2bn), not from profit; normalising that swing leaves $111.5bn, a 2.2% FCF yield and 45x P/FCF. Research and development grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation, both capping the margin expansion the multiple assumes. Shareholders have received $438.6bn of repurchases and $75.0bn of dividends in the five fiscal years to FY2025, and a further $82.2bn and $15.6bn in the twelve months to June 2026, against a $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025; equity capital raised across the six periods is nil and total debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S6, S1, S5].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The grid shows why the answer is contested: the market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%. That is the whole question, whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap to $344.63 is what investors pay for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133, and a simple re-rating to 27x forward earnings is $264. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple's June quarter set a record for earnings per share, the shares have beaten the S&P 500 over twelve months, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its five-year range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and FCF for FY2027-28 and a sell-side price target, none of which is publicly disclosed here.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle.

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-03-28 and 2026-06-27, at a gross margin roughly 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures fully confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, which is the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, the personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb the cost of frontier training. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android and can price the licence at renewal, and Apple's own research output, while still credible, now sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability.

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation that is rebuilt while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, and they give owners a reason to upgrade and a reason not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside the Wearables line and has no confirmed successor, which makes it a research option rather than a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

arguments.markdown:
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures fully confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, which is the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, the personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb the cost of frontier training. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android and can price the licence at renewal, and Apple's own research output, while still credible, now sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. [S111]

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation that is rebuilt while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, and they give owners a reason to upgrade and a reason not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside the Wearables line and has no confirmed successor, which makes it a research option rather than a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) Apple's market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn and its enterprise value $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that valuation needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021. On forward earnings the shares look less stretched — 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x — but that is still a premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium that only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near, while Alphabet, growing faster over the last year, trades at 14.6x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls it [S7, S6, S97, S14].

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and management guided the September quarter to 9-11% growth with iPhone in the mid-teens. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money in the same quarter for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure flatters. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but nine-month operating cash flow rose $35.2bn year on year of which $25.2bn came from a swing in other current and non-current liabilities (+$10.0bn against -$15.2bn), not from profit; normalising that swing leaves $111.5bn, a 2.2% FCF yield and 45x P/FCF. Research and development grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation, both capping the margin expansion the multiple assumes. Shareholders have received $438.6bn of repurchases and $75.0bn of dividends in the five fiscal years to FY2025, and a further $82.2bn and $15.6bn in the twelve months to June 2026, against a $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025; equity capital raised across the six periods is nil and total debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S6, S1, S5].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap to $344.63 is what investors pay for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133, and a simple re-rating to 27x forward earnings is $264. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple's June quarter set a record for earnings per share, the shares have beaten the broad market over the past year, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and free cash flow for the next two fiscal years and a sell-side price target, none of which is publicly disclosed here.

rows.implication: Continuity is high and the product-integration model is safe, but the skills most tested in 2026-28 (AI platform economics, regulatory negotiation, tariffs) are not the ones on his record, which argues for a wait-for-evidence stance rather than paying a new-CEO premium.
rows.mechanism: Promoting the hardware engineering head keeps the integrated product model intact but transfers the CEO role from a commercial operator who built the China supply chain and services pricing to an engineer whose record is product development.
rows.weakens: Ternus has run the largest product organisation at Apple for five years, which is broader than the title suggests; internal promotion is also the pattern that worked in 2011.

rows.benchmark: Q3 FY2026 revenue growth of 16% and the July 2026 statement that Siri AI shipped at WWDC26 are the test of whether the reorganisation delivered.
rows.confidence: high on the reorganisation; medium on whether accountability is now clear, which the company has not disclosed.
rows.finding: On 2025-12-01 Apple announced John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, with Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety moved into the software organisation, and the rest of the AI org split between Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue.
rows.follow_up: Who now owns Siri roadmap and model strategy, and does Subramanya report to the CEO or only to Federighi?
rows.implication: Treat AI execution as an unresolved item requiring a milestone (shipped Siri AI adoption and a disclosed AI roadmap) before adding to a position.
rows.mechanism: AI accountability was spread across a standalone SVP, the software org and the operations org; folding models and safety under Software Engineering shortens the path from model to product but leaves the P&L owner for AI undisclosed.
rows.weakens: Apple shipped the all-new Siri AI by WWDC26, so the reorganisation produced a deliverable within seven months; the delay that triggered it is not quantified in any filing.

rows.benchmark: Products gross margin of 36.8% in FY2025 rests on custom silicon and is the line at risk if silicon leadership weakens.
rows.confidence: medium - single media report, denied by nobody and confirmed by nobody; no departure has been disclosed.
rows.finding: On 2025-12-06 it was reported that Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, told Tim Cook he was seriously considering leaving the company; no departure or new role has been disclosed in any filing since.
rows.follow_up: Has Srouji been given a new title, retention award or CTO role, and who is his designated successor?
rows.implication: This is the single most underpriced key-person risk in the holding; ask for the retention arrangement before sizing a position.
rows.mechanism: Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and hardware margin; losing the executive who built it threatens a multi-year roadmap that competitors cannot copy quickly.
rows.weakens: The report is unconfirmed and Apple has disclosed no change; promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be exactly the move that retains silicon talent.

rows.benchmark: Microsoft's Nadella at $96.5m reported for FY2025 and Alphabet's Pichai at $10.9m reported for 2025 but with a 2026 target equity award of $210m and a 1.35m-share PSU vesting in February 2026.
rows.confidence: high on Apple's numbers; medium on peers, where one figure comes from reporting rather than the proxy itself.
rows.finding: Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m (base $3m unchanged since 2016, target cash $6m, target equity $50m, 75% performance-based); the other named executive officers each target about $23m (base $1m, 200% cash target, $20m equity); Parekh's CFO package was $1m base with 175% cash target and $16.75m target equity.
rows.follow_up: What are the 2026 awards to Ternus and to the non-NEO SVPs, and do they include multi-year retention grants?
rows.implication: Shareholders get a chief executive paid well below mega-cap peers, which is a real plus, but the same restraint applied to undisclosed SVPs is a poaching risk in the AI labour market.
rows.mechanism: Apple pays small annual awards with long vesting (about 4.5 years) and no employment contracts, so retention depends on unvested equity rather than contractual protection; peers use front-loaded mega-grants that make leaving expensive.
rows.weakens: Pay follows performance: 92% say-on-pay in 2025 and a 2,162% cumulative TSR from 2011 to 2025 make the structure defensible, and unvested RSUs are large in absolute terms.

rows.benchmark: The 2026 proxy names only six named executive officers and four current executives in the ownership table, against a peer group whose CEOs are covered individually in sector research.
rows.confidence: high - the set of filers and titles comes from the Form 4 list itself.
rows.finding: Apple's Section 16 population is narrow: the Form 4 filers in the twelve months to 2026-10-29 are Cook (now Executive Chair), Ternus, O'Brien, Parekh, Newstead, principal accounting officer Borders and director Levinson; Craig Federighi, Eddy Cue, Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak do not appear, so their ownership and trades are not publicly disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Will Apple designate its AI and silicon leaders as Section 16 officers, and what does the 2027 proxy disclose about their awards?
rows.implication: Information asymmetry is material for a people-dependent thesis; the report should carry an explicit disclosure limitation and the investor should seek management access before sizing.
rows.mechanism: Non-disclosure of the operating bench means outside holders cannot price succession, retention or internal competition for the CEO role from filings alone.
rows.weakens: The named group still covers operations, finance, legal and retail, i.e. every function with external reporting exposure, so the disclosure gap is about product and technology leaders rather than the whole bench.

rows.benchmark: Apple's 2011 transition had one CEO change with no simultaneous CFO, COO, GC or AI-lead change.
rows.confidence: high on dates and roles; the causation between turnover and execution is an interpretation.
rows.finding: In roughly eighteen months Apple changed CFO (Parekh, 2025-01-01), COO (Khan, 2025), general counsel (Newstead from 2026-03-01, with Adams moving to government affairs until retirement in late 2026), lost its AI chief (2025-12-01) and its environment chief (Lisa Jackson, announced 2025-12-04), and named a new CEO (2026-09-01).
rows.follow_up: Which of these roles is now filled by an external hire, and what is the average tenure of the current executive team?
rows.implication: A cluster of senior turnover into a CEO change raises execution risk; it supports a conditions-based entry rather than buying the transition narrative.
rows.mechanism: Simultaneous turnover in finance, operations, legal, environment and AI removes institutional knowledge at the moment the company must re-price its services rent and defend antitrust cases.
rows.weakens: Apple describes each move as a planned transition, the CFO and COO successors were internal, and there is no filing evidence of dispute or dysfunction.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and net buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.5x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to about 1% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below roughly $270, where the three-year return spans 5-13% around a 10% central case, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and a source of correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple trades $13.8bn a day, so a position of any size a long-only fund would take can be liquidated inside a week at a market impact measured in single-digit basis points, and the exit is never closed. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they all mark the same multiple down together [S7].

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on a $5,029.6bn market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2026E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.0% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return, multiple unchanged | 9.9% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return, multiple reverts to 31.0x | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does most of the work in that growth, and at 39.5x it buys a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar spent — below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury — so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. The mechanism is not a scandal; it is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 39.5x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.5% of the price, or 7.7% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. That is the mechanism the higher-rate regime exerts on a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than it was when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually since 2012 | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

The precedents are all capital returns, because that is the only exit a company of this size has ever offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 20-30% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 39.5x is making the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

| Entry price | Exit at 27x | Exit at 31x | Exit at 34x |
|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 (2026-10-30) | -3.2% | 1.3% | 4.5% |
| $300 | 1.4% | 6.1% | 9.4% |
| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% |
| $240 | 9.2% | 14.3% | 17.9% |

Three-year annualised return on FY2029E EPS of $11.45 and $3.55 of dividends; exit multiples of 27x, 31x and 34x, the range Apple has traded in over four years [S6, S7, S97].

The sell discipline follows from that table. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from roughly $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who already owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12% rather than the 9.9% consensus assumes for iPhone revenue. The conditions that would make me raise the entry price are specific and all observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The conditions that force a sale are equally specific: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, roughly $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The bear case sets the drawdown to expect, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on about $242: a reversion to Apple's 2022 multiple of 24.6x on FY2027E earnings, and the $243.42 low the shares actually printed within the past twelve months. That is a 30% drawdown, and it is the realistic bad case for a fund holding the shares. The DCF bear of $133 is a different animal — it assumes gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a 9.5% discount rate together — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback is what limits it: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down mechanically raises the forward earnings growth the buyer is getting [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong for two years. Apple has compounded 27.5% over the past twelve months while the technology sector fell 8.3% in the last month alone, and a fund that sold at 35x in FY2025 would have forgone a third of that gain. Multiples of this quality have stayed high through a 4.93% ten-year yield that most models said would compress them. That is a reason to size the position modestly and to buy on weakness rather than to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real and growing, and the only thing standing between the current price and a 9% return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation.

Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years — one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit — but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit at Apple's own age-75 ceiling, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality.

### What a buyer actually owns

Apple Inc. is a California corporation incorporated on 1977-01-03, listed on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars. At 2026-01-02 it had 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding against 50,400,000,000 authorised, all of a single class of $0.00001 par common stock with one vote per share. There is no dual-class structure, no VIE, no nominee shareholder and no contractual control chain — verified in the balance sheet and the 2026 proxy, not assumed. Float is effectively the whole company: directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares, or 0.06%, leaving 99.94%. Vanguard (9.63%) and BlackRock (7.10%) are the only disclosed 5% holders — and BlackRock's figure rests on a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the 2026 register is partly unknown. ### Cash conversion is real; the 2026 step-up is partly working capital

Nine-month operating cash flow rose 43.1% to $116,996M while net income rose 20.0%, and the balance sheet shows why: receivables fell to $31,398M from $39,777M and vendor non-trade receivables to $27,509M from $33,180M, cutting days sales outstanding to 24.5 from 34.9, while inventory rose to $11,092M from $5,718M and payables fell to $64,525M from $69,860M, shortening the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1. Part of the record is therefore a release of working capital that reverses as memory is pre-bought, not a permanent lift in earning power. The top line is not being smoothed either: deferred revenue of $14.9B is 3.2% of trailing revenue, and only $7,260M of nine-month revenue came out of the opening deferred balance. [S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. The FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B payable within twelve months and $37.0B of future interest, commercial paper ran at a 4.19% weighted rate, leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need a question rather than a red flag: $2,604M of unrealised losses on the securities book, and intangible assets that rose to $25,417M net from $13,301M — $38,220M gross, $12,803M accumulated amortisation — without the 10-Q disaggregating what was bought. ### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: free cash flow of $136,683M over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 71.2%, against 57.3% in FY2025. With a ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, any plausible cost of equity of 9-11% is cleared several times; the constraint is the price, because a $5,072B market capitalisation on $128,930M of trailing net income is a 2.5% earnings yield. Capital allocation supports that reading rather than contradicting it: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M are 67.0% of free cash flow, net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. This is not a debt-funded buyback story. [S6, S7]

### What the next print has to clear

No audited fiscal 2026 exists yet: Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026, two days after this analysis, and the only forward numbers are management's guidance of 9-11% revenue growth for that quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B) with iPhone growth in the mid-teens, against consensus of $56.4B of iPhone revenue for the quarter, $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%). Sensitivity on trailing figures after a 17.3% tax rate: 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of EPS (6.0%), 500 basis points is $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment is $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue at the 39.9% product margin is $0.55 (6.3%). Gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue while a unit miss applies only to hardware. The implication for an investor is that earnings quality is not the constraint on this name — the price is, since 39x trailing net income already assumes the 2026 margin is a base rather than a peak. The open diligence is specific: what gross margin does management guide for the December 2026 quarter, how much of FY2027 memory is contracted at fixed prices, and what was acquired for the $12,116M increase in net intangibles?
