arguments.markdown:
The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era — hardware, operations, finance — and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation after the Siri delay, the chip chief was reported to be considering leaving, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition. Apple is run by career insiders — Cook has been at the company since March 1998 (28 years), Ternus since 2001 (25 years), and the 2025 CFO and COO appointments were internal promotions. Ternus's hardware organisation and the silicon team invent; Cook built worldwide sales before 2005 and O'Brien runs retail; Cue's organisation holds the App Store rent; Parekh allocates the capital, $106.1bn returned in FY2025; Federighi's software organisation took over AI on 2025-12-01. [S11, S56]

| Executive | Degree | Institution | Year | Focus | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tim Cook, CEO 2011-2026, Executive Chair from 2026-09-01 | Not disclosed in proxy or 10-K | — | — | — | S11, S56 |
| John Ternus, CEO from 2026-09-01 | B.S. Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics; minor in psychology | University of Pennsylvania | 1997 | Mechanical engineering | S130 |
| Kevan Parekh, CFO from 2025-01-01 | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Sabih Khan, COO from 2025 | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Deirdre O'Brien, SVP Retail + People | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Jennifer Newstead, SVP, General Counsel from 2026-03-01 | Not disclosed in Apple filings | — | — | — | S132 |
| Amar Subramanya, VP of AI from 2025-12 | Not disclosed in Apple filings | — | — | — | S127 |

Apple's proxy is unusual among mega-caps in disclosing no degrees for any named executive; only Ternus's 1997 Penn engineering degree is established from a university record. The gap is material because the CEO's technical formation is the main public evidence of whether he can referee a models-and-silicon roadmap.

| Period | Executive | Role | Evidence of scope | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1998-03 to 2000-10 | Tim Cook | SVP, Worldwide Operations | Supply and operations remit | S11 |
| 2002-02 to 2005-10 | Tim Cook | EVP, Worldwide Sales and Operations | Sales added to operations | S11 |
| 2005-10 to 2011-08 | Tim Cook | Chief Operating Officer | Ran the company through product cycles | S11 |
| 2011-08 to 2026-09-01 | Tim Cook | CEO | Cumulative TSR +2,162% and market capitalisation +$3.4trn, 2011-2025 | S11 |
| 2001 to 2013 | John Ternus | Product design team, then VP Hardware Engineering from 2013 | Product development | S56, S130 |
| 2021 to 2026-09-01 | John Ternus | SVP, Hardware Engineering | Largest product organisation | S56 |
| 2025-01-01 to present | Kevan Parekh | SVP, CFO | Previously VP, Financial Planning and Analysis | S11 |
| 2025 to present | Sabih Khan | SVP, COO | On the executive team since 2019, previously SVP Operations | S11 |
| 2017 to 2026-03 | Kate Adams | SVP, General Counsel and Secretary | Moved to government affairs until retirement in late 2026 | S128, S132 |
| 2026-01 to present | Jennifer Newstead | SVP; General Counsel from 2026-03-01 | External hire, reports to the CEO | S132 |

Pay is where the team is most unusual. Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m — a $3m salary unchanged since 2016, a $6m target cash award and a $50m equity award, 75% performance-based — against Satya Nadella's $96.5m reported for Microsoft's fiscal 2025 and Sundar Pichai's $10.9m reported for 2025, though Pichai's 2026 target equity award is $210m and a 1,348,607-share 2022 award vested to him in February 2026. Apple's other named executives each target about $23m: $1m salary, a 200% cash target and $20m of equity. There are no employment contracts, no change-of-control payments and time-based RSUs vest over roughly four and a half years, so retention runs through unvested stock rather than contractual protection — cheap for shareholders and defensible at 92% say-on-pay, but exposed where pay is not disclosed at all. [S11, S129, S125]

::: evidence
**The AI organisation has been rebuilt around software, but no filing names an owner of the AI P&L.**
On 2025-12-01 Apple announced that John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, taking Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety, while the rest of the organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue [S127]. Seven months later the July 2026 results release had Cook announcing "the all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 [S17] — delivery, but through a structure in which model, product and commercial accountability sit with three different executives.
:::

The reporting on silicon is the sharpest counter-evidence to a continuity story. In December 2025 Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, was reported to have told Cook he was seriously considering leaving; no departure or new role has been disclosed since. Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and the 36.8% products gross margin, so the loss of its architect would threaten a roadmap competitors cannot copy quickly. Promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be the retention move that keeps that bench together — or it may not, and the filings will not say which. [S131, S5]

The 2024-26 turnover cluster is the part a reference check should attack. Within about eighteen months Apple changed CFO (2025-01-01), COO (2025), general counsel (2026-03-01, with Adams retained for government affairs until late 2026), AI leadership (2025-12-01), environment leadership (announced 2025-12-04) and CEO (2026-09-01). Apple calls each a planned transition and two successors were internal, which is real bench evidence; but keeping the outgoing general counsel on government affairs signals how heavy the regulatory load has become, and it also means the person who ran the DOJ and DMA fights is leaving while those cases are live. [S11, S128, S132]

| Dimension | Cook | Ternus | Parekh | Khan | Team |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Years at Apple | 28 | 25 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Deep insider bench |
| Technical depth | Operations and supply chain | Hardware engineering | Finance and FP&A | Operations | Strong on hardware and cost |
| Scaling record | CEO through 15 years and $3.4trn of value added | Largest product organisation | CFO through a 16% growth year | COO across the supply chain | Proven at scale |
| Capital markets | $263.2bn of buybacks in three years | Not evidenced | CFO since 2025 | Not evidenced | Adequate |
| Regulatory and policy | Testified through antitrust era | Not evidenced | Not evidenced | Not evidenced | Thin |
| Prior exits or founder roles | None disclosed | None disclosed | None disclosed | None disclosed | No founder experience |
| Key-person dependency | High as Executive Chair | High as new CEO | Medium | Medium | High |
| Retention risk | Low; retirement provisions in place | Low; first-year CEO | Medium | Medium | Medium-high |

What public records confirm is narrow and clean: titles, dates, pay, the $59m target, the 2,162% cumulative TSR under Cook and the 92% say-on-pay. What they contradict or cannot settle is larger — no degrees for six of seven executives, no pay or ownership for Federighi, Cue, Srouji or Joswiak because they are not Section 16 filers, no disclosed outcome to the Srouji report, and no named AI owner. For a people-dependent thesis that is a real information discount. Diligence should verify Ternus's non-hardware operating scope and any retention award, the Srouji title and succession, the 2026 awards to non-NEO SVPs, and who signs off the AI roadmap and budget. The company's leadership biographies, which would settle degrees and prior employers, could not be retrieved in this run, so those cells stay "not disclosed" rather than inferred. [S41, S11]

The financials section is robust and consistent with mine. Key differences:
- They use FCF $136,683M and conversion 1.06x, treating the step-up as "partly working capital" (receivables/DSO, inventory, payables) — they attribute the WC release to receivables, inventory and payables, while I attribute $25.2B to "other current and non-current liabilities". Both are in the 10-Q. Their explanation focuses on DSO and CCC; mine is the liability line. They're complementary, not contradictory. They do say "Part of the record is therefore a release of working capital that reverses as memory is pre-bought" — consistent with my normalisation.
- They say market cap $5,072B (diluted shares) — I use $5,029.6B. Minor.
- They note "the ability to capitalise 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%". My DCF uses 33% operating margin flat, consistent with ~47-48% GM.
- Their EPS sensitivity: losing the $20B search payment = $1.12 (12.9%). Mine: SOTP impact ~$27-36/share. Different methods, both fine.

One inconsistency to check: they say "nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M" while I cite "$82.2bn and $15.6bn in the twelve months to June 2026" — different periods, both correct (9M vs TTM). Fine.

Their effective tax rate TTM 17.3% matches mine.

They say "reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026, two days after this analysis" ✓ consistent with S72.

Now, is there a note worth leaving for the Fundamentals Analyst? Their conversion claim "1.06x" and the statement "Apple's profit is unusually cash-true" is reasonable. But they attribute the OCF step-up to receivables/DSO/payables — the 10-Q shows "other current and non-current liabilities +$10,016M vs -$15,161M" is a $25.2B swing, which is bigger than the receivables effect. If their section implies the WC release is receivables-driven, that's incomplete. But they did mention inventory and payables too. Their conclusion (reverses) is the same as mine.

Hmm — the cash conversion cycle computation: receivables fell $8.4B, vendor receivables fell $5.7B, inventory rose $5.4B, payables fell $5.3B. Net WC change: +8.4 + 5.7 - 5.4 - 5.3 = +3.4B. That doesn't explain $35B of OCF increase. The "other liabilities" +$25.2B swing is the dominant driver, and they don't mention it. That's worth a note: it's a fact their section needs, with the source ID S6.

Note to Fundamentals (max 600 chars): "The $35.2bn nine-month OCF increase is dominated by a $25.2bn swing in 'other current and non-current liabilities' (+$10,016M vs -$15,161M, 10-Q 2026-06-27, S6), larger than the receivables, inventory and payables effects combined (~$3.4bn net). | Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units, and the sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at 1.26B units and a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% a year earlier on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every geographic segment in double digits; that is genuine pricing power [S17, S87, S84]. But IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases, and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down more than 20%. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months.

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects it to ship more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a global advertising pool of $1.34T in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables are a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era — hardware, operations, finance — and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation after the Siri delay, the chip chief was reported to be considering leaving, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition. Apple is run by career insiders — Cook has been at the company since March 1998 (28 years), Ternus since 2001 (25 years), and the 2025 CFO and COO appointments were internal promotions. Ternus's hardware organisation and the silicon team invent; Cook built worldwide sales before 2005 and O'Brien runs retail; Cue's organisation holds the App Store rent; Parekh allocates the capital, $106.1bn returned in FY2025; Federighi's software organisation took over AI on 2025-12-01. Apple's proxy is unusual among mega-caps in disclosing no degrees for any named executive; only Ternus's 1997 Penn engineering degree is established from a university record. Pay is where the team is most unusual. Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m — a $3m salary unchanged since 2016, a $6m target cash award and a $50m equity award, 75% performance-based — against Satya Nadella's $96.5m reported for Microsoft's fiscal 2025 and Sundar Pichai's $10.9m reported for 2025, though Pichai's 2026 target equity award is $210m and a 1,348,607-share 2022 award vested to him in February 2026. Apple's other named executives each target about $23m: $1m salary, a 200% cash target and $20m of equity. There are no employment contracts, no change-of-control payments and time-based RSUs vest over roughly four and a half years, so retention runs through unvested stock rather than contractual protection — cheap for shareholders and defensible at 92% say-on-pay, but exposed where pay is not disclosed at all. [S11, S129, S125]

::: evidence
**The AI organisation has been rebuilt around software, but no filing names an owner of the AI P&L.**
On 2025-12-01 Apple announced that John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, taking Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety, while the rest of the organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. By the July 2026 results release, Cook was announcing "the all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 — delivery, but through a structure in which model, product and commercial accountability sit with three different executives. [S127, S17]
:::

The reporting on silicon is the sharpest counter-evidence to a continuity story. In December 2025 Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, was reported to have told Cook he was seriously considering leaving; no departure or new role has been disclosed since. Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and the 36.8% products gross margin, so the loss of its architect would threaten a roadmap competitors cannot copy quickly. Promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be the retention move that keeps that bench together — or it may not, and the filings will not say which. [S131, S5]

The 2024-26 turnover cluster is the part a reference check should attack. Within about eighteen months Apple changed CFO (2025-01-01), COO (2025), general counsel (2026-03-01, with Adams retained for government affairs until late 2026), AI leadership (2025-12-01), environment leadership (announced 2025-12-04) and CEO (2026-09-01). Apple calls each a planned transition and two successors were internal, which is real bench evidence; but keeping the outgoing general counsel on government affairs signals how heavy the regulatory load has become, and the general counsel who oversaw those defences is leaving while the DOJ and DMA cases are live. [S11, S128, S132]

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, the highest Apple has reported. Part of that is structural: services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue. Part is not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 percentage points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to those refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average, Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%, and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The 30 July 2026 release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); nine-month products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9% a year earlier on mix and refunds, while memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and Apple's 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off the trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of the $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real; the 2026 step-up is partly working capital

Nine-month operating cash flow rose 43.1% to $116,996M while net income rose 20.0%, and the balance sheet shows why: receivables fell to $31,398M from $39,777M and vendor non-trade receivables to $27,509M from $33,180M, cutting days sales outstanding to 24.5 from 34.9, while inventory rose to $11,092M from $5,718M and payables fell to $64,525M from $69,860M, shortening the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1. Part of the record is therefore a release of working capital that reverses as memory is pre-bought, not a permanent lift in earning power. The top line is not being smoothed either: deferred revenue of $14.9B is 3.2% of trailing revenue, and only $7,260M of nine-month revenue came out of the opening deferred balance. [S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. The FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B payable within twelve months and $37.0B of future interest, commercial paper ran at a 4.19% weighted rate, leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: free cash flow of $136,683M over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 71.2%, against 57.3% in FY2025. With a ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, any plausible cost of equity of 9-11% is cleared several times; the constraint is the price, because a $5,072B market capitalisation on $128,930M of trailing net income is a 2.5% earnings yield. Capital allocation supports that reading rather than contradicting it: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M are 67.0% of free cash flow, net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. This is not a debt-funded buyback story. [S6, S7]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,993 characters)
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while payments for property, plant and equipment fell, as the metrics show. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up of that size with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

| A20 Pro process node | 2nm (A19: 3nm) | Apple launch specification | S113, S112 |

| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

Google owns the model, the training chips and the Android channel; Apple owns the device, the interface and the privacy architecture.

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |

| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |
| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Owns TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC design, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity, App Store, 76.3% services margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite moat** | **Strong hardware, weak AI** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | Years on hardware | S113, S6 |

The replication test is unfriendly to the AI narrative and friendly to the hardware one. A funded engineering team with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge within a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed rather than built, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which treats the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening while questioning whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a chronic-signal alert over a month, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical and pricing claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. These products deepen the installed base and create upgrade reasons; they are sold as hardware features, not as platforms with their own economics.

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline, leaving Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking; the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. No individual patent number is cited here because none could be verified against a USPTO record; freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where that verification matters most. If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If Apple used the Gemini term as a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patents."}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era — hardware, operations, finance — and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation, the chip chief was reported to be considering leaving, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition. Apple is run by career insiders — Cook has been at the company since March 1998 (28 years), Ternus since 2001 (25 years), and the 2025 CFO and COO appointments were internal promotions. Ternus's hardware organisation and the silicon team invent; Cook built worldwide sales before 2005 and O'Brien runs retail; Cue's organisation holds the App Store rent; Parekh allocates the capital, $106.1bn returned in FY2025; Federighi's software organisation took over AI on 2025-12-01. [S11, S56]

| Executive | Degree | Institution | Year | Focus | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tim Cook, CEO 2011-2026, Executive Chair from 2026-09-01 | Not disclosed in proxy or 10-K | — | — | — | S11, S56 |
| John Ternus, CEO from 2026-09-01 | B.S. Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics; minor in psychology | University of Pennsylvania | 1997 | Mechanical engineering | S130 |
| Kevan Parekh, CFO from 2025-01-01 | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Sabih Khan, COO from 2025 | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Deirdre O'Brien, SVP Retail + People | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Jennifer Newstead, SVP, General Counsel from 2026-03-01 | Not disclosed in Apple filings | — | — | — | S132 |
| Amar Subramanya, VP of AI from 2025-12 | Not disclosed in Apple filings | — | — | — | S127 |

Apple's proxy is unusual among mega-caps in disclosing no degrees for any named executive; only Ternus's 1997 Penn engineering degree is established from a university record. The gap is material because the CEO's technical formation is the main public evidence of whether he can referee a models-and-silicon roadmap.

| Period | Executive | Role | Evidence of scope | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1998-03 to 2000-10 | Tim Cook | SVP, Worldwide Operations | Supply and operations remit | S11 |
| 2002-02 to 2005-10 | Tim Cook | EVP, Worldwide Sales and Operations | Sales added to operations | S11 |
| 2005-10 to 2011-08 | Tim Cook | Chief Operating Officer | Ran the company through product cycles | S11 |
| 2011-08 to 2026-09-01 | Tim Cook | CEO | Cumulative TSR +2,162% and market capitalisation +$3.4trn, 2011-2025 | S11 |
| 2001 to 2013 | John Ternus | Product design team, then VP Hardware Engineering from 2013 | Product development | S56, S130 |
| 2021 to 2026-09-01 | John Ternus | SVP, Hardware Engineering | Largest product organisation | S56 |
| 2025-01-01 to present | Kevan Parekh | SVP, CFO | Previously VP, Financial Planning and Analysis | S11 |
| 2025 to present | Sabih Khan | SVP, COO | On the executive team since 2019, previously SVP Operations | S11 |
| 2017 to 2026-03 | Kate Adams | SVP, General Counsel and Secretary | Moved to government affairs until retirement in late 2026 | S128, S132 |
| 2026-01 to present | Jennifer Newstead | SVP; General Counsel from 2026-03-01 | External hire, reports to the CEO | S132 |

Pay is where the team is most unusual. Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m — a $3m salary unchanged since 2016, a $6m target cash award and a $50m equity award, 75% performance-based — against Satya Nadella's $96.5m reported for Microsoft's fiscal 2025 and Sundar Pichai's $10.9m reported for 2025, though Pichai's 2026 target equity award is $210m and a 1,348,607-share 2022 award vested to him in February 2026. Apple's other named executives each target about $23m: $1m salary, a 200% cash target and $20m of equity. There are no employment contracts, no change-of-control payments and time-based RSUs vest over roughly four and a half years, so retention runs through unvested stock rather than contractual protection — cheap for shareholders and defensible at 92% say-on-pay, but exposed where pay is not disclosed at all. [S11, S129, S125]

::: evidence
**The AI organisation has been rebuilt around software, but no filing names an owner of the AI P&L.**
On 2025-12-01 Apple announced that John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, taking Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety, while the rest of the organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Siri AI reached users only as a beta in English with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14, running on a Gemini model licensed from Google — delivery, but through a structure in which model, product and commercial accountability sit with three different executives. [S127, S113, S111]
:::

The reporting on silicon is the sharpest counter-evidence to a continuity story. In December 2025 Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, was reported to have told Cook he was seriously considering leaving; no departure or new role has been disclosed since. Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and the 36.8% products gross margin, so the loss of its architect would threaten a roadmap competitors cannot copy quickly. Promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be the retention move that keeps that bench together — or it may not, and the filings will not say which. [S131, S5]

The 2024-26 turnover cluster is the part a reference check should attack. Within about eighteen months Apple changed CFO (2025-01-01), COO (2025), general counsel (2026-03-01, with Adams retained for government affairs until late 2026), AI leadership (2025-12-01), environment leadership (announced 2025-12-04) and CEO (2026-09-01). Apple calls each a planned transition and two successors were internal, which is real bench evidence; but keeping the outgoing general counsel on government affairs signals how heavy the regulatory load has become, and the general counsel who oversaw those defences is leaving while the DOJ and DMA cases are live. [S11, S128, S132]

| Dimension | Cook | Ternus | Parekh | Khan | Team | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Years at Apple | 28 | 25 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Deep insider bench | S11, S56 |
| Technical depth | Operations and supply chain | Hardware engineering | Finance and FP&A | Operations | Strong on hardware and cost | S11, S56 |
| Scaling record | CEO for 15 years; $3.4trn of value added | Largest product organisation | CFO through a 16% growth year | COO across the supply chain | Proven at scale | S11 |
| Capital markets | $263.2bn of buybacks in three years | Not evidenced | CFO since 2025 | Not evidenced | Adequate | S11, S5 |
| Regulatory and policy | Testified through the antitrust era | Not evidenced | Not evidenced | Not evidenced | Thin | S11 |
| Prior exits or founder roles | None disclosed | None disclosed | None disclosed | None disclosed | No founder experience | S11 |
| Key-person dependency | High as Executive Chair | High as new CEO | Medium | Medium | High | S11, S131 |
| Retention risk | Low; retirement vesting in place | Low; first-year CEO | Medium | Medium | Medium-high | S11, S131 |

What public records confirm is narrow and clean: titles, dates, pay, the $59m target, the 2,162% cumulative TSR under Cook and the 92% say-on-pay. What they contradict or cannot settle is larger — no degrees for six of seven executives, no pay or ownership for Federighi, Cue, Srouji or Joswiak because they are not Section 16 filers, no disclosed outcome to the Srouji report, and no named AI owner. For a people-dependent thesis that is a real information discount. Diligence should verify Ternus's non-hardware operating scope and any retention award, the Srouji title and succession, the 2026 awards to non-NEO SVPs, and who signs off the AI roadmap and budget. ### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, the highest Apple has reported. Part of that is structural: services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue. Part is not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 percentage points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to those refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average, Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%, and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The 30 July 2026 release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); nine-month products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9% a year earlier on mix and refunds, while memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and Apple's 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off the trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of the $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real; the 2026 step-up is partly working capital

Nine-month operating cash flow rose 43.1% to $116,996M while net income rose 20.0%, and the balance sheet shows why: receivables fell to $31,398M from $39,777M and vendor non-trade receivables to $27,509M from $33,180M, cutting days sales outstanding to 24.5 from 34.9, while inventory rose to $11,092M from $5,718M and payables fell to $64,525M from $69,860M, shortening the cash conversion cycle to −56.8 days from −71.1. Part of the record is therefore a release of working capital that reverses as memory is pre-bought, not a permanent lift in earning power. The top line is not being smoothed either: deferred revenue of $14.9B is 3.2% of trailing revenue, and only $7,260M of nine-month revenue came out of the opening deferred balance. [S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. The FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B payable within twelve months and $37.0B of future interest, commercial paper ran at a 4.19% weighted rate, leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need a question rather than a red flag: $2,604M of unrealised losses on the securities book, and intangible assets that rose to $25,417M net from $13,301M — $38,220M gross, $12,803M accumulated amortisation — without the 10-Q disaggregating what was bought. ### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. arguments.markdown:
Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years — one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit — but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit at Apple's own age-75 ceiling, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality. Apple Inc. is a California corporation incorporated on 1977-01-03, listed on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars. At 2026-01-02 it had 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding against 50,400,000,000 authorised, all of a single class of $0.00001 par common stock with one vote per share. There is no dual-class structure, no VIE, no nominee shareholder and no contractual control chain — verified in the balance sheet and the 2026 proxy, not assumed. Float is effectively the whole company: directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares, or 0.06%, leaving 99.94%. Vanguard (9.63%) and BlackRock (7.10%) are the only disclosed 5% holders — and BlackRock's figure rests on a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the 2026 register is partly unknown. [S11]

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Share classes and votes | 1 class, 1 vote; 50.4bn authorised; 14.70bn outstanding | Alphabet issues Class C alongside voting shares | good | S5, S11, S125 |
| Free float | 99.94% (insiders 9,079,765 shares) | No strategic or state holder | good | S11 |
| Board independence | 7 of 8 directors; 7 of 9 from 2026-09-01 | Majority independent | warn | S11, S56 |
| Independent director tenure | 12.0-year average; longest 26 years | Apple's age-75 re-election guideline | warn | S11 |
| Capital returned vs free cash flow | $106.1bn vs $98.8bn (107%), FY2025 | 100% of free cash flow | warn | S5 |
| Effective tax rate | 15.6% FY2025 vs 24.1% FY2024 | Prior year | warn | S5 |
| iPhone share of revenue | 53.9% in 9M FY2026 vs 51.2% in 9M FY2025 | Prior year | warn | S17 |
:::

### The entity map is simple; the profit map was not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Inc. | California, US | Corporation (registrant) | Group parent; designs, sells, holds IP | 100% of group | No controlling holder | S5, S11 |
| Apple Operations International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Non-US holding and operations | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Operations Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Irish operations | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Distribution International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Non-US distribution | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Asia Ltd | Hong Kong | Limited company | Regional sales and procurement | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Braeburn Capital, Inc. | Nevada, US | Corporation | Treasury vehicle; function not disclosed | 100% | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Insurance Company, Inc. | Arizona, US | Corporation | Captive insurance; function not disclosed | 100% | Apple Inc. | S5 |

Every listed subsidiary is wholly owned; Exhibit 21 omits entities that are not significant in aggregate, so no complete group list is public, and the 10-K does not say which two Irish subsidiaries held the branches at issue. The structure that mattered economically was profit allocation, not ownership: Irish branches operated under tax opinions issued in 1991 and 2007, which the Commission treated as state aid on 2016-08-30. The General Court annulled that decision on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice set the annulment aside on 2024-09-10, and Apple booked a one-time $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 — $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit. Irish law had already closed the opinions from January 2015. Two consequences follow: the tax rate is now policy-driven rather than engineered, at 24.1% in FY2024 and 15.6% in FY2025 with no filing supporting a return to the pre-2015 structure; and the entity map carries no enforceability premium, because the legal risk attached to it is regulatory rather than structural — a materially better position than a contractually controlled China VIE. [S5]

### Business model: one platform, one rent, one budget owner

Apple sells integrated hardware to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, then monetises the installed base through Services. FY2025 net sales were $416,161m, split $307,003m products and $109,158m services, with 40% direct and 60% indirect distribution. The end user is usually the buyer, but the budget owner for the highest-margin line is the developer and the subscriber: Services earned a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products. Growth comes from installed-base expansion and price/mix, not unit share — Apple states it holds a minority share of global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 iPhone was 53.9% of revenue against 51.2% a year earlier and Services 25.2%, so concentration is rising again rather than falling. [S5, S17]

### Governance: senior, stable, slow to refresh

Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus the CEO. Independent tenure averages 12.0 years — Levinson 26 years and chair since 2000, Jung 18, Sugar 16, Wagner 12, Lozano and Gorsky 5, Austin 2 — and two of the seven (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75. Committees are conventional and fully independent: Audit under Sugar (nine meetings in 2025), People and Compensation under Jung, Nominating under Wagner; 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025. From 2026-09-01 the structure shifts in a way that matters: Ternus joins as CEO and Cook becomes Executive Chair, taking non-independent directors to two of nine (77.8%) and replacing an independent chair with a lead independent director. [S11, S56]

### A clean structure is not a clean earnings record

The forensic problem is optical, not legal. FY2025 returned $106.1bn — $90.7bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends — against free cash flow of $98.8bn, or 107% of it, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%. Diluted shares fell 6.9%, from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026, and $263.2bn of buybacks over three years bought the arithmetic. That is how a mature hardware company reports high-teens EPS growth; it is also what stops working the year the buyback slows. Counter-evidence is genuine: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% and gross margin reached 50.1%, so FY2026 is not an optical year; no audited FY2026 accounts had been filed on 2026-10-31. [S5, S17]

### Where the judgement breaks, and what to settle

Three events would change the call: a structural remedy in the DOJ monopolisation suit or the DMA Article 6(4) file that reaches commission economics would compress the 75.4% services margin; a board that keeps the executive-chair arrangement past 2027 would entrench a post-CEO chair; and a buyback slowdown would expose the underlying operating growth rate. Confidence is high on identity, ownership and capital-return facts and medium on the board's appetite for refresh, because its own age guideline is already being waived for two members. Diligence should settle whether that waiver was formal and who chairs the board after 2027; whether BlackRock's stake has moved since 2023; what share of Services revenue depends on US third-party payment rules; and the FY2026 buyback pace under the $100bn authorisation of 2025-05-01. [S11, S5]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,993 characters)
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while payments for property, plant and equipment fell, as the metrics show. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up of that size with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro process node | 2nm (A19: 3nm) | Apple launch specification | S113, S112 |
| Siri AI availability | Beta, English, from 2026-09-14 | Apple release | S113 |
| Assistant model scale | 1.2tn parameters, reported | Press reports, unconfirmed | S122 |
| R&D, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $34.04bn, +33% | 10-Q | S6 |
| Capex, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $6.80bn (prior year $9.47bn) | 10-Q cash-flow statement | S6 |
| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures fully confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, which is the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, the personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb the cost of frontier training. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android and can price the licence at renewal, and Apple's own research output, while still credible, now sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. [S111]

| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation that is rebuilt while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, and they give owners a reason to upgrade and a reason not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside the Wearables line and has no confirmed successor, which makes it a research option rather than a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. Nominees for Election
The matrix on the following page highlights
the mix of key skills and experiences of the nominees that, among other factors, led the Board and the Nominating Committee to
recommend these nominees for election to the Board. The matrix is intended to depict notable areas of focus for each director based
on the current composition of the Board, and not having a mark does not mean that a particular director does not possess that qualification
or skill. Nominees have developed competencies in these skills through education, direct experience, and oversight responsibilities.
The Nominating Committee assesses the directors’ mix of skills on an annual basis. Additional biographical information on each
nominee is set out starting on page 27.

Core
Leadership
Experience serving in a significant leadership position, including as a chief executive officer, chief financial officer, or other senior leadership role, equips directors with valuable insight into organizational behavior and processes and a deep understanding of the various aspects of modern organizations, including strategic planning, financial reporting, compliance, values, and culture.
Corporate Governance
Experience on public company boards promotes an understanding of the dynamics and operation of a corporate board and its relationship with the chief executive officer and other senior management, as well as deep knowledge of corporate governance practices and policies and an appreciation of how they can impact Apple.
Risk Management
Experience identifying, managing, or mitigating risks develops a director’s ability to effectively oversee Apple’s risk management.
Financial
Knowledge of financial markets, financing, and financial reporting processes helps our directors understand and oversee our financial position, results of operations, and related financial reporting, as well as our broader financing activities and capital structure.
Strategic
People and Culture
Because Apple operates in a competitive talent market, directors with experience managing people and teams, including recruitment, retention, development, compensation, and incentivization of key talent, provide strategic value in overseeing these areas and in determining compensation for our CEO and other senior leaders.
Global Business and Operations
Experience in global business and operations, including exposure to global business cultures, consumer preferences, and economic, regulatory, and political conditions, helps directors oversee Apple’s global footprint and complex supply chain.
Innovation and Technology
Directors with an understanding of innovation and technology, through experience in technology-related businesses or driving scientific innovation, are strategically equipped to oversee Apple’s innovation-focused product and services roadmap.
Brand and Marketing
Experience with the marketing and branding of products, building brand awareness, and enhancing corporate reputation can help directors successfully guide and advise management and oversee related efforts.
Privacy and Security
At Apple, we believe privacy is a fundamental human right. Directors with experience in information security, data privacy, and cybersecurity are uniquely qualified to oversee our product and services roadmap, as well as privacy and cybersecurity risks.
Public Policy and Government
Experience in government relations, regulatory matters, or regulated industries provides a valuable perspective as Apple operates in an increasingly regulated global environment.
Environment and Climate
At Apple, we believe business can and should be a force for good. Directors with experience leading efforts to mitigate environmental impacts are well qualified to oversee our environmental programs and product development.

Art Levinson
Chair of the Board
Director since 2000
People and Compensation Committee
Key Skills and Qualifications
Art Levinson brings to the Board executive leadership experience, including
through his service as a chairman and chief executive officer of a large international public company, along with extensive
financial expertise and brand marketing experience. Through his experiences at biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies,
he also brings significant expertise in the health sector and technology and innovation.
Career Highlights
Dr. Levinson, 75, has served as the Chief Executive Officer of Calico, a company
focused on health, aging, and well-being, since September 2013.
Dr. Levinson previously served as Chief Executive Officer of Genentech,
Inc., a medical drug developer, from July 1995 to April 2009, and served as Genentech’s Chairman from September
1999 to September 2014.
Dr. Levinson also serves on the Board of Directors of the Broad Institute of
MIT and Harvard and on the Board of Scientific Consultants at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
Dr. Levinson was awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, the
nation’s highest honor for achievement and leadership in advancing the fields of science and technology, and the
Biotechnology Heritage Award from the Biotechnology Industry Organization and the Chemical Heritage Foundation. Dr. Levinson
has been inducted into the Biotech Hall of Fame.
Other Public Company Boards:
None
Tim Cook
Chief Executive Officer
Director since 2011
Key Skills and Qualifications
Tim Cook brings to the Board extensive executive leadership experience in the
technology industry, including the management of worldwide operations, sales, service, and support.
Career Highlights
Mr. Cook, 65, has served as Apple’s Chief Executive Officer since
2011, having previously served as Apple’s Chief Operating Officer from October 2005.
Mr. Cook joined Apple in March 1998 and served as Executive Vice
President, Worldwide Sales and Operations from February 2002 to October 2005. From October 2000 to February
2002, Mr. Cook served as Senior Vice President, Worldwide Operations, Sales, Service and Support. From March
1998 to October 2000, Mr. Cook served as Senior Vice President, Worldwide Operations.
Mr. Cook serves on the Board of Directors of The National Football Foundation
& College Hall of Fame, Inc., the Board of Trustees of Duke University, and on the Leadership Council for
the Malala Fund, an international non-profit organization that advocates for girls’ education.
Other Public Company Boards:
Current: NIKE, Inc.

Wanda Austin brings to the Board executive leadership experience through her service
as president and chief executive officer of a large research and development organization, significant expertise in advanced technology
and innovation, experience with environment, cybersecurity, and public policy, and a global business perspective from her service
on other boards.
Career Highlights
Dr. Austin, 71, is the retired President and Chief Executive Officer of The Aerospace
Corporation, an independent, non-profit organization performing objective technical analyses and assessments for a variety of
government, civil, and commercial customers, operating the only federally funded research and development center committed exclusively
to the space enterprise. Dr. Austin served in this role from January 2008 until October 2016. Dr. Austin joined The Aerospace
Corporation in 1979, serving in various positions of increasing responsibility.
Dr. Austin is also a Member of the National Academy of Engineering and is a
co-founder of MakingSpace, Inc., a leadership and science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) consulting
firm. Dr. Austin was the Interim President of the University of Southern California from 2018 to 2019 and has served on
the American Energy Innovation Council since 2017. Dr. Austin also served on the Defense Policy Board from 2017 to 2019,
the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology from 2015 to 2017, the Defense Science Board from
2009 to 2017, and the NASA Advisory Council from 2005 to 2007 and 2014 to 2016.

European Commission State Aid Decision
On August 30, 2016, the Commission announced its decision that Ireland granted state aid to the Company by providing tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 concerning the tax allocation of profits of the Irish branches of two subsidiaries of the Company (“State Aid Decision”). The State Aid Decision ordered Ireland to calculate and recover additional taxes from the Company for the period June 2003 through December 2014. Irish legislative changes, effective as of January 2015, eliminated the application of the tax opinions from that date forward.
The Company and Ireland appealed the State Aid Decision to the General Court of the Court of Justice of the European Union (“General Court”). On July 15, 2020, the General Court annulled the State Aid Decision. On September 25, 2020, the Commission appealed the General Court’s decision to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”). On September 10, 2024, the ECJ announced that it had set aside the 2020 judgment of the General Court and confirmed the Commission’s 2016 State Aid Decision. As a result, during the fourth quarter of 2024 the Company recorded a one-time income tax charge of $ 10.2 billion, net, which represented $ 15.8 billion payable to Ireland via release of amounts held in escrow, partially offset by a U.S. foreign tax credit of $ 4.8 billion and a decrease in unrecognized tax benefits of $ 823 million.

arguments.claims: On 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down to serve as an advisor before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, leading Apple Foundation Models, ML research, and AI Safety and Evaluation; the balance of Giannandrea's organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue.

 April 20, 2026
 PRESS RELEASE
 Johny Srouji named Apple’s Chief Hardware Officer
 CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced that, effective immediately, Apple executive Johny Srouji will become chief hardware officer. Srouji, who most recently served as senior vice president of Hardware Technologies, will assume an expanded role leading Hardware Engineering, which John Ternus most recently oversaw, as well as the hardware technologies organization.
 “Johny is one of the most talented people I have ever had the privilege to work with,” said Apple CEO Tim Cook. “He has played a singular role in driving Apple’s silicon strategy, and his influence has been felt deeply not just inside the company, but across the industry. He has always led his organization with remarkable deftness and judgment, and time and again, his team has delivered breakthrough innovations that have transformed our products. We are incredibly fortunate to have him as Apple’s chief hardware officer.”
 “Johny has been an incredible partner on the executive team, and is going to be an extraordinary chief hardware officer,” said incoming Apple CEO John Ternus. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with him in our new roles.”
 Srouji has built one of the world’s strongest and most innovative teams of silicon and technology engineers, driving leading breakthroughs in custom chips and hardware technologies including Apple silicon, batteries, cameras, storage controllers, sensors, displays, cellular modems, and other critical areas across Apple’s entire product line.
 Apple’s world-class hardware engineering team turns bold ideas into beautifully integrated products people rely on every day. They create and build all of Apple’s hardware products, leading everything from product design to system engineering to reliability and durability testing. The team works closely with industrial design, hardware technologies, software engineering, and operations to deliver the world’s most innovative products.
 Srouji joined Apple in 2008 to lead development of A4, the first Apple-designed system-on-a-chip. Prior to Apple, Srouji held senior positions at Intel and IBM in the area of processor development and design. He earned both a bachelor’s and master’s degree in Computer Science from Technion, Israel’s Institute of Technology.
 About Apple
 Apple revolutionized personal technology with the introduction of the Macintosh in 1984. Today, Apple leads the world in innovation with iPhone, iPad, Mac, AirPods, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro. Apple’s six software platforms — iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, visionOS, and tvOS — provide seamless experiences across all Apple devices and empower people with breakthrough services including the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Pay, iCloud, and Apple TV+. Apple’s more than 150,000 employees are dedicated to making the best products on earth and to leaving the world better than we found it.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured, turning one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Ownership moved before the deal did: on 2025-12-01 Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation passed under software chief Craig Federighi with Amar Subramanya as vice president of AI, and John Giannandrea stepped down before retiring in spring 2026. Apple bought the part it could not ship and put the rest under the software organisation. [S111, S122, S127]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while capital spending fell. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up of that size with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A20 Pro process node | 2nm (A19: 3nm) | Apple launch specification | S113, S112 |
| Siri AI availability | Beta, English, from 2026-09-14 | Apple release | S113 |
| Assistant model scale | 1.2tn parameters, reported | Press reports, unconfirmed | S122 |
| R&D, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $34.04bn, +33% | 10-Q | S6 |
| Capex, nine months to 2026-06-27 | $6.80bn (prior year $9.47bn) | 10-Q cash-flow statement | S6 |
| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |
| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Owns TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| AI organisation | Software Engineering since 2025-12-01 | DeepMind | Own research | Own research | S127 |
| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC design, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity, App Store, 76.3% services margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite moat** | **Strong hardware, weak AI** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | Years on hardware | S113, S6 |

The replication test favours the hardware story. A funded engineering team with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge within a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed rather than built, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which questions whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a monthly alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. These deepen the installed base and add upgrade reasons; they are sold as features, not as platforms with their own economics.

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Shipping | 2026-09-18 | iPhone $54.25bn in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by model | December 2026 mix | S113, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Shipping | Announced 2026-09-09 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Durability and returns | S114 |
| Services | Shipping | Ongoing | $91.73bn in nine months, +14% | 76.3% | DMA compliance | S6 |
| Wearables and Vision Pro | Shipping | Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3 in FY2025 | Not separately disclosed | Not disclosed | Health-feature adoption | S5, S124 |

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline, leaving Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking; the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. No individual patent number is cited because none could be verified against a USPTO record; freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where verification matters most. [S117]

| Patent or portfolio | Area | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. utility grants, 2025 | Silicon, RF, display, health | US | — | 2,722 grants | Granted, down 12% | Breadth, no blocking family | S117 |
| Foldable hinge and display assemblies | Hinge, crease, lamination | US, CN, EU (reported) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Pending and granted, unverified | Duo durability | S114 |
| On-device inference efficiency | Routing, model compression | Not verified | — | — | Published research, no patent number | Inference cost | S52, S53 |

If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If Apple used the Gemini term as a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patents.
