Nothing on a large accrual. The other non-current liabilities increase is unexplained in the 10-Q (condensed). Could be deferred taxes/unrecognized tax benefits. It's fine to flag it as a diligence question and not over-attribute.

Now, what is the correct normalisation? I have:
- TTM other-liabilities inflow: +$14,101M
- Of which 9M FY2026: +$10,016M (other current -$4,128M; other non-current +$13,531M), after an $8.8bn deemed repatriation tax payment.
- Prior-year 9M: -$15,161M, which includes the State Aid payment (9M FY2025 cash taxes $37,332M vs provision $15,381M → $22.0bn excess, of which ~$15.8bn State Aid).
- FY2023: +$3,031M; FY2024: +$15,552M (State Aid accrual); FY2025: -$11,076M (payment).

So the "clean" run rate of the line is roughly +$3bn/yr (FY2023) and maybe +$4.7bn (FY2025 ex-State-Aid). A reasonable normalisation is ~$3bn, meaning TTM FCF should be reduced by ~$11bn → ~$125.7bn. Conversion 0.975x.

Alternatively, one could argue that since the build is in non-current liabilities (long-dated), it doesn't reverse in the next twelve months. But it is a non-cash source that flatters TTM OCF by $14bn relative to a normal $3bn.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures fully confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, which is the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research output, while still credible, now sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. [S111]

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

The agreement was confirmed on 2026-01-12 under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the team that negotiated the licence: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query would turn the AI bill into a visible services-margin item rather than an R&D line. [S111, S98]

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down to advise before retiring in spring 2026, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest of the organisation going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |
| Siri AI out of beta, with five more languages | From 2026-10 | Beta in English since 2026-09-14 | That a licensed model can be made to feel like an Apple product | S113 |
| Standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 | Spring 2027, reported | Unlaunched | A two-cycle year and 2nm volume | S112 |
| Duo durability and return data | FY2027 | Not disclosed | Whether the foldable is a franchise or a flagship experiment | S114 |
| Renewal of India production incentives | After the 2026-03-31 expiry | Unresolved in the sources reviewed | The true cost of the China hedge | S115 |
| DMA interoperability decisions and appeals | Ongoing; 56 requests by 2026-03-22 | In progress | Whether services defaults survive regulation | S119 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. [S111]

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

The agreement was confirmed on 2026-01-12 under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. [S111, S98]

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |
| Siri AI out of beta, with five more languages | From 2026-10 | Beta in English since 2026-09-14 | That a licensed model can be made to feel like an Apple product | S113 |
| Standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 | Spring 2027, reported | Unlaunched | A two-cycle year and 2nm volume | S112 |
| Duo durability and return data | FY2027 | Not disclosed | Whether the foldable is a franchise or a flagship experiment | S114 |
| Renewal of India production incentives | After the 2026-03-31 expiry | Unresolved in the sources reviewed | The true cost of the China hedge | S115 |
| DMA interoperability decisions and appeals | Ongoing; 56 requests by 2026-03-22 | In progress | Whether services defaults survive regulation | S119 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. The agreement was confirmed under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. [S111, S98]

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |
| Siri AI out of beta, with five more languages | From 2026-10 | Beta in English since 2026-09-14 | That a licensed model can be made to feel like an Apple product | S113 |
| Standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 | Spring 2027, reported | Unlaunched | A two-cycle year and 2nm volume | S112 |
| Duo durability and return data | FY2027 | Not disclosed | Whether the foldable is a franchise or a flagship experiment | S114 |
| Renewal of India production incentives | After the 2026-03-31 expiry | Unresolved in the sources reviewed | The true cost of the China hedge | S115 |
| DMA interoperability decisions and appeals | Ongoing; 56 requests by 2026-03-22 | In progress | Whether services defaults survive regulation | S119 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation.

The structure that mattered economically was profit allocation, not ownership: Irish branches operated under tax opinions issued in 1991 and 2007, which the Commission treated as state aid on 2016-08-30. The General Court annulled that decision on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice set the annulment aside on 2024-09-10, and Apple booked a one-time $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 — $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit. Irish law had already closed the opinions from January 2015. Two consequences follow: the tax rate is now policy-driven rather than engineered, at 24.1% in FY2024 and 15.6% in FY2025 with no filing supporting a return to the pre-2015 structure; and the entity map carries no enforceability premium, because the legal risk attached to it is regulatory rather than structural — a materially better position than a contractually controlled China VIE. [S5]

### Business model: one platform, one rent, one budget owner

Apple sells integrated hardware to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, then monetises the installed base through Services. FY2025 net sales were $416,161m, split $307,003m products and $109,158m services, with 40% direct and 60% indirect distribution. The end user is usually the buyer, but the budget owner for the highest-margin line is the developer and the subscriber: Services earned a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products. Growth comes from installed-base expansion and price/mix, not unit share — Apple states it holds a minority share of global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 iPhone was 53.9% of revenue against 51.2% a year earlier and Services 25.2%, so concentration is rising again rather than falling. [S5, S17]

### Governance: senior, stable, slow to refresh

Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus the CEO. Independent tenure averages 12.0 years — Levinson 26 years and chair since 2000, Jung 18, Sugar 16, Wagner 12, Lozano and Gorsky 5, Austin 2 — and two of the seven (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75. Committees are conventional and fully independent: Audit under Sugar (nine meetings in 2025), People and Compensation under Jung, Nominating under Wagner; 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025. From 2026-09-01 the structure shifts in a way that matters: Ternus joins as CEO and Cook becomes Executive Chair, taking non-independent directors to two of nine (77.8%) and replacing an independent chair with a lead independent director. [S11, S56]

### A clean structure is not a clean earnings record

The forensic problem is optical, not legal. FY2025 returned $106.1bn — $90.7bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends — against free cash flow of $98.8bn, or 107% of it, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%. Diluted shares fell 6.9%, from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026, and $263.2bn of buybacks over three years bought the arithmetic. That is how a mature hardware company reports high-teens EPS growth; it is also what stops working the year the buyback slows. Counter-evidence is genuine: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% and gross margin reached 50.1%, so FY2026 is not an optical year; no audited FY2026 accounts had been filed on 2026-10-31. [S5, S17]

### Where the judgement breaks, and what to settle

Three events would change the call: a structural remedy in the DOJ monopolisation suit or the DMA Article 6(4) file that reaches commission economics would compress the 75.4% services margin; a board that keeps the executive-chair arrangement past 2027 would entrench a post-CEO chair; and a buyback slowdown would expose the underlying operating growth rate. Confidence is high on identity, ownership and capital-return facts and medium on the board's appetite for refresh, because its own age guideline is already being waived for two members. Diligence should settle whether that waiver was formal and who chairs the board after 2027; whether BlackRock's stake has moved since 2023; what share of Services revenue depends on US third-party payment rules; and the FY2026 buyback pace under the $100bn authorisation of 2025-05-01. [S11, S5]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 3 by Company Analyst, 8,205 characters)
The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era — hardware, operations, finance — and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation, the chip chief was reported to be considering leaving, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition. Apple is run by career insiders — Cook has been at the company since March 1998 (28 years), Ternus since 2001 (25 years), and the 2025 CFO and COO appointments were internal promotions. Ternus's hardware organisation and the silicon team invent; Cook built worldwide sales before 2005 and O'Brien runs retail; Cue's organisation holds the App Store rent; Parekh allocates the capital, $106.1bn returned in FY2025; Federighi's software organisation took over AI on 2025-12-01. Pay is where the team is most unusual. Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m — a $3m salary unchanged since 2016, a $6m target cash award and a $50m equity award, 75% performance-based — against Satya Nadella's $96.5m reported for Microsoft's fiscal 2025 and Sundar Pichai's $10.9m reported for 2025, though Pichai's 2026 target equity award is $210m and a 1,348,607-share 2022 award vested to him in February 2026. Apple's other named executives each target about $23m: $1m salary, a 200% cash target and $20m of equity. There are no employment contracts, no change-of-control payments and time-based RSUs vest over roughly four and a half years, so retention runs through unvested stock rather than contractual protection — cheap for shareholders and defensible at 92% say-on-pay, but exposed where pay is not disclosed at all. [S11, S129, S125]

::: evidence
**The AI organisation has been rebuilt around software, but no filing names an owner of the AI P&L.**
On 2025-12-01 Apple announced that John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, taking Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety, while the rest of the organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. The reporting on silicon is the sharpest counter-evidence to a continuity story. Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and the 36.8% products gross margin, so the loss of its architect would threaten a roadmap competitors cannot copy quickly. Promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be the retention move that keeps that bench together — or it may not, and the filings will not say which. [S131, S5]

The 2024-26 turnover cluster is the part a reference check should attack. Within about eighteen months Apple changed CFO (2025-01-01), COO (2025), general counsel (2026-03-01, with Adams retained for government affairs until late 2026), AI leadership (2025-12-01), environment leadership (announced 2025-12-04) and CEO (2026-09-01). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,974 characters)
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured, turning one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Ownership moved first: on 2025-12-01 Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation passed under software chief Craig Federighi with Amar Subramanya as VP of AI, as John Giannandrea stepped down ahead of retirement. Apple bought the part it could not ship and reorganised the rest. [S111, S122, S127]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while capital spending fell. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

| Services gross margin, nine months | 76.3% | 10-Q | S6 |
| U.S. patent grants, 2025 | 2,722, down 12% | IFI CLAIMS | S117 |

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. [S112]

| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |

| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC design, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |
| OS and installed-base switching costs | 9 | Continuity, App Store, 76.3% services margin | 7+ years | S6 |
| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite moat** | **Strong hardware, weak AI** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | Years on hardware | S113, S6 |

The replication test favours the hardware story. A funded engineering team with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge within a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed rather than built, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which questions whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a monthly alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. These deepen the installed base and add upgrade reasons; they are sold as features, not as platforms with their own economics.

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

U.S. grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024, a 12% decline, leaving Apple seventh in the U.S. ranking; the portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family. No individual patent number is cited because none could be verified against a USPTO record; freedom-to-operate risk sits in foldable hinges, displays and health sensing, where verification matters most. If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing Apple's integration beating standalone assistants, the AI layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after the 2026-11-02 results would confirm the current reading. If the Gemini term is a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patents."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,963 characters)
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. The agreement was confirmed under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. [S111, S98]

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |
| Siri AI out of beta, with five more languages | From 2026-10 | Beta in English since 2026-09-14 | That a licensed model can be made to feel like an Apple product | S113 |
| Standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 | Spring 2027, reported | Unlaunched | A two-cycle year and 2nm volume | S112 |
| Duo durability and return data | FY2027 | Not disclosed | Whether the foldable is a franchise or a flagship experiment | S114 |
| Renewal of India production incentives | After the 2026-03-31 expiry | Unresolved in the sources reviewed | The true cost of the China hedge | S115 |
| DMA interoperability decisions and appeals | Ongoing; 56 requests by 2026-03-22 | In progress | Whether services defaults survive regulation | S119 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,744 characters)
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year, +2% YoY; Omdia 1.25B (+2%) | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7% YoY, steepest annual fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP); 2026 = $196.5B x 4/3 / $613B | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC, +1.7%; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |
| Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units, and the sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at 1.26B units and a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% a year earlier on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every geographic segment in double digits; that is genuine pricing power [S17, S87, S84]. But IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases, and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down more than 20%. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months.

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects it to ship more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a global advertising pool of $1.34T in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables are a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. Foldables and services can add; the non-phone device pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

| Region | Market size (latest dated) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Americas | Regional value not published; global $613B (2026E) | Apple +11.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; home market; 42.9% of FY2025 revenue | US tariffs (Section 232 and 301); platform antitrust | Samsung, Google, Motorola | S84, S5, S6 |
| Europe | Not published | Apple +16.1% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 26.7% of revenue | DMA take-rate cuts from 2026-10-01; GDPR | Samsung, Xiaomi, Google | S77, S6 |
| Greater China | 66M units in Q2 2026; 134M in H1 2026 | Market -4.3% in Q2 2026; H2 2026 decline could reach 20%; Apple +30.0% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 18.1% handset share versus Huawei 22.6% | Market access; local champion; data rules | Huawei, OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi, Honor | S87, S6 |
| Japan | Not published | Apple +10.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 6.9% of revenue | Yen weakness; carrier-controlled channel | Samsung, Google, Sharp | S6 |
| Rest of Asia-Pacific | Not published; emerging markets forecast down more than 20% in 2026 | Apple +19.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 8.1% of revenue; India manufacturing and retail expansion | Price sensitivity; tariffs | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, OPPO, Transsion | S84, S6 |

Geography splits the durability question, and policy is a live variable in every region [S6, S87, S77]. Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue but produced 30% growth in the first nine months of FY2026; Europe is 26.7% and grew 16%, the Americas 42.9% and 11%, Japan 6.9% and 10%, and Rest of Asia-Pacific 8.1% and 19%. The China number is the most fragile: the market fell 4.3% in Q2 2026, Apple's 18.1% share trailed Huawei's 22.6%, and the top six vendors hold 96%. The EU's DMA terms cut the commission on externally distributed digital transactions to 5% from 1 October 2026. US tariffs moved twice in 2026: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026 and Section 301 duties were imposed since, while the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs on Apple products on 14 January 2026. Demand is organic consumer replacement, not policy-created: China's subsidies faded in 2026 and India's incentives are supply-side manufacturing support. The budget owner is the consumer or carrier financing plan; the procurement cycle follows the annual September launch; willingness to pay is being tested by the 27.6% ASP increase. What would change the conclusion: services growth above 15% with user growth, a foldable cycle adding IDC's $45.7B category value, or China stabilising after H2 2026. Confidence is high on 2026 data and low on 2027-2030 regional sizing, because regional market values are paywalled and Apple does not disclose units; the open questions are what share of iPhone growth is units versus price, whether services growth is users or price, how much China demand was pulled forward, and how much memory cost Apple can pass through in FY2027.

::: evidence
**Apple's markets are growing in dollars while shrinking in units, so its growth is price- and share-led, not market-led.**

The global pool is $613B of smartphone value in 2026 against just over 1.0B units, with a 27.6% ASP increase doing the work volume used to do (IDC, S84). Premium concentration (29% of units) and Apple's 65% share of it explain why Apple captures 36-43% of value on 20-24% of units (Counterpoint, S94; Apple filings, S5, S6). Foldables ($45.7B of category value by 2027) and services ($120.5B TTM at 76.0% gross margin) are the only pools large enough to move group growth; wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030 (IDC, S85).
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,871 characters)
Apple is winning the competition for profit and price while ceding unit share in China: it holds 65% of premium phone units and a 40% product gross margin, but Huawei is taking premium share in a shrinking China market and regulation is capping the services take rate, so its competitive position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and weakening at the margin in China. Apple's own 10-K concedes a minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables and says some of its markets have experienced little or no growth; the useful analysis is therefore per product, because the iPhone, Mac, wearables and services each face a different rival set [S5].

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Apple | Weaknesses vs Apple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung | Galaxy S26, Z Fold 7 | Android; Exynos 2600 or Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 | Unrestricted | Flagship parity; foldable incumbent | Premium | 19% global 2025; 23% in Q3 2026 | Foldable head start; carrier breadth | MX division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 | S91, S92, S120 |
| Huawei | Mate and Pura; HarmonyOS | Kirin silicon; HarmonyOS | China scale; US export restrictions | Premium camera and battery | Premium | 22.6% China in Q2 2026 | Domestic supply chain; holds prices | Little share outside China | S87, S86 |
| Xiaomi | Xiaomi 17 series | Android; Snapdragon | Unrestricted | Value flagship | Mid-premium | 11.5% global in Q2 2026 | Price-performance; AIoT and EV ecosystem | 8.5% handset gross margin; profit -42.6% | S90 |
| Google | Pixel 11 | Android; Tensor; Gemini | Unrestricted | AI-first software | Premium | Not disclosed | Gemini integration; search distribution | Small hardware distribution | S15, S50 |
| Lenovo, HP, Dell | PC lines | Windows on x86 | Unrestricted | Enterprise and channel strength | $600-2,000 | 24.4%, 19.1%, 13.6% in Q2 2026 | Enterprise channel; price tiers | No in-house OS-silicon integration | S95 |
| Spotify | Music streaming and app distribution | App; DMA alternative distribution | EU DMA beneficiary | 300M paying subscribers | Subscription | Twice Apple Music's subscriber base | Cross-platform; podcasts | No hardware bundle | S93, S77 |
| Alphabet | Search, YouTube, Play | Android; Gemini | Antitrust scrutiny | Advertising scale | Ad-funded | $471B TTM revenue | Search and advertising scale | AI capex dilution | S15, S50 |
| Status quo | Longer device life, refurbished | None | None | Adequate for most users | Zero | Not disclosed | Free and familiar | No new capability | S87 |

Huawei is the most dangerous competitor to Apple's profit pool, and Samsung is the most dangerous to its unit position [S87, S86, S91, S92, S84]. Huawei led China with 22.6% in Q2 2026 against Apple's 18.1%, after its highest share since Q4 2020 in the prior quarter, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026; Huawei funds that push with CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of CNY880.9B of 2025 revenue. Samsung is broader, with 19% global share in 2025 and 23% in Q3 2026, a foldable incumbent and the only rival with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth, so it cannot buy share indefinitely. Huawei takes price and profit; Samsung takes volume and loses money doing it.

Share trends from 2025 to 2026 show Apple gaining value and premium ground while its unit share moves sideways [S92, S120, S94, S84, S17]. Apple led 2025 with 20% of global units and 10% growth and Samsung followed at 19%; in Q3 2026 Samsung held 23% to Apple's 22% as the market fell 20%. The premium layer is where Apple's position improves: its 65% of $600-plus units in H1 2026 came with 9% growth, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% share in 2026. Pricing power shows in the gross margin, 40.1% on products in Q3 FY2026 versus 34.5% a year earlier, with iPhone revenue up 22% in nine months. The caveat is that the price increase is imposed by a memory shock rather than earned by innovation alone: NAND and DRAM costs are up more than 300% year over year, and Apple's signalling of further rises pulled Chinese demand forward.

China is the one region where the competitive position is deteriorating on share even as revenue rises [S87, S6, S86]. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in the first nine months of FY2026, but that came against a market down 4.2% in H1 2026 and with Apple at 18.1% share to Huawei's 22.6%; Huawei grew 19.4% and Apple 24.4% in Q2 2026, both by holding prices while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi raised theirs and lost 9.7%, 11.4% and 21.7% respectively. The top six vendors hold 96% of the market, so the fight is for premium share inside a contracting pool, and Huawei's HarmonyOS scale gives it a domestic platform Apple cannot match on localisation. Apple's revenue growth is a price-hold plus pull-forward effect, not evidence that it has regained structural leadership in China.

Regulation is now a competitive force that transfers rent from Apple to its rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. The practical effect is to lower switching costs out of the App Store in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and to hand Spotify, Epic and alternative storefronts a distribution channel on iOS; Spotify already has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. The DMA is the template, and its spread to other jurisdictions is the regulatory risk to monitor.

| Product | Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche player | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (premium) | Leader in premium value, second in units | Apple | Samsung | Google Pixel | Huawei in China; foldables | S94, S87 |
| Mac | Share gainer from a small base | Lenovo by units | Apple | HP and Dell premium tiers | Snapdragon Windows PCs | S95 |
| Wearables | Leader by value, third by units | Xiaomi by units, Apple by value | Huawei | Oura in rings, Meta in glasses | AI glasses | S85 |
| Services (apps and advertising) | Challenger in advertising, leader in app distribution | Alphabet in advertising | Apple in app distribution | Spotify in music | DMA-enabled alternative stores | S15, S93, S77 |

The status quo is a formidable competitor: consumers are holding devices longer, IDC expects China's recovery only in 2028-2029 and forecasts a smaller, more concentrated market after the memory crisis, and the cheapest segment is disappearing [S87, S84, S17, S93]. Pipeline threats are Apple's own foldable in H2 2026, Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion, Google's Gemini-integrated Pixel and AI agents that could move the assistant layer off the operating system. Apple's wedge is the integration of silicon, OS and an installed base that reached an all-time high in Q3 FY2026, which lets it earn 40% product gross margins while rivals earn single digits or lose money; that wedge supports profit-share gains but not unit-share gains. The competitive position therefore supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated ceiling on services, not a share-gain growth story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China and medium on services because take rates are in flux. Diligence questions: how much of the premium gain is price inflation, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS, and whether Apple's foldable holds 40% of the category beyond 2027.

| Weaknesses | 18.1% China share behind Huawei; 15.5% wearables unit share; no advertising scale; revenue concentrated in one product | S87, S85, S5 |

**Apple's competitive advantage is profit capture, not unit share.**

Apple holds 20% of phone units but 65% of premium units and 36-43% of market value (Counterpoint, S94; IDC, S84). Its 40.1% product gross margin compares with Xiaomi's 8.5% handset margin and a loss at Samsung's mobile division (S17, S90, S91). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 7,773 characters)
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,072B, or 39.3x trailing EPS of $8.72; the price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::"}],"isError":false}
