{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 2 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,996 characters)
Apple's regulatory exposure, not its ESG record, is what can change a long-only case. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn and Services revenue $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin, so App Store commissions and the Google default-search payment sit inside the profit pool carrying the premium multiple [S5]. Fines are not the mechanism; remedies and fee schedules are. Bear case: a 10-15% operating-income tail from losing or repricing search placement and a structurally lower App Store take rate over 2026-2028. The mechanism is that a dollar of commission or default rent carries almost no marginal cost, so losing it hits operating income faster than revenue.

### The EU fine is small; the fee schedule is not

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation, 0.1% of FY2025 net sales. The material part is the fee schedule: from 2026-10-01 Apple's unified EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase (down from 30%), 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and 5% on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web. Apple says the terms resolve its disagreements with the Commission; EU developer groups call them unacceptable, so the settlement is contested. The General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08, with an interoperability ruling unlikely before late 2027. Apple does not disclose EU App Store revenue; at a 75.4% Services margin, each $1bn of commission lost equals $0.75bn of gross profit. The consequence is a permanently lower take rate on the most profitable services [S78, S77, S82, S5].

### The $20 billion Google payment is the largest policy-sensitive cash flow

Apple does not disclose the Google default-search payment, but the US v. Google trial record put it at $20bn in 2022, or 36% of Google's Safari search revenue: a litigated estimate, not a company disclosure. That is 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue and, if near-pure margin, 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's final judgment of 2025-12-05 preserved non-exclusive payments, banned exclusivity and capped default deals at 12 months; the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026 seeking a payment ban. A negotiated lower rate is more likely than zero, but either compresses Services growth, and an appellate decision is likely in 2027. The payment is worth more as Apple profit than as Google cost, which points to a lower rate rather than zero [S80, S76, S5].

### US courts are already narrowing the App Store take rate

On 2025-12-11 the Ninth Circuit affirmed that Apple willfully violated the Epic injunction, upheld the steering remedy and limited any fee on linked transactions to Apple's costs; the Supreme Court granted certiorari on 2026-06-30. Separately, the DOJ and 16 states and DC have sued Apple for monopolization in "performance smartphones" and "smartphones" since 2024-03-21, seeking equitable relief, not damages; the case is in pre-trial litigation with no trial date in Apple's 2026 filings. A federal appellate court finding willful violation raises the odds of stricter remedies and weakens management's "substantial defenses" posture. US courts can reset App Store economics before the DOJ case reaches trial [S79, S81, S6].

### Tariffs have flipped from cost to refund, not to a new margin level

Q3 FY2026 revenue was $109.4bn and gross margin 50.1%, including 2 percentage points from tariff refunds; EPS of $2.02 included $0.11 from refunds. The underlying margin is 48.1%, against 46.9% for FY2025, when products gross margin fell on tariff costs. The refund follows the Supreme Court's 2026-02-20 ruling striking down certain IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 semiconductor initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products, but Section 301 duties have since been imposed and further actions remain possible. For valuation, normalise the margin rather than extrapolate the refund: underwrite 47-48%, not 50% [S17, S5, S6].

### Governance is a strength; the ESG gaps are disclosure and labour

Governance is not the discount. Apple has eight directors, three of them women (37.5%), an independent chair separate from the CEO, no dual-class stock, a $120,000 related-party review threshold, Audit Committee ownership of privacy and cybersecurity, and 92% Say-on-Pay support in 2025. The gaps are supply-chain labour and disclosure: 166,000 employees at 2025-09-27, a 10-K concession that supplier code violations "occur from time to time", and no audit metrics in the filing. Climate claims are unverified company statements. None has changed demand, so the economic read is that ESG is a tail-risk and discount-rate input, not a revenue driver [S11, S5].

{"url":"https://www.antitrustinstitute.org/work-product/aai-urges-dc-circuit-to-affirm-googles-liability-but-strengthen-remedy-in-landmark-search-monopoly-case/","title":"AAI Urges D.C. Circuit to Affirm Google’s Liability But Strengthen the Remedy in Landmark Search Monopoly Case (United States v. Google) - American Antitrust Institute","text":"On August 4, 2026, the American Antitrust Institute (AAI) filed an amicus brief in United States v. Google LLC, No. 26-5023, asking the D.C. Circuit to affirm the district court’s finding that Google unlawfully maintained its search monopoly but remand the remedial order with instructions to prohibit Google’s payment-for-default mechanism, which the district court’s liability opinion condemned but its remedy opinion left in place.
After a nine-week bench trial, the district court found that Google entered revenue-sharing arrangements with browser makers, device manufacturers, and other search access points, conditioning those payments on Google’s status as the distributor’s exclusive default search engine. The court found that these arrangements foreclosed a substantial share of the market, prevented rivals from gaining scale, and diminished rivals’ incentives to invest and innovate. It entered equitable relief that, among other things, imposed data and syndication remedies but permitted Google to continue paying for default placement. On appeal, Google argues, among other things, that its conduct was not exclusionary but rather competition on the merits, contending that plaintiffs must show that a rival would have won default placement in a counterfactual world without Google’s payments.
AAI’s brief argues that the district court committed no error in finding liability but erred in fashioning the remedy. On liability, AAI explains that Google’s proposed “but-for world” exclusionary-conduct standard—which would require plaintiffs to prove that a rival would have obtained default status absent Google’s payments—has no basis in Supreme Court or D.C. Circuit precedent and would defeat the consumer-welfare purpose of Section 2. The standard contravenes Microsoft, which declined to condition a finding of exclusionary conduct on proof that rivals would have prevailed in a counterfactual market, and it systematically warps the balance of error costs by effectively immunizing the most entrenched monopolists, whose conduct makes counterfactual reconstruction impossible. A monopolist that pays distributors out of its monopoly profits to foreclose rivals—rather than competing on the merits of its product—is engaged in precisely the conduct antitrust law is designed to prevent.
On the remedy, AAI argues that while the district court’s data and syndication remedies should be affirmed, the court erred by permitting Google to continue paying for default placement, the very bargain its liability opinion condemned. Antitrust remedial discretion, although broad, is bounded by a non-negotiable effectiveness requirement: relief must reach the whole of the violation. By preserving the payment-for-default mechanism while acknowledging that doing so “could blunt the effectiveness of the remedies imposed,” the district court allowed a consideration governing the choice among effective remedies to excuse its failure to impose one.
The brief was written by AAI Vice President Kathleen Bradish and AAI President Randy Stutz, with assistance from AAI General Counsel Mark Hegedus and AAI Senior Counsel David O. Fisher.
Read the full brief: AAI Amicus Brief in United States v. Google LLC","truncated":false}

{"url":"https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260930-13258.html","title":"AI Server Demand Sustains Memory Contract Price Increases in 4Q26, While Consumer-Side Pressure Persists, Says TrendForce","text":"Conventional DRAM contract prices are projected to grow 10–15% QoQ in 4Q26, while NAND Flash contract prices are expected to increase 15–20%
	Enterprise SSDs are the only category expected to see price growth accelerate due to strong demand from CSPs

TrendForce’s latest memory industry research reveals that DRAM suppliers continue to prioritize advanced-process capacity for high-performance server products in 4Q26, keeping the overall market undersupplied. However, the pace of contract price increases is expected to moderate, with conventional DRAM prices projected to rise 10–15% QoQ. 

Meanwhile, the NAND Flash market is seeing a divergence between accelerating AI demand and weak consumer demand, although prices are still rising across segments. Overall NAND Flash contract prices are projected to increase 15–20% QoQ.

For PC DRAM, notebook inventories are increasingly reflecting higher component costs in the fourth quarter, weighing on end-market sales. Nevertheless, PC OEMs continue to procure aggressively amid expectations that DRAM supply will remain tight in 2027, providing continued support for prices. On the supply side, DRAM suppliers have been fulfilling agreed volumes to PC OEMs and module makers every quarter throughout 2026. However, the PC DRAM supply could decline in 2027 as more capacity shifts to server applications.

In the server DRAM market, improving server CPU availability has prompted CSPs and server OEMs to increase bit procurement from suppliers to meet growing RDIMM demand for general servers supporting agentic AI workloads. Memory suppliers have increased the share of lower-capacity RDIMMs in their product mix to better address customer demand. However, constraints in component supply, packaging and testing capacity, and front-end DRAM production flexibility continue to prevent supply from fully aligning with demand. Server DRAM is therefore expected to remain undersupplied in 4Q26. On the pricing front, increases for some suppliers are expected to lag the market average due to pricing mechanisms stipulated in long-term agreements (LTAs).

For mobile DRAM, rising costs and the depletion of low-cost inventories continue to weigh on smartphone production, suppressing overall bit demand. At the same time, strong demand and higher margins in AI-related applications are prompting suppliers to continue shifting capacity toward server products, leaving mobile DRAM allocations tight. Consequently, the upward price trend remains firmly in place. However, because substantial increases were already priced in during previous quarters, growth is expected to moderate in 4Q26.

In graphics DRAM, some PC brands are reconsidering GDDR6 as a means of reducing overall BOM costs. GDDR7 demand, meanwhile, continues to be driven primarily by AI chips, with procurement momentum outperforming the PC market.
 
On the supply side, suppliers continue to scale back GDDR6 production while gradually exiting the market. GDDR7 output also remains limited as advanced-process capacity is increasingly allocated to applications such as server DRAM. These constraints are expected to keep graphics DRAM prices on an upward trajectory.

For consumer DRAM, recent incremental demand has come primarily from SSD customers, supplementing existing demand from consumer networking and TV applications. In particular, the improved outlook for QLC SSD demand has increased corresponding demand for DRAM components. However, major suppliers remain committed to production cuts, leaving the market heavily reliant on Taiwanese suppliers. Prices are therefore expected to continue rising—albeit at a slower pace.

Turning to client SSDs, PC OEMs can rely on finished-goods inventories and channel stock built during the first half of the year to support fourth-quarter shipments, limiting procurement largely to components in short supply. PC brands are also reducing SSD capacities in mainstream models to lower BOM costs, resulting in declines in both procurement volumes and average capacity per device. With buyers holding sufficient inventories and purchasing requirements remaining limited, NAND Flash suppliers have adopted a more flexible pricing stance, restraining the magnitude of price increases.

The enterprise SSD market presents a markedly different picture. Bit demand for enterprise SSDs is projected to grow by more than 80% YoY in 2026 as CSPs continue to expand AI inference infrastructure. Demand is also shifting from LLM training toward actual AI deployment. Additionally, the large-scale rollout of agentic AI is driving exponential growth in data volumes for real-time retrieval and caching, while QLC penetration in vector databases continues to rise. 

In response, suppliers are expanding QLC capacity and the availability of high-capacity products, while PCIe 6.0 adoption is ramping alongside next-generation AI server platforms. However, most incremental supply has already been committed, leaving little available on the open market. Enterprise SSD price growth is therefore expected to accelerate in 4Q26, making it the only memory product category to see a larger increase than in the previous quarter.

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue; products are not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to them. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

The 30 July 2026 release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9% a year earlier, while memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and the 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off the trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of the $8.72.

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M: non-cash add-backs added $1,956M more and working capital $16,366M more. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against -$15,161M a year earlier, a $25,177M swing concentrated in other non-current liabilities, up to $55,080M from $41,549M; without that line working capital was an $8,811M drag. ### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. {"url":"https://www.theantitrustattorney.com/apples-gemini-siri-deal-is-the-next-microsoft-antitrust-case-not-the-next-app-store-fight/","title":"Apple’s Gemini-Siri Deal Is the Next Microsoft Antitrust Case, Not the Next App Store Fight","text":"The Gate to the Kingdom May Be Closing for Good: Apple Puts Google Inside Siri
Author: Luis Blanquez
On January 12, 2026, Apple and Google announced a multi-year deal—reported at roughly $1 billion a year—under which a custom Google Gemini model will run as the backend “brain” of the rebuilt Siri and the next generation of Apple Intelligence. Apple plans to unveil the new assistant at WWDC on June 8, 2026, and ship it with iOS 27 in September. Apple’s own on-device Foundation Models will handle simpler, privacy-sensitive tasks. Heavier queries will route to Gemini on Apple’s private cloud. Siri’s cognitive core will no longer be Apple’s. It will be Google’s.
Meanwhile, ChatGPT—the model Apple spent 18 months positioning as the future of iPhone AI, and the one still at the center of the xAI antitrust lawsuit pending in the Northern District of Texas—continues to sit where it has always sat: in a separate, opt-in, off-by-default layer that users have to turn on themselves. In iOS 27, Apple will expand that layer into an “Extensions” framework that lets users pick from Claude, Grok, Copilot, Perplexity, and a user-selectable Gemini chatbot app alongside ChatGPT.
On the surface, the Gemini deal looks like Apple conceding ground—admitting it cannot build a frontier AI model of its own and paying Google to fill the gap. It is not. Apple does not fear a better chatbot. It fears losing the user to one. By routing Siri’s cognition through a supplier Apple controls contractually, it keeps the interface, the invocation, the defaults, the billing, and the brand—everything that makes an operating system a platform—while outsourcing the only layer it never wanted to own: the AI model. It is classic Apple, but this time with Google as an ally instead of a threat.
Where The xAI Case Stands
Elon Musk’s X Corp. and xAI sued Apple and OpenAI on August 25, 2025, in the Northern District of Texas.
The theory of harm has two layers. First, ChatGPT’s integration into iOS, iPadOS, and macOS—announced in June 2024—delivers billions of iPhone-originated prompts to a single model. Second, the complaint alleges that Apple deprioritized rival chatbots in App Store rankings, making it harder for Grok and others to reach users even outside the system layer.
In late September 2025, Apple and OpenAI moved to dismiss. Apple argued the deal is “expressly not exclusive.” OpenAI called the suit part of a “lawfare” campaign. Judge Mark T. Pittman denied both motions on November 13, 2025, in a one-page order signaling the case is “more well-suited for adjudication through a motion(s) for summary judgment.” Discovery opened on October 10, 2025, and closes on May 22, 2026.
Two rulings tell us the real story.
The source-code ruling: Courts don’t want to become engineers, they just want evidence of platform foreclosure
On January 22, 2026, Magistrate Judge Hal R. Ray Jr. denied X’s motion to compel OpenAI to produce ChatGPT’s source code. X argued it needed the code to rebut any defense of lack of feasibility, to establish whether Apple could integrate Grok into the Apple iOS, and whether it would be feasible to integrate multiple AI products from various providers on the iPhone. The court disagreed on both relevance and proportionality.
On relevance, the order is blunt: “At this stage, it is unclear how the source code is relevant to whether Apple unlawfully excluded Grok from its products and conspired with the other defendants to create a monopoly.” On proportionality, the court noted that OpenAI had already produced API documentation and offered to stipulate that neither side would rely on proprietary source code. X refused the compromise. The court refused the production.
For a platform-exclusion case, that ruling is not a setback. It is a roadmap. Courts do not want plaintiffs dissecting competitor IP to infer what could have happened. They want direct evidence of platform misconduct—integration terms, routing logic, default settings, App Store treatment. That is where antitrust liability lives in a case like this. The court said so in plain terms, and future plaintiffs should take the hint.
The April 2026 motion to compel: Valuation and training data
X filed a second motion to compel on April 10, 2026, this one aimed squarely at OpenAI’s document production. The motion accuses OpenAI of having “persistently evaded its discovery obligations,” noting that OpenAI had produced 7,475 documents compared with X’s 32,116. The requested materials include valuation studies, financial projections through 2030, ChatGPT usage by country, and documents about OpenAI’s use of X data to train its models.
The valuation request is the one to watch. X tells the court that OpenAI’s valuation grew by more than $500 billion in the past year—from $300 billion at the end of March 2025. X argues the jump “does not make sense unless OpenAI and its investors understand that ChatGPT’s exclusive deal with Apple is cementing OpenAI’s dominance.” That is a causation theory built on investor behavior, not technology.
The training-data request matters for a different reason. OpenAI has defended the case in part by arguing that Grok’s foreclosure from iPhone-originated prompts is insubstantial because xAI has asymmetrical access to X data. X’s response is direct: if OpenAI also trains on X data, the asymmetry disappears. That question—who gets to learn from where—sits at the center of every theory of harm in generative AI.
Both motions, taken together, ask the court to analyze platform foreclosure through evidence: deal terms, integration architecture, valuation impact, data flows. None of it is specific to OpenAI nor depends on getting inside OpenAI’s code.
That same framework applies to Gemini.
Gemini Isn’t Apple’s Competitor. It’s Apple’s Supplier.
Apple’s decision to build Siri on Gemini at the backend, while offering third-party chatbots through Extensions on top, reshapes the competitive picture more than any filing in Texas has.
Apple did not retreat

European Commission State Aid Decision
On August 30, 2016, the Commission announced its decision that Ireland granted state aid to the Company by providing tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 concerning the tax allocation of profits of the Irish branches of two subsidiaries of the Company (“State Aid Decision”). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 3 by Valuation Analyst, 8,917 characters)
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and net buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.5x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. As the table shows, Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so the exit is never closed and market impact is measured in basis points. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on a $5,029.6bn market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2026E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.0% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return, multiple unchanged | 9.9% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return, multiple reverts to 31.0x | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 39.5x it buys a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar spent, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is not a scandal; it is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 39.5x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.5% of the price, or 7.7% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than it was when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS continuous auction | $13.8bn a day; exit complete in days | Any trading day | Near-certain, and the default route | S7 |
| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

| Precedent realisation | Year | Value | Multiple at the time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repurchases, FY2022 | 2022 | $89.4bn | 24.6x year-end P/E | S2, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2023 | 2023 | $77.6bn | 27.9x | S3, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2024 | 2024 | $94.9bn | 37.5x | S4, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2025 | 2025 | $90.7bn | 34.2x | S5, S7 |
| Observed drawdown, twelve months to 2026-10-30 | 2026 | $243.42 low | 29.4% below $344.63 | S7 |

The precedents are all capital returns, because that is the only exit a company of this size has ever offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 20-30% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 39.5x makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

| Entry price | Exit at 27x | Exit at 31x | Exit at 34x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 (2026-10-30) | -3.2% | 1.3% | 4.5% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $300 | 1.4% | 6.1% | 9.4% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $240 | 9.2% | 14.3% | 17.9% | S6, S7, S97 |

The sell discipline follows from that table, which assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12% rather than the 9.9% consensus assumes for iPhone revenue. The conditions that would make me raise the entry price are specific and observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The conditions that force a sale are equally specific: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The bear case sets the drawdown to expect, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $242: a reversion to Apple's 2022 multiple of 24.6x on FY2027E earnings, and the $243.42 low the shares actually printed within the past twelve months. That is a 30% drawdown, and it is the realistic bad case for a fund holding the shares. The DCF bear of $133 is a different animal — gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a 9.5% discount rate together — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded strongly while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That is a reason to size modestly and buy on weakness rather than to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real and growing, and the only thing between today's price and the fund's required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is publicly disclosed in the sources here and both set the floor under the services multiple."}],"isError":false}

(2) As of September 28, 2024, cash and cash equivalents included $ 2.6 billion held in escrow and restricted from general use. These restricted cash and cash equivalents were designated to settle the Company’s obligation related to the State Aid Decision (refer to Note 7, “Income Taxes”).
(3) As of September 28, 2024, current marketable securities included $ 13.2 billion held in escrow and restricted from general use. These restricted marketable securities were designated to settle the Company’s obligation related to the State Aid Decision (refer to Note 7, “Income Taxes”).
European Commission State Aid Decision
On August 30, 2016, the Commission announced its decision that Ireland granted state aid to the Company by providing tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 concerning the tax allocation of profits of the Irish branches of two subsidiaries of the Company (“State Aid Decision”). The State Aid Decision ordered Ireland to calculate and recover additional taxes from the Company for the period June 2003 through December 2014. Irish legislative changes, effective as of January 2015, eliminated the application of the tax opinions from that date forward.
The Company and Ireland appealed the State Aid Decision to the General Court of the Court of Justice of the European Union (“General Court”). On July 15, 2020, the General Court annulled the State Aid Decision. On September 25, 2020, the Commission appealed the General Court’s decision to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”). On September 10, 2024, the ECJ announced that it had set aside the 2020 judgment of the General Court and confirmed the Commission’s 2016 State Aid Decision. As a result, during the fourth quarter of 2024 the Company recorded a one-time income tax charge of $ 10.2 billion, net, which represented $ 15.8 billion payable to Ireland via release of amounts held in escrow, partially offset by a U.S. foreign tax credit of $ 4.8 billion and a decrease in unrecognized tax benefits of $ 823 million.

plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63.
plan.mechanism: Each risk transmits to value through one of two channels: a cost shock against a 48.7% gross margin that applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, or a legal remedy against two near-pure-margin services tolls, and a 39.5x multiple capitalises both at a 2.5% earnings yield so either shock is amplified by the exit multiple.
plan.comparison_set: Peer median 20.2x P/E against Apple's 39.5x; Apple's own four-year mean 31.0x and FY2022 trough 24.6x; the $243.42 52-week low (-29.4%); Samsung's mobile division losing KRW0.8tn and Xiaomi at an 8.5% handset margin show what the memory shock does to weaker hardware models.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple grew iPhone revenue 22.4% through a 16.7% industry unit decline, gained 4.8 points of China share to 19.5% in Q3 2026, holds $62.2bn of net cash, and the district court remedy preserved Google's payments; the multiple has held above 34x for two years.
plan.decision_question: At what entry price do the memory, search-payment, DMA and China risks still leave a long-only fund a 9% three-year return, and which signpost would invalidate that entry?
plan.why_different: This is the only section that prices the left tail and the multiple: it separates fatal risks from execution risks, stress-tests the base case against smaller markets, lower FCF and higher discount rates, and gives each risk a dated signpost.
plan.visual: risk-matrix of nine risks with probability, impact, level, timing, signpost and mitigation, plus a danger card on the gross-margin risk
plan.prohibited: generic risk lists, 'risks are manageable', unquantified probabilities, a risk without an early-warning signpost, repeating the thesis without stress-testing it

rows.finding: The June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; TrendForce projects 4Q26 conventional DRAM contract prices +10-15% QoQ and NAND +15-20%, with DRAM tight into 2027.
rows.mechanism: A cost shock hits a hardware line priced months ahead: Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, so the gross margin absorbs the increase before any price offset arrives.
rows.benchmark: iPhone 18 Pro BOM +38% YoY with memory 34% of BOM against ~10% a year earlier; 200bp of gross margin = $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of trailing $8.72.
rows.weakens: Q4 guidance of 47-48% reported already assumes part of the increase, and memory price growth is moderating from the 146% first-quarter 2026 jump; services at 76.3% margin cushion the blend.
rows.implication: A 46% gross margin takes FY2027 EPS to about $9.3 and, at 29x, fair value to $270 - the entry price becomes the base case, not the bear case.
rows.confidence: high on the cost data, medium on the pass-through because Apple's price elasticity is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What gross margin does management guide for the December 2026 quarter, and how much FY2027 memory is contracted at fixed prices?

rows.finding: The trial record put the Google payment at $20bn in 2022, 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and about 15% of operating income at near-pure margin; the district court remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the D.C. Circuit appeal No. 26-5023 with a DOJ cross-appeal seeking a ban is live into 2027.
rows.mechanism: A rent with almost no marginal cost is capitalised in the services multiple; a ban removes operating income and de-rates the line that carries most of the terminal value.
rows.benchmark: A ban is -10% to -13% of EPS and, at 30-35x, -$35 to -$45 a share; a lower rate is the more likely outcome and is worth less than the market's implied perpetuity.
rows.weakens: The payment survived the district court remedy, Apple has filed in support of it, and appellate courts defer on remedies; the 2022 figure may understate or overstate the 2026 rate.
rows.implication: Price a 20-25% probability of loss into any entry; do not pay a services multiple on the full toll.
rows.confidence: medium: the legal record is high-confidence, the outcome and the payment's current size are not
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment and term, and when is the D.C. Circuit argument scheduled?

rows.finding: From 2026-10-01 Apple's EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase, 20% on alternative payment, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission; Europe was 26.7% of nine-month FY2026 revenue.
rows.mechanism: Regulated take-rate compression on the highest-margin line transfers rent to developers and alternative storefronts and lowers switching costs out of the App Store.
rows.benchmark: EU band of 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere; each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of trailing operating income.
rows.weakens: Apple retains 26% on in-app purchase; EU App Store revenue is not disclosed and the direct hit may be 1-2% of operating income.
rows.implication: The EU amount is manageable; the template is not. Underwrite services growth at 10-12%, not 15%, and treat a US move to a 5-15% band as the bear case.
rows.confidence: medium: the fee schedule is high-confidence, the revenue exposure is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: How much EU App Store commission revenue is at stake, and how fast are developers migrating to external distribution?

rows.finding: Apple trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median and a 31.0x four-year mean, while the DCF is $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity and $193 at 9.5%.
rows.mechanism: Almost all of the value is terminal, so the discount rate and the exit multiple dominate: each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%.
rows.benchmark: Reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 38%; the 52-week low of $243.42 is a 29.4% drawdown.
rows.weakens: Forward 35.2x equals the twelve-month average of 35.7x, and quality franchises have held premium multiples through a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.implication: Zero position at $344.63; a starter only at $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% across 27-34x exits.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the timing of any re-rating
rows.follow_up: What would the ten-year yield have to do for a 7.0% cost of equity to be defensible, and how sticky is the passive bid?

rows.finding: China shipments fell 10% YoY in Q3 2026 on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%; Apple gained 4.8 points of share in the quarter, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in H2 2026.
rows.mechanism: A shrinking unit pool with a fixed premium layer means revenue growth comes from price and share, both of which reverse when demand is pulled forward.
rows.benchmark: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; Apple grew 30% in the nine months against a market down 4.3% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Apple gained share and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor; the two trackers disagree by 1.7 points on Apple's Q3 share, so the data are noisy.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 30% China growth; a 20% China decline is about 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS.
rows.confidence: medium-high on the direction, medium on the magnitude because the trackers disagree
rows.follow_up: What share of the China growth was pull-forward ahead of Apple's H2 2026 price rises?

rows.finding: Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14 on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capex fell to $6.80bn; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation.
rows.mechanism: Rented intelligence is operating expense with no asset behind it: the marginal AI dollar is a margin cost, and the supplier also owns Android, so renewal terms carry the bargaining power.
rows.benchmark: A $1bn licence is 0.6% of trailing operating income; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would be several times that and would land in the 76.3% services margin.
rows.weakens: Apple keeps distribution, personal context and Private Cloud Compute, and a better assistant may sell handsets even if Apple does not own the model.
rows.implication: Treat AI as a cost line, not a moat; the upgrade cycle must show up in units and ASP before it is worth paying for.
rows.confidence: low-to-medium: the licence price is reported, not confirmed, and the AI P&L structure is an absence of disclosure
rows.follow_up: What are the Gemini renewal terms, and who signs off the AI budget?

rows.finding: Trailing free cash flow of $136.7bn includes $14.1bn from a rise in other liabilities; normalised FCF is $122.6-125.1bn, while intangibles rose $12.1bn in nine months and inventory is $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end.
rows.mechanism: Working-capital accruals and acquisitions convert into free cash flow without being earnings; inventory build is the channel through which a demand miss becomes a write-down.
rows.benchmark: Conversion of 0.95-0.97x normalised against 1.06x headline, still ahead of Microsoft at 0.50x; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of trailing operating income.
rows.weakens: Apple's cash conversion is genuinely better than peers and the liability swing may be a timing item that reverses as memory is pre-bought.
rows.implication: Use the normalised $122.6-125.1bn for valuation; a 30% lower FCF of $95.7bn no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback plus dividends.
rows.confidence: medium: the swing is filed, its cause is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What is acquired for $12.1bn of net intangibles, and what sits in the $13.5bn rise in other non-current liabilities?

rows.finding: The board waived its age-75 guideline for Levinson (75) and Sugar (77); from 2026-09-01 Apple has nine directors, two non-independent, with Cook Executive Chair. Srouji was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20, superseding the December 2025 departure report. FY2025 returned $106.1bn, 107% of $98.8bn FCF but 93% of the $114.6bn normalised for the Irish tax payment.
rows.mechanism: Key-person and board-refresh risk affects the roadmap rather than the near-term cash flow; capital return is sustainable on normalised cash but not on the depressed FY2025 figure.
rows.benchmark: 92% say-on-pay, no dual-class stock, internal CFO and COO promotions; underlying FY2025 EPS growth of about 10.6% once the prior year's $10.2bn tax charge is added back, not the 22.7% headline.
rows.weakens: Srouji was promoted and retained, the CEO transition was planned over two years, and the payout ratio is a tax artefact.
rows.implication: Carry as a low-level monitor, not a thesis risk; anchor EPS growth on 8-11% operating growth plus the buyback, not the headline.
rows.confidence: high on the records, medium on the retention outcome because no succession is disclosed
rows.follow_up: When do Levinson and Sugar leave the board, and what retention award keeps Srouji through the 2028 silicon roadmap?

Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet: at $344.63 on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, with a $212 base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity. [S7, S97, S10] Nine risks are ranked below; two are fatal to the current price and the rest are execution risks a long-only fund can own through, provided it buys near $270. Detectability varies more than severity: memory costs and China shipments print monthly or quarterly, while the D.C. Circuit's remedy decision is a single binary event with no partial hedge.

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The record 50.1% gross margin in the June 2026 quarter carried 2 percentage points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS, and the refunds will not recur. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast has conventional DRAM contract prices up 10-15% quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher, with PC DRAM supply tightening in 2027 as capacity shifts to servers. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from about 10% a year earlier. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of the base case's 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to about $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if price increases meet elastic demand. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% is the one risk that breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, the company cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and the 39.5x multiple leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: the same 200bp that costs $0.52 of EPS also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x four-year mean, which together is a 25-30% drawdown from $344.63. The signpost is the December-quarter gross-margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The US v. Google trial record put Apple's search revenue share at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and about 15% of operating income at near-pure margin. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, a reading the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 amicus brief confirms when it asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the payment mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value once the services multiple de-rates; a lower rate is the likelier outcome and is worth less than the perpetuity the market capitalises. The EU fee schedule in force from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is smaller in situ, because Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but larger as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth from 12-14% to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### AI is a cost line before it is a moat

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; the distribution layer is also litigious, with X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI in the Northern District of Texas surviving motions to dismiss and closing discovery on 2026-05-22, and the same default-placement theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would be several times that and would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is therefore not capability but whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at a $1,199 starting price. [S111, S6, S127, S137]

### China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war

Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% year on year on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%; Apple gained 4.8 points of share in the quarter and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half that pulled purchases forward ahead of Apple's own price rises; a 20% China decline is about 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: about 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where smartphone production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

arguments.markdown:
Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. [S7, S97, S10] Nine risks are ranked below; two are fatal to the current price, the rest are execution risks a fund can own through at the right entry. Memory and China print quarterly and are cheap to monitor; the D.C. Circuit's remedy is a binary event with no partial hedge.

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp; -25% to -30% of value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin below 37%; DRAM and NAND contract prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -21.5% at 31x; -38% at 24.6x | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield above 5%; forward P/E above 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services growth | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails to lift ASP; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin step-down | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Tariffs and supply-chain shock | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -3% to -5% at a 10-point product-margin hit | Medium | Ongoing | New Section 301 lists; India incentive renewal | India at 25% of assembly | S115, S6, S17 |
| Earnings quality: liability swing, intangibles, inventory | Medium, 30-50% | EPS -2% on a 30% inventory write-down | Medium | FY2026 10-K, 2026-11-02 | FCF conversion below 0.9x | Use normalised free cash flow | S6, S5 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | Director retirements; Srouji title | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The record 50.1% gross margin in the June 2026 quarter carried 2 percentage points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts conventional DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher, with PC DRAM supply tightening in 2027. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38% year on year, with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of the base case's 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to roughly $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if higher prices meet elastic demand. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The US v. Google trial record put Apple's search revenue share at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income at near-pure margin. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 amicus brief confirms that reading when it asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the payment mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value once the services multiple de-rates; a lower rate is likelier and worth less than the perpetuity the market capitalises. The EU fee schedule in force from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ, since Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but material as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### AI is a cost line before it is a moat

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; the distribution layer is also litigious, with X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI surviving dismissal and closing discovery on 2026-05-22, and the same default-placement theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is not capability but whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at a $1,199 starting price. [S111, S6, S127, S137]

### China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war

Q3 2026 China shipments fell 10% year on year on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%; Apple gained 4.8 points of share and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half that pulled purchases forward ahead of Apple's own price rises; a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x trailing, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and the multiple is the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough costs 38%, and the realistic drawdown is the $242 on which two independent methods converge. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%, so a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied required return is the whole debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $95.7bn, or 52x, and no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and what would change the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors, not thesis risks. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The FY2025 payout that looks stretched is a tax artefact of the Irish State Aid payment, not cash the company cannot spare. What remains genuinely unknown sits outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption that would stop 2nm A20 Pro supply, an appellate remedy that treats the Gemini default as the next search payment, and the liability line matching most of the intangibles added in nine months, which the filing does not explain. None changes the recommendation: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if the December quarter confirms the margin trough.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) Apple's market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn and its enterprise value $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that valuation needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021. Forward, 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium that only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near, while Alphabet, growing faster over the last year, trades at 14.6x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls it [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung Electronics and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed here, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and management guided the September quarter to 9-11% growth with iPhone in the mid-teens. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The year-on-year swing of $25.2bn overstates the problem, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement released from escrow in the year to September 2025. Netting the line to zero, or to its $2.5bn three-year average of +$3.0bn, +$15.6bn and -$11.1bn, gives normalised FCF of $122.6-125.1bn — 0.95-0.97x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and about 41x P/FCF, still ahead of Microsoft's 1.5% and Alphabet's 0.6%. The $122.6bn end treats the whole build as deferred consideration for the $13.3bn of gross intangibles added, in which case the cash is an unpaid purchase and the payment falls due in a later year. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation, both capping the margin expansion the multiple assumes. Shareholders have received $438.6bn of repurchases and $75.0bn of dividends in the five fiscal years to FY2025, plus $82.2bn and $15.6bn in the twelve months to June 2026, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025; no equity has been raised and total debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S5, S6, S1].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The normalisation above does not move it: the model capitalises NOPAT and gives no credit for a working-capital source. The grid shows why the answer is contested: the market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%. That is the whole question, whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap is the premium paid for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple's June quarter set a record for earnings per share, the shares have beaten the broad market over the past year, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and free cash flow for the next two fiscal years and a sell-side price target, none of which is publicly disclosed here.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. [S7, S97, S10] Nine risks are ranked below: two are fatal to the current price, the rest are execution risks a fund can own through at the right entry. Memory and China print quarterly; the D.C. Circuit's remedy is a binary event with no partial hedge.

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp; -25% to -30% of value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM and NAND prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -21.5% at 31x; -38% at 24.6x | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield above 5%; forward P/E above 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services growth | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin step-down | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Tariffs and supply-chain shock | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -3% to -5% at a 10-point product hit | Medium | Ongoing | New Section 301 lists; India incentive renewal | India at 25% of assembly | S115, S6, S17 |
| Earnings quality: liabilities, intangibles, inventory | Medium, 30-50% | EPS -2% on a 30% inventory write-down | Medium | FY2026 10-K, 2026-11-02 | FCF conversion below 0.9x | Use normalised free cash flow | S6, S5 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | Director retirements; Srouji title | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The record 50.1% gross margin carried 2 percentage points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts conventional DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38% year on year, memory at 34% of it against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of the base case's 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to roughly $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if higher prices meet elastic demand. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The US v. Google trial record put Apple's search revenue share at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 amicus brief confirms that reading when it asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the payment mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value once the services multiple de-rates; a lower rate is likelier. The EU fee schedule in force from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ, since Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but material as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### AI is a cost line before it is a moat

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal, and the same default-placement theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is not capability but whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at a $1,199 starting price. [S111, S6, S127, S137]

### China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war

Q3 2026 China shipments fell 10% year on year on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%; Apple gained 4.8 points of share and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half that pulled purchases forward; a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x trailing, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and the multiple is the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough costs 38%, and the realistic drawdown is the $242 on which two independent methods converge. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%, so a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied required return is the whole debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $95.7bn, or 52x, and no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and what would change the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors, not thesis risks. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The FY2025 payout that looks stretched is a tax artefact, not cash the company cannot spare. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption that would stop 2nm A20 Pro supply, an appellate remedy that treats the Gemini default as the next search payment, and the liability line matching most of the intangibles added in nine months. None changes the recommendation: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if the December quarter confirms the margin trough.

At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) Apple's market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn and its enterprise value $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that valuation needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, with the September quarter guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The year-on-year swing of $25.2bn overstates the problem, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement released from escrow in the year to September 2025. Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple's June quarter set a record for earnings per share, the shares have beaten the broad market over the past year, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and free cash flow for the next two fiscal years and a sell-side price target, none of which is publicly disclosed here.

The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The FY2025 payout that looks stretched is a tax artefact, not cash the company cannot spare. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption that would stop 2nm A20 Pro supply, an appellate remedy that treats the Gemini default as the next search payment, and the liability line matching most of the intangibles added in nine months. None changes the recommendation: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if the December quarter confirms the margin trough.
