arguments.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and net buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.5x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. As the table shows, Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so the exit is never closed and market impact is measured in basis points. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on a $5,029.6bn market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2026E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.0% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return, multiple unchanged | 9.9% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return, multiple reverts to 31.0x | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 39.5x it buys a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar spent, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is not a scandal; it is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 39.5x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.5% of the price, or 7.7% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than it was when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS continuous auction | $13.8bn a day; exit complete in days | Any trading day | Near-certain, and the default route | S7 |
| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

| Precedent realisation | Year | Value | Multiple at the time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repurchases, FY2022 | 2022 | $89.4bn | 24.6x year-end P/E | S2, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2023 | 2023 | $77.6bn | 27.9x | S3, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2024 | 2024 | $94.9bn | 37.5x | S4, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2025 | 2025 | $90.7bn | 34.2x | S5, S7 |
| Observed drawdown, twelve months to 2026-10-30 | 2026 | $243.42 low | 29.4% below $344.63 | S7 |

The precedents are all capital returns, because that is the only exit a company of this size has ever offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 20-30% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 39.5x makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

| Entry price | Exit at 27x | Exit at 31x | Exit at 34x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 (2026-10-30) | -3.2% | 1.3% | 4.5% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $300 | 1.4% | 6.1% | 9.4% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $240 | 9.2% | 14.3% | 17.9% | S6, S7, S97 |

The sell discipline follows from that table, which assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12% rather than the 9.9% consensus assumes for iPhone revenue. The conditions that would make me raise the entry price are specific and observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The conditions that force a sale are equally specific: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The bear case sets the drawdown to expect, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $242: a reversion to Apple's 2022 multiple of 24.6x on FY2027E earnings, and the $243.42 low the shares actually printed within the past twelve months. That is a 30% drawdown, and it is the realistic bad case for a fund holding the shares. The DCF bear of $133 is a different animal — gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a 9.5% discount rate together — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded strongly while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That is a reason to size modestly and buy on weakness rather than to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real and growing, and the only thing between today's price and the fund's required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is publicly disclosed in the sources here and both set the floor under the services multiple.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. [S7, S97, S10] Nine risks follow: two are fatal to the current price, the rest are execution risks. Memory prints quarterly; the D.C. Circuit ruling is binary.

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp; -25% to -30% of value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM and NAND prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -21.5% at 31x; -38% at 24.6x | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield over 5%; forward P/E over 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin step-down | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Tariffs and supply-chain shock | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -3% to -5% at a 10-point product hit | Medium | Ongoing | New Section 301 lists; India incentive renewal | India at 25% of assembly | S115, S6, S17 |
| Earnings quality: liabilities, intangibles, inventory | Medium, 30-50% | EPS -2% on a 30% inventory write-down | Medium | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | FCF conversion below 0.9x | Use normalised free cash flow | S6, S5 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | Director retirements; Srouji title | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The record 50.1% gross margin carried 2 percentage points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts conventional DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38% year on year, memory at 34% of it against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to roughly $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if higher prices meet elastic demand. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the search payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief confirms that when it asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value once the services multiple de-rates; a lower rate is likelier. The EU fee schedule in force from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ, since Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but material as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal, and the same default-placement theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is not capability but whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at a $1,199 starting price. China is the other half, and it is a shrinking pool rather than a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point share gain, and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half that pulled purchases forward; a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and the multiple is the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough costs 38%, and the realistic drawdown is the $242 on which two independent methods converge. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%, so a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied required return is the whole debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $95.7bn, or 52x, and no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors, not thesis risks. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The stretched payout ratio is a tax artefact. arguments.markdown:
Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. [S7, S97, S10] Nine risks follow: two are fatal to the current price, the rest are execution risks. Memory prints quarterly; the D.C. Circuit ruling is binary.

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp; -25% to -30% of value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM/NAND prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -21.5% at 31x; -38% at 24.6x | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield over 5%; forward P/E over 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin step-down | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Tariffs and supply-chain shock | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -3% to -5% at a 10-point product hit | Medium | Ongoing | New Section 301 lists; India incentive renewal | India at 25% of assembly | S115, S6, S17 |
| Earnings quality: liabilities, intangibles, inventory | Medium, 30-50% | EPS -2% on a 30% inventory write-down | Medium | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | FCF conversion below 0.9x | Use normalised free cash flow | S6, S5 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | Director retirements; Srouji title | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The record 50.1% gross margin carried 2 percentage points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts conventional DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to roughly $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if higher prices meet elastic demand. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief confirms that when it asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value once the services multiple de-rates; a lower rate is likelier. The EU fee schedule in force from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ, since Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but material as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal, and the same theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is not capability but whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at a $1,199 starting price. China is the other half, and it is a shrinking pool rather than a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point share gain, and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half of pull-forward demand; a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and the multiple is the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough costs 38%, and the realistic drawdown is the $242 two methods converge on. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%, so a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied required return is the whole debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $95.7bn, or 52x, and no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors, not thesis risks. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The stretched payout ratio is a tax artefact. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption that would stop 2nm supply, an appellate remedy that treats the Gemini default as the next search payment, and the liability line matching most of the intangibles added in nine months. Economically the downside is a de-rating rather than insolvency, so position size carries the risk, and open diligence is narrow: the December-quarter margin guide, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if the December quarter confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S11, S5]

::: risk-matrix

| Tariffs and supply-chain shock | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -3% to -5% at a 10-point product hit | Medium | Ongoing | New Section 301 lists; India incentive renewal | India at 25% of assembly | S115, S6, S17 |
| Earnings quality: liabilities, intangibles, inventory | Medium, 30-50% | EPS -2% on a 30% inventory write-down | Medium | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | FCF conversion below 0.9x | Use normalised free cash flow | S6, S5 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | Director retirements; Srouji title | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts conventional DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to roughly $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if higher prices meet elastic demand. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief confirms that when it asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value once the services multiple de-rates; a lower rate is likelier. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ, since Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but material as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal, and the same theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is not capability but whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at a $1,199 starting price. China is the other half: a shrinking pool, not a lost share war. Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point share gain, and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half of pull-forward demand; a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%, so a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied required return is the whole debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $95.7bn, or 52x, and no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

Governance and key-person risk are monitors. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The stretched payout ratio is a tax artefact. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption that would stop 2nm supply, an appellate remedy that treats the Gemini default as the next search payment, and the liability line matching most of the intangibles added in nine months. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk, and open diligence is narrow: the December-quarter margin guide, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if the December quarter confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S11, S5]

Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. [S7, S97, S10] Nine risks follow: two are fatal to the current price, the rest are execution risks. Memory prints quarterly; the D.C. Circuit ruling is binary. The strategic risk is that AI defends the price without widening the moat; the economic risk is that a 48.7% gross margin meets a memory cycle.

::: risk-matrix

| Earnings quality: liabilities, intangibles, inventory | Medium, 30-50% | EPS -2% on a 30% inventory write-down | Medium | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | FCF conversion below 0.9x | Use normalised FCF | S6, S5 |

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Because the margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point of gross margin is $4.7bn of operating income, and 39.5x capitalises it: that is the economic mechanism. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts conventional DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to roughly $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if demand proves elastic. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value; a lower rate is likelier. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ, since Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but material as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability, books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal, and the same theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at $1,199. China is the other half: a shrinking pool, not a lost share war. Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point share gain, and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half of pull-forward demand; a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and the multiple is the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough costs 38%, and the realistic drawdown is $242. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the whole debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $95.7bn, or 52x, and no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The stretched payout ratio is a tax artefact. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment, and the liability line matching most of the intangibles added in nine months. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk, and open diligence is narrow: the December-quarter margin guide, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S11, S5]"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 2 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,996 characters)
Apple's regulatory exposure, not its ESG record, is what can change a long-only case. FY2025 net sales were $416.2bn and Services revenue $109.2bn at a 75.4% gross margin, so App Store commissions and the Google default-search payment sit inside the profit pool carrying the premium multiple [S5]. Fines are not the mechanism; remedies and fee schedules are. Bear case: a 10-15% operating-income tail from losing or repricing search placement and a structurally lower App Store take rate over 2026-2028. The mechanism is that a dollar of commission or default rent carries almost no marginal cost, so losing it hits operating income faster than revenue.

### The EU fine is small; the fee schedule is not

On 2025-04-23 the European Commission fined Apple €500m for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation, 0.1% of FY2025 net sales. The material part is the fee schedule: from 2026-10-01 Apple's unified EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase (down from 30%), 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and 5% on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web. Apple says the terms resolve its disagreements with the Commission; EU developer groups call them unacceptable, so the settlement is contested. The General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08, with an interoperability ruling unlikely before late 2027. Apple does not disclose EU App Store revenue; at a 75.4% Services margin, each $1bn of commission lost equals $0.75bn of gross profit. The consequence is a permanently lower take rate on the most profitable services [S78, S77, S82, S5].

### The $20 billion Google payment is the largest policy-sensitive cash flow

Apple does not disclose the Google default-search payment, but the US v. Google trial record put it at $20bn in 2022, or 36% of Google's Safari search revenue: a litigated estimate, not a company disclosure. That is 18.3% of FY2025 Services revenue and, if near-pure margin, 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's final judgment of 2025-12-05 preserved non-exclusive payments, banned exclusivity and capped default deals at 12 months; the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026 seeking a payment ban. A negotiated lower rate is more likely than zero, but either compresses Services growth, and an appellate decision is likely in 2027. The payment is worth more as Apple profit than as Google cost, which points to a lower rate rather than zero [S80, S76, S5].

### US courts are already narrowing the App Store take rate

On 2025-12-11 the Ninth Circuit affirmed that Apple willfully violated the Epic injunction, upheld the steering remedy and limited any fee on linked transactions to Apple's costs; the Supreme Court granted certiorari on 2026-06-30. Separately, the DOJ and 16 states and DC have sued Apple for monopolization in "performance smartphones" and "smartphones" since 2024-03-21, seeking equitable relief, not damages; the case is in pre-trial litigation with no trial date in Apple's 2026 filings. A federal appellate court finding willful violation raises the odds of stricter remedies and weakens management's "substantial defenses" posture. US courts can reset App Store economics before the DOJ case reaches trial [S79, S81, S6].

### Tariffs have flipped from cost to refund, not to a new margin level

Q3 FY2026 revenue was $109.4bn and gross margin 50.1%, including 2 percentage points from tariff refunds; EPS of $2.02 included $0.11 from refunds. The underlying margin is 48.1%, against 46.9% for FY2025, when products gross margin fell on tariff costs. The refund follows the Supreme Court's 2026-02-20 ruling striking down certain IEEPA tariffs; Section 232 semiconductor initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products, but Section 301 duties have since been imposed and further actions remain possible. For valuation, normalise the margin rather than extrapolate the refund: underwrite 47-48%, not 50% [S17, S5, S6].

### Governance is a strength; the ESG gaps are disclosure and labour

Governance is not the discount. Apple has eight directors, three of them women (37.5%), an independent chair separate from the CEO, no dual-class stock, a $120,000 related-party review threshold, Audit Committee ownership of privacy and cybersecurity, and 92% Say-on-Pay support in 2025. The gaps are supply-chain labour and disclosure: 166,000 employees at 2025-09-27, a 10-K concession that supplier code violations "occur from time to time", and no audit metrics in the filing. Climate claims are unverified company statements. None has changed demand, so the economic read is that ESG is a tail-risk and discount-rate input, not a revenue driver [S11, S5].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,933 characters)
Apple's profit is unusually cash-true. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 operating cash flow was $146,724M, capital expenditure $10,041M and free cash flow $136,683M against net income of $128,930M — a headline conversion of 1.06x, or 0.95-0.97x once a liability accrual is normalised, on capex of 2.2% of revenue, against 0.50x and 34.9% at Microsoft and 0.08x and 33.9% at Alphabet. The income statement behind that cash grew revenue from $383,285M in FY2023 to $416,161M in FY2025 and $466,823M trailing, with operating margin of 29.8%, 32.0% and 33.2%. The nine months to 27 June 2026 produced an incremental operating margin of 43.0% — $21,809M more operating income on $50,662M more revenue — which is the bull case in one line. The question is how much of that increment is repeatable. [S5, S6]

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue; products are not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to them. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The 30 July 2026 release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9% a year earlier, while memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 and the 10-Q warns cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off the trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of the $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M: non-cash add-backs added $1,956M more and working capital $16,366M more. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against -$15,161M a year earlier, a $25,177M swing concentrated in other non-current liabilities, up to $55,080M from $41,549M; without that line working capital was an $8,811M drag. The prior-year figure is distorted: the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid payment ran through the same line in the nine months to June 2025 (cash taxes paid of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision), and the $15,552M added to it in FY2024 is within $250M of the $15.8B payable; the clean swing is nearer $9.4B. Trailing free cash flow of $136,683M carries $14,101M from that line. Normalising it to zero, or to its $2.5B clean three-year average, gives $122.6-125.1B, conversion of 0.95-0.97x — still ahead of both peers — a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.5-41.4x price to free cash flow. The $111.5B that subtracting the full $25.2B swing implies is too low because it treats a settlement-hit year as the baseline. The line is unexplained: a $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities against $13,270M of gross intangibles added and investing "other" of $1,780M points to deferred consideration, in which case that cash is an unpaid purchase, not earnings. Deferred revenue is no cushion either: 3.2% of trailing revenue, with only $7,260M of nine-month revenue out of the opening balance. [S5, S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B due within twelve months; leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need a question: $2,604M of unrealised losses on the securities book, and intangibles up to $25,417M net from $13,301M, $12,116M in nine months, without the 10-Q saying what was bought. ### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: normalised free cash flow of about $125B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 65.2%, against 57.3% in FY2025. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, a cost of equity of 9-11% is cleared several times; the constraint is the price: $5,072B of market capitalisation on $128,930M of trailing net income is a 2.5% earnings yield. Capital allocation agrees: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M are 67.0% of free cash flow, net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 7,773 characters)
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,072B, or 39.3x trailing EPS of $8.72; the price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).

The reviewer argues that a **D.C. Circuit ban** would cost **10–13% of EPS** and, with a services de-rating, **15–20% of value**. **The second candidate is the gross margin.** The base case capitalises **47–48%**, after the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% included two points of tariff refunds. **TrendForce** has DRAM contract prices up **10–15% in the fourth quarter of 2026** and NAND up **15–20%**, with supply tight into 2027. At 29x, the scenario base case gives **$284**, so $270 is only a **5% discount to base** and sits **above the $242 realistic bear case**. The reviewer's conclusion is that the recommendation survives but the entry price does not: stage the entry rather than treat $270 as a margin of safety.

**What the franchise can survive.** A market 50% smaller takes revenue down about 35% and EPS to roughly **$6**, worth **$120–150** at 20–25x, but **$62.2bn of net cash** means the company survives and the buyback stops rather than the balance sheet breaking. Revenue 30% lower gives operating income of about **$95bn** and EPS of **$5.4** — exactly the **$133** DCF bear case. Free cash flow 30% lower is **$95.7bn**, **52x**, and no longer covers the **$82.2bn** buyback; net cash absorbs three or more years of the gap. Multiple compression to **24.6x** is a **38%** drawdown.

But R&D is already up **33% to $34.04bn** with no disclosed AI revenue, and a per-device or per-query price across the **2.5bn** installed base would be several times $1bn and would land in the **76.3% services margin** — a **2–4% EPS risk** the entry price and starter size do not adjust for. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,871 characters)
Apple is winning the competition for profit and price while ceding unit share in China: it holds 65% of premium phone units and a 40% product gross margin, but Huawei is taking premium share in a shrinking China market and regulation is capping the services take rate, so its competitive position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and weakening at the margin in China. Apple's own 10-K concedes a minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables and says some of its markets have experienced little or no growth; the useful analysis is therefore per product, because the iPhone, Mac, wearables and services each face a different rival set [S5].

| Huawei | Mate and Pura; HarmonyOS | Kirin silicon; HarmonyOS | China scale; US export restrictions | Premium camera and battery | Premium | 22.6% China in Q2 2026 | Domestic supply chain; holds prices | Little share outside China | S87, S86 |
| Xiaomi | Xiaomi 17 series | Android; Snapdragon | Unrestricted | Value flagship | Mid-premium | 11.5% global in Q2 2026 | Price-performance; AIoT and EV ecosystem | 8.5% handset gross margin; profit -42.6% | S90 |
| Google | Pixel 11 | Android; Tensor; Gemini | Unrestricted | AI-first software | Premium | Not disclosed | Gemini integration; search distribution | Small hardware distribution | S15, S50 |
| Lenovo, HP, Dell | PC lines | Windows on x86 | Unrestricted | Enterprise and channel strength | $600-2,000 | 24.4%, 19.1%, 13.6% in Q2 2026 | Enterprise channel; price tiers | No in-house OS-silicon integration | S95 |
| Spotify | Music streaming and app distribution | App; DMA alternative distribution | EU DMA beneficiary | 300M paying subscribers | Subscription | Twice Apple Music's subscriber base | Cross-platform; podcasts | No hardware bundle | S93, S77 |
| Alphabet | Search, YouTube, Play | Android; Gemini | Antitrust scrutiny | Advertising scale | Ad-funded | $471B TTM revenue | Search and advertising scale | AI capex dilution | S15, S50 |
| Status quo | Longer device life, refurbished | None | None | Adequate for most users | Zero | Not disclosed | Free and familiar | No new capability | S87 |

Huawei is the most dangerous competitor to Apple's profit pool, and Samsung is the most dangerous to its unit position [S87, S86, S91, S92, S84]. Huawei led China with 22.6% in Q2 2026 against Apple's 18.1%, after its highest share since Q4 2020 in the prior quarter, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026; Huawei funds that push with CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of CNY880.9B of 2025 revenue. Samsung is broader, with 19% global share in 2025 and 23% in Q3 2026, a foldable incumbent and the only rival with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth, so it cannot buy share indefinitely. Huawei takes price and profit; Samsung takes volume and loses money doing it.

Share trends from 2025 to 2026 show Apple gaining value and premium ground while its unit share moves sideways [S92, S120, S94, S84, S17]. Apple led 2025 with 20% of global units and 10% growth and Samsung followed at 19%; in Q3 2026 Samsung held 23% to Apple's 22% as the market fell 20%. The premium layer is where Apple's position improves: its 65% of $600-plus units in H1 2026 came with 9% growth, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% share in 2026. Pricing power shows in the gross margin, 40.1% on products in Q3 FY2026 versus 34.5% a year earlier, with iPhone revenue up 22% in nine months. The caveat is that the price increase is imposed by a memory shock rather than earned by innovation alone: NAND and DRAM costs are up more than 300% year over year, and Apple's signalling of further rises pulled Chinese demand forward.

China is the one region where the competitive position is deteriorating on share even as revenue rises [S87, S6, S86]. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in the first nine months of FY2026, but that came against a market down 4.2% in H1 2026 and with Apple at 18.1% share to Huawei's 22.6%; Huawei grew 19.4% and Apple 24.4% in Q2 2026, both by holding prices while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi raised theirs and lost 9.7%, 11.4% and 21.7% respectively. The top six vendors hold 96% of the market, so the fight is for premium share inside a contracting pool, and Huawei's HarmonyOS scale gives it a domestic platform Apple cannot match on localisation. Apple's revenue growth is a price-hold plus pull-forward effect, not evidence that it has regained structural leadership in China.

Regulation is now a competitive force that transfers rent from Apple to its rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. The practical effect is to lower switching costs out of the App Store in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and to hand Spotify, Epic and alternative storefronts a distribution channel on iOS; Spotify already has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. The DMA is the template, and its spread to other jurisdictions is the regulatory risk to monitor.

| Mac | Share gainer from a small base | Lenovo by units | Apple | HP and Dell premium tiers | Snapdragon Windows PCs | S95 |
| Wearables | Leader by value, third by units | Xiaomi by units, Apple by value | Huawei | Oura in rings, Meta in glasses | AI glasses | S85 |
| Services (apps and advertising) | Challenger in advertising, leader in app distribution | Alphabet in advertising | Apple in app distribution | Spotify in music | DMA-enabled alternative stores | S15, S93, S77 |

The status quo is a formidable competitor: consumers are holding devices longer, IDC expects China's recovery only in 2028-2029 and forecasts a smaller, more concentrated market after the memory crisis, and the cheapest segment is disappearing [S87, S84, S17, S93]. Pipeline threats are Apple's own foldable in H2 2026, Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion, Google's Gemini-integrated Pixel and AI agents that could move the assistant layer off the operating system. Apple's wedge is the integration of silicon, OS and an installed base that reached an all-time high in Q3 FY2026, which lets it earn 40% product gross margins while rivals earn single digits or lose money; that wedge supports profit-share gains but not unit-share gains. The competitive position therefore supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated ceiling on services, not a share-gain growth story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China and medium on services because take rates are in flux. Diligence questions: how much of the premium gain is price inflation, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS, and whether Apple's foldable holds 40% of the category beyond 2027.

Pay is where the team is most unusual. Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m — a $3m salary unchanged since 2016, a $6m target cash award and a $50m equity award, 75% performance-based — against Satya Nadella's $96.5m reported for Microsoft's fiscal 2025 and Sundar Pichai's $10.9m reported for 2025, though Pichai's 2026 target equity award is $210m and a 1,348,607-share 2022 award vested to him in February 2026. Apple's other named executives each target about $23m: $1m salary, a 200% cash target and $20m of equity. There are no employment contracts, no change-of-control payments and time-based RSUs vest over roughly four and a half years, so retention runs through unvested stock rather than contractual protection — cheap for shareholders and defensible at 92% say-on-pay, but exposed where pay is not disclosed at all. The reporting on silicon is the sharpest counter-evidence to a continuity story. In December 2025 Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, was reported to have told Cook he was seriously considering leaving; no departure or new role has been disclosed since. Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and the 36.8% products gross margin, so the loss of its architect would threaten a roadmap competitors cannot copy quickly. Promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be the retention move that keeps that bench together — or it may not, and the filings will not say which. [S131, S5]

The 2024-26 turnover cluster is the part a reference check should attack. Apple calls each a planned transition and two successors were internal, which is real bench evidence; but keeping the outgoing general counsel on government affairs signals how heavy the regulatory load has become, and the general counsel who oversaw those defences is leaving while the DOJ and DMA cases are live. Apple seeks to conduct business ethically, honestly,

In China last quarter, it is exactly what happened to Apple. According to preliminary figures from IDC, smartphone shipments in China fell 15.4% year on year in the third quarter of 2026. Apple’s own shipments dropped 4.3%, but because almost everyone else fell further, its share of the market rose from 15.8% to 17.8%.

The one brand that grew strongly was Huawei.

The Numbers

BrandQ3 2026 shareQ3 2025 shareYear-on-year shipmentsHuawei21.1%15.2%+17.3%Apple17.8%15.8%-4.3%Wiko0.8%2.6%-74%Whole market-15.4%

Huawei’s 17.3% rise made it the clear leader, although its shipments still dropped 17.6% from the previous quarter. Lenovo was the only other top-10 brand to grow year on year, by a modest 1.1%. Wiko, which sells phones built with Huawei’s help, had the worst quarter in the top 10, with shipments down 74%.

Quarter on quarter, the picture is different. Apple fell 15.1% from the second quarter, while Lenovo, Honor and Samsung all grew, Samsung by 106.5% from a small base.

Why the Market Is Shrinking

IDC’s explanation comes down to cost. Component prices have risen sharply, phone makers have passed that on in higher retail prices, and buyers in China are responding by keeping their phones longer. It is the same squeeze that has pushed prices up elsewhere, including the $100 rise on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this year.

IDC credits Huawei’s strong run to a broad range of phones and “relatively restrained price increases”. On Apple, it says the new iPhones received a “better-than-expected market reception”, and that shipments dipped only because Apple has fewer models on sale this year. That is most likely a reference to Apple’s split launch schedule, with the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo arriving in the autumn and the standard iPhone 18 held back until spring. The iPhone Duo also had not gone on sale by the end of the quarter.

The quarter-on-quarter drop for Apple looks worse than it is. The third quarter ends in September, so it includes less than two weeks of iPhone 18 Pro sales (they went on sale on 18 September), while the previous quarter included the 618 shopping festival in June, when Chinese retailers and Apple’s own store cut prices heavily.

What Comes Next

IDC is not expecting a quick recovery. It says component costs will “remain elevated over the next several quarters” and that pressure will last “through much of 2027, with the market likely to continue experiencing significant declines.” Higher prices and longer upgrade cycles look set to become normal.

For Apple, the fourth quarter should look better on paper. The iPhone Duo goes on sale on 23 October, and the iPhone has historically done well in China during the end-of-year shopping season. Whether a phone starting at $1,999 sells in volume in a market where buyers are holding on to their handsets is another matter. Huawei has had foldables on sale in China for years, and it will not give up that ground easily.

It is a long way from spring 2025, when Apple’s sales in China slumped as local brands surged. Apple has steadied itself, but Huawei now has a clear lead.

Over to You

Would higher prices make you keep your current phone for an extra year, or is your next upgrade already planned? Let us know in the comments.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,744 characters)
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year, +2% YoY; Omdia 1.25B (+2%) | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7% YoY, steepest annual fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP); 2026 = $196.5B x 4/3 / $613B | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC, +1.7%; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |
| Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units, and the sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at 1.26B units and a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% a year earlier on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every geographic segment in double digits; that is genuine pricing power [S17, S87, S84]. But IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases, and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026 and emerging markets are forecast down more than 20%. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months.

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one is large enough to change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects it to ship more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth more than $45.7B. Services: $120.5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a global advertising pool of $1.34T in 2026 and an App Store ecosystem Apple says carried $149B of digital goods and services in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables are a 2.4% CAGR market to 2030 with smartwatches shrinking 3.7% in 2026 while glasses grow 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. Foldables and services can add; the non-phone device pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.
