{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 2 by Lead Analyst, 8,877 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap, and the base rate they must beat is modest: revenue compounded 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value where this report sees an 18% overvaluation: the median twelve-month target is $338-355, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price proposed below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and a peak multiple at once.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value at $291.5, 15% below the price. Bull ($357, 25%): the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return, with the upside coming from a multiple that stays elevated. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with the break-up rejected and conduct remedies imposed: the asset survived, but the overhang ran for three years and the resolution did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225 or on evidence that FY2027 EPS growth is tracking above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the three tranches exist to price that. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the twelve months to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, neither of which the register holds. Sell above $380 or above 45 times forward earnings ($441), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 6 by Lead Analyst, 8,214 characters)
The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S146]. The DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212, the bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the market price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. The sell side's median target of $338-355 offers flat to +3%, so there is no analyst catalyst to close the gap either.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 41.2 times.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. The score table below carries the figures and their sources.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter, and the table below carries the mechanics. At the current price the probability-weighted return across the three scenarios is negative, so the Kelly fraction is zero; at the first tranche the odds support a fractional Kelly well above the cap, so the cap binds rather than the calculation. The market regime reinforces patience: an elevated volatility percentile, a ten-year yield at 4.93% and a month of technology underperformance against the index are the profile the regime playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10]. The open diligence is the FY2026 10-K detail on working capital and intangibles, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, and the appellate outcome on the search payment.

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue; products are not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to them. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% with the 10-Q warning that cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M: non-cash add-backs added $1,956M more and working capital $16,366M more. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 7,773 characters)
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.9% gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.3% gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | products gross margin 39.9% | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% a year earlier, and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,990 characters)
Apple is winning on profit and price and, since the September 2026 quarter, on share in a shrinking China market: it holds 65% of premium phone units at a 40.1% product gross margin, Huawei leads China 21.3% to 19.5% but Apple gained 4.8 points, and regulation caps the services take rate, so its position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and exposed to market size rather than share loss [S5]. Apple's 10-K concedes a minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables, so the analysis is per product: each faces a different rival set.

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Apple | Weaknesses vs Apple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung | Galaxy S26, Z Fold 7 | Android; Exynos 2600 or Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 | Unrestricted | Flagship parity; foldable | Premium | 19% global 2025; 23% in Q3 2026 | Foldable head start; carrier breadth | MX division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 | S91, S92, S120 |
| Huawei | Mate and Pura; HarmonyOS | Kirin silicon; HarmonyOS | China scale; US export restrictions | Premium camera and battery | Premium | 21.3% China Q3 2026; 21.1% on IDC | Domestic supply chain; holds prices | Little share outside China | S139, S140, S86 |
| Xiaomi | Xiaomi 17 series | Android; Snapdragon | Unrestricted | Value flagship | Mid-premium | 11.5% global in Q2 2026 | Price-performance; AIoT and EV ecosystem | 8.5% handset gross margin; profit -42.6% | S90 |
| Google | Pixel 11 | Android; Tensor; Gemini | Unrestricted | AI-first software | Premium | Not disclosed | Gemini integration; search distribution | Small hardware distribution | S15, S50 |
| Lenovo, HP, Dell | PC lines | Windows on x86 | Unrestricted | Enterprise and channel strength | $600-2,000 | 24.4%, 19.1%, 13.6% in Q2 2026 | Enterprise channel; price tiers | No in-house OS-silicon integration | S95 |
| Spotify | Music streaming and app distribution | App; DMA alternative distribution | EU DMA beneficiary | 300M paying subscribers | Subscription | Twice Apple Music's subscriber base | Cross-platform; podcasts | No hardware bundle | S93, S77 |
| Alphabet | Search, YouTube, Play | Android; Gemini | Antitrust scrutiny | Advertising scale | Ad-funded | $471B TTM revenue | Search and advertising scale | AI capex dilution | S15, S50 |
| Status quo | Longer device life | None | None | Adequate for most users | Zero | Not disclosed | Free and familiar | No new capability | S87 |

Huawei is the most dangerous rival to Apple's profit pool, Samsung to its unit position. Huawei led China with 21.3% to Apple's 19.5% in Q3 2026, after 22.6% to 18.1% in Q2 2026, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026; Huawei funds that push with CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of CNY880.9B of 2025 revenue [S96, S139, S140, S91, S92, S86, S87]. Samsung is broader, with 19% global share in 2025 and 23% in Q3 2026, the only rival with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth, so it cannot buy share indefinitely. Huawei takes price and profit; Samsung takes volume and loses money doing it.

Share trends show Apple gaining value and premium ground while its global unit share moves sideways [S92, S120, S94, S84, S17]. Apple led 2025 with 20% of global units, Samsung 19%; in Q3 2026 Samsung held 23% to Apple's 22% as the market fell 20%. The premium layer is where Apple's position improves: its 65% of $600-plus units in H1 2026 came with 9% growth, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% share in 2026. Pricing power shows in the gross margin, 40.1% on products in Q3 FY2026 versus 34.5% a year earlier, with iPhone revenue up 22% in nine months. The caveat is that the price rise is imposed by a memory shock, not earned by innovation: NAND and DRAM costs are up more than 300%.

China is the region where the risk has flipped from share loss to market contraction [S139, S140, S87, S6]. In Q3 2026 China's smartphone shipments fell 10% to the lowest third-quarter level since 2012 on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's; Apple took 19.5%, second, up 4.8 points year on year, with iPhone 18 Pro sales up 23.5% in the first three weeks, while Huawei led at 21.3% (21.1% on IDC, shipments up 17.3%). Huawei and Apple were the only top brands to gain, taking 40% between them. That is not share loss: Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in the first nine months of FY2026 in a market down 4.2% in H1 2026. The vulnerability is the size and price level of the pool. IDC expects component costs elevated through much of 2027 with significant further declines, Apple raised iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max prices by $100 and holds the standard iPhone 18 to spring 2027, so part of the Q3 gain is pull-forward and launch timing, not a durable recovery. Apple has steadied China and gained premium share without regaining structural leadership; Huawei's HarmonyOS scale still gives it a localisation advantage Apple cannot match.

Regulation transfers rent from Apple to its rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. The effect is to lower switching costs out of the App Store in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and hand Spotify, Epic and alternative storefronts an iOS distribution channel; Spotify has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. Its spread to other jurisdictions is the regulatory risk to monitor.

| Product | Position | Leader | Challenger | Niche player | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (premium) | Leader in premium value and China share gainer; second in units | Apple | Samsung | Google Pixel | Huawei in China; foldables | S94, S139, S140 |
| Mac | Share gainer from a small base | Lenovo by units | Apple | HP and Dell premium tiers | Snapdragon Windows PCs | S95 |
| Wearables | Leader by value, third by units | Xiaomi by units, Apple by value | Huawei | Oura in rings, Meta in glasses | AI glasses | S85 |
| Services (apps and advertising) | Challenger in advertising, leader in app distribution | Alphabet in advertising | Apple in app distribution | Spotify in music | DMA-enabled alternative stores | S15, S93, S77 |

The status quo is formidable: consumers hold devices longer, IDC expects China's recovery only in 2028-2029 and a smaller, more concentrated market, and the cheapest segment is disappearing [S87, S84, S93]. Pipeline threats are Apple's foldable in H2 2026, Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion, Google's Gemini-integrated Pixel and AI agents that could move the assistant layer off the operating system. Apple's wedge is silicon, OS and an installed base at an all-time high in Q3 FY2026, letting it earn 40% product gross margins while rivals earn single digits or lose money; that supports profit-share gains and, in 2026, share gains inside a contracting market, but not unit growth. The competitive position therefore supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated ceiling on services, not a share-gain growth story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China, medium on services, because take rates are in flux. Diligence questions: how much of the premium and China gain is price inflation, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS, and whether the foldable holds 40% beyond 2027.

| Threats | DMA 5% take rate on external distribution; Huawei premium share; memory costs up more than 300%; AI assistants commoditising the OS layer | S77, S87, S84 |
:::

::: evidence
**Apple's competitive advantage is profit capture, and in 2026 also China premium share, not unit leadership.**

Apple holds 20% of phone units but 65% of premium units and 36-43% of market value (Counterpoint, S94; IDC, S84). Its 40.1% product gross margin compares with Xiaomi's 8.5% handset margin and a loss at Samsung's mobile division (S17, S90, S91). In China, Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% yet Apple's share rose 4.8 points to 19.5% behind Huawei's 21.3% (Counterpoint, S139, S96); the vulnerability is the shrinking pool and regulation (S140, S77), not lost share.

At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) Apple's market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn and its enterprise value $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that valuation needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021. Forward, 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls it [S7, S6, S97, S14].

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, with the September quarter guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn year-on-year swing overstates it, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement in the year to September 2025. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 39.5-41.0x P/FCF (40.2x at the midpoint on the $5,029.6bn market value, 40.5x diluted), still ahead of Microsoft's 1.5% and Alphabet's 0.6%. The $122.6bn floor treats the whole build as deferred consideration for the $13.3bn of gross intangibles added, which would make that cash an unpaid purchase; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x diluted. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation, both capping the margin expansion the multiple assumes. Shareholders have received $438.6bn of repurchases and $75.0bn of dividends in the five fiscal years to FY2025, plus $82.2bn and $15.6bn in the twelve months to June 2026; nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised nine-month free cash flow, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised and total debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S5, S6, S1].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%. That is the whole question, whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,894 characters)
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year, +2% YoY; Omdia 1.25B (+2%) | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7% YoY, steepest annual fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP); 2026 = $196.5B x 4/3 / $613B | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC, +1.7%; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |
| Global advertising pool (services) | $1.34T | 2026E | WARC, +11.9% | S89 |

Two independent methods agree that the market is growing in dollars while shrinking in units, and the sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48% [S6, S17].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. A discounted cash flow gives $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at the stock's own mean of 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price [S7, S97, S146].

Two facts would change the call. A gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it; an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133. The one question below decides which of the two the next twelve months delivers.

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence; the difference lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. As the table shows, Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so the exit is never closed and market impact is measured in basis points. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 39.5x it buys a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar spent, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is not a scandal; it is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 39.5x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.5% of the price, or 7.7% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than it was when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

arguments.markdown:
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48% [S6, S17].

Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over. Those are the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. A discounted cash flow gives $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at the stock's own mean of 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price [S7, S97, S146].

Two facts would change the call. A gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it; an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S17, S76].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence; the difference lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

::: one-question
Will the Google default-search payment survive the D.C. Circuit appeal, and at what annual rate?

The payment is the largest single item in services and runs at near-pure margin. A ban or a materially lower rate resets the services multiple that carries most of the valuation and moves fair value from the base case toward the bear case, regardless of how well the hardware cycle trades.
:::

::: takeaways
1. Watchlist, not ownership: at $344.63 the shares trade at 35.2 times forward earnings against 18.09 for the index, and the 18% discount in the base case depends on a 29 times exit, itself 18% below today's multiple [S7, S97, S146].
2. The franchise is not the problem: services earn 40.3% of gross profit, cash conversion is 0.97x, 0.95x at the band floor, and net cash is $62,173M, so a 30% revenue fall leaves the company solvent [S6].
3. The entry is a price, not a narrative: 0.75-1.0% at $270, a second tranche at $245 and the 5% cap below $225, with $270 above the $242 bear case and a 1.5% maximum loss at the cap [S6, S7].
:::

Definitions: free cash flow = operating cash flow - capital expenditure; net cash = cash and equivalents + current and non-current marketable securities - debt; trailing twelve months (TTM) = last fiscal year + this year to date - last year to date (for EPS an approximation). ROE = net income / average stockholders' equity; ROA = net income / average total assets; ROIC (approximate) = operating income x (1 - effective tax rate) / average invested capital, where the tax rate is income tax / pretax income (21% when pretax income is not positive) and invested capital = equity + debt - cash and marketable securities; an average is of the opening and closing balances, or the closing one alone when the opening one is missing. DSO = receivables / revenue x 365; DIO = inventory / cost of revenue x 365; DPO = accounts payable / cost of revenue x 365, all from closing balances; cash conversion cycle = DSO + DIO - DPO. Interest coverage = operating income / interest expense; goodwill and intangibles count what is tagged; capex / D&A = capital expenditure / depreciation and amortization. n/m = not meaningful (a base that is not positive). Interest expense = InterestExpense as tagged. Debt = LongTermDebtNoncurrent + LongTermDebtCurrent + CommercialPaper as tagged; finance leases are not included.

arguments.markdown:
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. A discounted cash flow gives $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at the stock's own mean of 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence; the difference lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

::: one-question

The payment is the largest single item in services and runs at near-pure margin. A ban or a materially lower rate resets the services multiple that carries most of the valuation and moves fair value from the base case toward the bear case, regardless of how well the hardware cycle trades.
:::

::: takeaways
1. Watchlist, not ownership: at $344.63 the shares trade at 35.2 times forward earnings against 18.09 for the index, and the 18% discount in the base case depends on a 29 times exit, itself 18% below today's multiple [S7, S97, S146].
2. The franchise is not the problem: services earn 40.3% of gross profit, cash conversion is 0.97x, 0.95x at the band floor, and net cash is $62,173M, so a 30% revenue fall leaves the company solvent [S6].
3. The entry is a price, not a narrative: 0.75-1.0% at $270, a second tranche at $245 and the 5% cap below $225, with $270 above the $242 bear case and a 1.5% maximum loss at the cap [S6, S7].

The Company is experiencing a period of supply constraints and increasing costs for components driven by factors such as industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND) and memory (DRAM). The Company expects these trends to intensify, which may materially negatively impact the Company’s revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations and financial condition. Actions, such as price increases, that have been and may in the future be taken by the Company may not effectively mitigate these negative impacts, and may also reduce demand for the Company’s products and materially adversely affect the Company’s revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations and financial condition.
Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new tariffs were announced on imports to the U.S., including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the European Union (“EU”), among others. In response, several countries have imposed, or threatened to impose, reciprocal tariffs on imports from the U.S. and other retaliatory measures. On January 14, 2026, initial results were published of the previously announced U.S. Department of Commerce investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, into imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products, including downstream products that contain semiconductors. The announcement of the initial results of the investigation did not impose any additional tariffs affecting the Company’s products. Separately, on February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court (“Supreme Court”) issued a ruling striking down certain tariffs previously imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977. The Company has applied for a refund of tariffs paid, following the processes established by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and has recognized any refunds received as a reduction of products cost of sales. Various modifications to U.S. tariffs have been announced, including the recent imposition of tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and further changes could be made in the future, which may include additional measures under the Section 232 semiconductor sector investigation, additional sector-based tariffs, further actions under Section 301, or other measures. Tariffs and other measures that are applied to the Company’s products or their components can have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition, including impacting the Company’s supply chain, the availability of rare earths and other raw materials and components, pricing and gross margin. The ultimate impact remains uncertain and will depend on several factors, including whether additional or incremental U.S. tariffs or other measures are announced or imposed, to what extent other countries implement tariffs or other retaliatory measures in response, and the overall magnitude and duration of these measures. Trade and other international disputes can have an adverse impact on the overall macroeconomic environment and result in shifts and reductions in consumer spending and negative consumer sentiment for the Company’s products and services, all of which can further adversely affect the Company’s business and results of operations.

Section plan:
- Decision question: What is Apple worth today, and what price makes it an attractive long for a long-only fund?
- Final-report thesis sentence: Apple is worth about $212 a share on a 9.0% cost of equity and no more than $277 in the bull case, so at $344.63 the buyer is paying for a 7% return and should wait for about $270 or for evidence that EPS grows above 12%.
- Why this section is different from the other sections: The other sections describe the business and its risks; this one converts them into a price, tests what the price already assumes, and separates repeatable cash earnings from a liability accrual.
- Evidence mechanism to explain: Almost all of the value is terminal, so the cost of equity and the exit multiple, not next year's revenue, set the return; normalising the other-liabilities accrual to a $2,502M three-year average gives a $122.6-127.3bn cash band and separates cash earnings from an unpaid purchase.
- Comparison set / base rate: Peers Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, Dell and HP; Apple's own five fiscal-year multiples and four-year mean; DCF at 7.0-9.5% discount rates and 3-5% terminal growth.

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts fourth-quarter DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to about $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, with the DOJ's cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue, and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income. It matters as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at $1,199 is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in the second half of 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's, and Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.5x diluted (40.2x basic) trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn, 39.8-41.4x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 38%, and the realistic drawdown is $242. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn on the band, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; the deferred-consideration case at $123.2bn, 41.2x, changes neither; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO. arguments.markdown:
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; at 8.5% it gives $277 and at 9.5% $133, so the whole band sits below the close. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth — assumptions that make the price exactly fair, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value here; the difference is arithmetic. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 33 times gives $323 (-6%) and 35 times — today's forward multiple — gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive. The operating case makes 29 times defensible: consensus capitalises a 50.1% June-quarter gross margin that included two points of tariff refunds. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 sets out the FY2027 build; $9.79 is our estimate, not a consensus figure, and a primary consensus feed is still missing. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean rather than a dated series [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights, the $291.5 weighted value and the entry price. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with the DCF at $212-277 below it. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF at a 9.5% cost of equity as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with conduct remedies: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the cloud, not the settlement, created the return. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007 and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record — 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not. At a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201) and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration, not extinction [S143, S145, S147].

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety. At $270 the scenarios return +32.2%, +5.2% and -10.7%, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; the implied Kelly fraction exceeds 100% of the fund, not a usable size for one name, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision and caps the loss at 1.5% of the fund on the 30% drawdown from $344.63 to $241. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the year to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed. Sell above $380, 38.8 times the FY2027 build, or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

arguments.markdown:
The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S146]. The discounted cash flow is $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; and the price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. On exit multiples the answer is a ladder: $284 at 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, $303 at 31 times, $323 at 33 times and $343 at 35 times, so the 18% discount to the base case is a de-rating call. It holds below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times; at 31 times the three-year return in section 12 is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, products earn 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 41.2 times.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. The score table below carries the figures and their sources.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter. At $344.63 the probability-weighted value of $291.5 is 15.4% below the price, so the position is zero. At the first tranche of $270 the three scenarios return +32.2% on the bull case, +5.2% on the base and -10.7% on the bear, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; a full Kelly on those inputs exceeds 100% of the fund, which no single name can carry, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision rather than a Kelly output. At the cap the loss on the 30% bear drawdown from $344.63 to $241 is 1.5% of the fund. The market regime reinforces patience: an elevated volatility percentile, a ten-year yield at 4.93% and a month of technology underperformance against the index are the profile the regime playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10]. The open diligence is the FY2026 10-K detail on working capital and intangibles, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, and the appellate outcome on the search payment.

::: takeaways
1. Do not own Apple at $344.63: the base case is $284 (-18%) on a 29 times exit, and at the stock's own 31 times mean it is $303 (-12%), so the price is full rather than extreme [S6, S7, S97].
2. The two facts that would change the call are a 46% gross margin, which takes fair value to $270 at 29 times, and a D.C. Circuit ban on the search payment, which removes 12.9% of EPS [S17, S99, S76].
3. Stage the entry: 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270, a second tranche at $245, the 5% cap below $225, and a maximum loss of 1.5% of the fund at the cap [S6, S7].
:::

Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured, turning one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Ownership moved first: on 2025-12-01 Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation passed under software chief Craig Federighi with Amar Subramanya as VP of AI, as John Giannandrea stepped down ahead of retirement. Apple bought the part it could not ship and reorganised the rest. [S111, S122, S127]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

The cost of rented intelligence sits in operating expense, not on the balance sheet: research and development rose by a third in nine months while capital spending fell. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and Apple avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A step-up with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one.

### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed retail price a node advantage becomes either margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives Apple control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. The replication test favours the hardware story. A funded engineering team with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge within a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed rather than built, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which questions whether the alerts are accurate and useful. It is a monthly alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. plan.decision_question: Is Apple gaining or losing competitive position, product by product and region by region, and is its pricing power durable?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is winning on profit and price and, since the September 2026 quarter, on share in a shrinking China market, but its services and assistant layer is now contested by OpenAI and Alphabet at a scale no handset rival has reached, so the position is strengthening in hardware, contested in services and exposed to market size rather than share loss.
plan.why_different: This section maps rivals per product with dated shares and prices; it does not re-argue the AI licence or product roadmap, which belong to the technology section, nor the valuation multiple.
plan.mechanism: Apple monetises an installed base through hardware margin and services rent; rivals attack either the hardware price tier (Huawei, Xiaomi, Samsung) or the assistant/subscription layer above the OS (OpenAI, Alphabet), while regulation lowers the rent Apple can charge for distribution.
plan.comparison_set: Per product: Samsung, Huawei and Xiaomi in phones; Lenovo/HP/Dell in PCs; Samsung and Xiaomi in wearables; Spotify, Alphabet and OpenAI in services and subscriptions; Microsoft in cloud and enterprise; the status quo of longer device life.
plan.counter_evidence: OpenAI reached 1.2B weekly users and about $50B annualised revenue by September 2026 without owning a device, and plans hardware with Jony Ive from February 2027; the pricing-power case rests on launch-window mix, not full-cycle elasticity; Android premiumisation and Huawei's HarmonyOS scale could compress Apple's premium share.
plan.visual: Per-product competitor table plus a positioning table by product
plan.prohibited: fierce competition, well positioned, strong team, about, many, recently, huge market, clear business model, high barriers to entry, risks are manageable

rows.finding: ChatGPT reached 1.2 billion weekly users by 2026-09-29 (from 1 billion in July 2026) and OpenAI told investors it reached about $50B annualised revenue at end-September 2026, with 77% total and 107% enterprise run-rate growth in Q3 2026.
rows.mechanism: An assistant can scale across iOS and Android without owning a device, capturing subscription and advertising spend that would otherwise accrue to the platform owner.
rows.benchmark: OpenAI's ~$50B is about 41% of Apple's $120.5B trailing-twelve-month services revenue to June 2026, but grows at 77% a quarter against Apple's 14.1% nine-month services growth.
rows.implication: Treat AI subscription as a real competitor for services wallet and assistant mindshare; it caps the multiple Apple's services can command rather than threatening iPhone units today.
rows.weakens: Profitability is not disclosed and the $50B is below the $68B figure reported in late September 2026, so the revenue base is less certain than the user number.
rows.follow_up: What share of ChatGPT's users pay, and what is its retention against Gemini and Copilot?
rows.confidence: high on users and revenue (two independent outlets, dated), medium on durability because OpenAI discloses no profit.

rows.finding: Microsoft FY2026 revenue was $331.8B, up 17.8%, with a 46.8% operating margin and $115.9B of capital expenditure; Azure held 20% of Q2 2026 cloud infrastructure spend against AWS 28% and Google 15% in a $143.4B quarter.
rows.mechanism: Cloud and AI infrastructure is a scale game funded by cash flow; Apple buys compute (Google TPUs) rather than owning the layer, so it depends on rivals for the capability it sells.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's 17.8% revenue growth is more than five times Apple's 3.3% FY2021-25 revenue CAGR, and its $115.9B capex is an order of magnitude above Apple's capital spending.
rows.implication: Microsoft is not an iPhone rival but a competitor for enterprise AI budgets and a supplier-dependency risk; it weakens the idea that Apple controls its own AI cost curve.
rows.weakens: Microsoft's consumer device and phone presence is negligible, so the threat is to services and AI relevance, not to hardware share.
rows.follow_up: How much of Apple's AI inference runs on third-party silicon, and at what gross-margin cost?
rows.confidence: high, from the FY2026 10-K and XBRL data.

rows.finding: A $100 iPhone 17 Pro price increase in September 2025 was followed by a record December 2025 quarter, with CIRP's US weighted average retail price at $1,077 versus $953 a year earlier; the iPhone 18 Pro then sold 23.5% more in its first three weeks after a further $100 increase.
rows.mechanism: Launch demand is driven by installed-base upgrades and mix toward Pro models, so a price rise raises revenue even if unit elasticity is negative; the observation cannot separate mix from willingness to pay.
rows.benchmark: Two consecutive launch cycles absorbed $100 increases, against the 27.6% market-wide ASP jump in 2026.
rows.implication: Pricing power is partially established at launch, not proven over a full cycle; do not capitalise the 2026 margin as permanent.
rows.weakens: Both observations are launch windows and mix-led, CIRP is US-only and survey-based, and neither gives unit elasticity, so the claim remains an anecdote plus one full-quarter observation.
rows.follow_up: What are iPhone units, not revenue, in the March and June 2027 quarters after the standard iPhone 18 ships?
rows.confidence: medium: two dated observations, different methods and geographies.

rows.finding: Apple took 19.5% of China smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, second and up 4.8 points, against Huawei's 21.3%, in a market down 10% (Counterpoint) or 15.4% (IDC, Apple 17.8%).
rows.mechanism: In a shrinking market, share gains can come from rivals' exit and from pull-forward ahead of price rises; both raise share while lowering the pool.
rows.benchmark: Q2 2026 was 18.1% for Apple against Huawei's 22.6%, so the direction reversed in one quarter.
rows.implication: The China risk is market size and price level, not lost share; underwrite China revenue off a smaller pool.
rows.weakens: The two trackers disagree on the depth of the decline (10% versus 15.4%) and on Apple's level (19.5% versus 17.8%).
rows.follow_up: How much of Apple's Q3 2026 China gain was pull-forward before the iPhone 18 Pro price rise?
rows.confidence: high on direction, medium on magnitude.

rows.finding: From 2026-10-01 the EU charges 5% on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web versus 26% on App Store in-app purchases, after a EUR500M DMA fine in 2025.
rows.mechanism: Regulation lowers switching costs out of the App Store, transferring distribution rent from Apple to developers and rival storefronts.
rows.benchmark: Europe is 26.7% of Apple revenue; Spotify has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music.
rows.implication: Services growth must come from users and new products rather than take rate; price the regulatory ceiling into the services multiple.
rows.weakens: The 5% commission still leaves Apple with a fee on external distribution, and adoption of alternative stores may be slow.
rows.follow_up: What share of EU developers has moved to external distribution since 2026-10-01?
rows.confidence: high on the terms, low on take-up.
