arguments.markdown:
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.1% trailing gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.0% trailing gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | 39.1% trailing; 39.9% 9M FY2026 | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% (9M FY2026) | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Nine-month products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% (the June quarter was 40.1%), and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 — 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield. The price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::

With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, a 9-11% cost of equity is cleared several times; the price is the constraint: $5,029.6bn of market capitalisation on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 is 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield; the $5,072B figure uses the June quarter's 14,715M diluted weighted-average count, 39.3x. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 7,916 characters)
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.1% trailing gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.0% trailing gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | 39.1% trailing; 39.9% 9M FY2026 | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% (9M FY2026) | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Nine-month products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% (the June quarter was 40.1%), and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 — 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield. The price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::"}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 and keeping 27 closures confidential, while challenging the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year, 0.65% of trailing operating income. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. The agreement was confirmed under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. [S111, S98]

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |
| Siri AI out of beta, with five more languages | From 2026-10 | Beta in English since 2026-09-14 | That a licensed model can be made to feel like an Apple product | S113 |
| Standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 | Spring 2027, reported | Unlaunched | A two-cycle year and 2nm volume | S112 |
| Duo durability and return data | FY2027 | Not disclosed | Whether the foldable is a franchise or a flagship experiment | S114 |
| Renewal of India production incentives | After the 2026-03-31 expiry | Unresolved in the sources reviewed | The true cost of the China hedge | S115 |
| DMA interoperability decisions and appeals | Ongoing; 56 requests by 2026-03-22 | In progress | Whether services defaults survive regulation | S119 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation.

rows.finding: Apple's iPhone 18 cycle launched on 2026-09-09 at higher prices: iPhone 18 Pro from $1,199 and Pro Max from $1,299, plus the first foldable, iPhone Duo; the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second Air slipped to spring 2027. iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the June 2026 quarter, +22% year on year, and $196.5bn for nine months, +22%.
rows.mechanism: Apple is defending revenue with price and form-factor mix (Pro, Pro Max, foldable) rather than unit growth, and spreading launches across two events to keep ASP and supply of 2nm parts under control.
rows.benchmark: Prior iPhone 17 cycle and FY2025 iPhone growth; Q3 FY2026 iPhone +22% versus total company +16.4%.
rows.weakens: MacRumors reports Apple raised prices and repriced the iPhone 17 to $899 while memory costs rise, so unit elasticity is untested; the Duo's durability and yield are unproven.
rows.implication: The hardware cycle is not maturing yet; it is being re-priced. Watch Q4 FY2026 (2026-11-02) for whether mix held through launch.
rows.confidence: high — launch and pricing from Apple's own release; revenue from the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What are Duo first-quarter units and return/warranty rates, and did Pro mix hold in the December 2026 quarter?

rows.finding: The rebuilt Siri shipped on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English only, running on a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed 2026-01-12; Bloomberg reported the model at 1.2 trillion parameters and about $1bn a year (neither company confirmed the price). Apple's own foundation-model papers describe on-device and server models.
rows.mechanism: Apple keeps the interface, personal context and Private Cloud Compute wrapper, but licenses frontier reasoning from a competitor; the differentiation moves from model quality to distribution and privacy architecture.
rows.benchmark: Google owns the model, the TPUs and Android; Apple owns the device and the assistant surface but rents the intelligence.
rows.weakens: A 1.2-trillion-parameter rented model versus a published on-device model shows the hardest queries are outsourced; the beta label two years after Apple Intelligence launched is a delay, not a launch.
rows.implication: Siri is a feature that protects the installed base, not a moat that expands it. Price Apple as a hardware-and-services company with an AI option.
rows.confidence: high on dates and the deal; medium on the $1bn and parameter count (press reports, not company disclosure)
rows.follow_up: When does Siri AI leave beta, what proportion of queries route to Gemini, and what does Apple disclose about the cost?

rows.finding: Apple spent $34.04bn on R&D in the first nine months of FY2026, +33% year on year, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. Its foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud.
rows.mechanism: Apple is running an opex-heavy AI strategy: pay for models and rented compute rather than build datacentres, which protects free cash flow but caps frontier scale and hands bargaining power to Google.
rows.benchmark: Hyperscalers capitalise AI infrastructure; Apple's nine-month capex is about 2% of revenue while R&D is running at roughly 30% growth.
rows.weakens: The R&D step-up is a real cost: +$8.4bn in nine months, with no separately disclosed AI revenue to offset it, so margin is the place the bill lands.
rows.implication: Free cash flow stays intact and buybacks continue, but there is no proprietary compute moat to underwrite a higher multiple on AI.
rows.confidence: high — both figures are in the 10-Q cash-flow and income statements
rows.follow_up: What share of the R&D increase is AI infrastructure and depreciation, and does Apple intend to keep renting frontier models after the Gemini term?

rows.finding: The reported $1bn Gemini licence is 0.65% of the $154,859M trailing operating income ($1,000M ÷ $154,859M) and $0.06 of EPS after a 17.3% tax rate on 14,750M diluted shares. Across the more than 2.5bn active devices Apple disclosed on 2026-01-29, per-device pricing at $0.50, $1.00 and $2.00 a year costs $1.25bn, $2.50bn and $5.00bn: EPS $0.07, $0.14 and $0.28, and services gross margin 75.3%, 74.2% and 72.2% if booked as a services cost against a 76.3% base. The reported $1bn implies $0.40 a device.
rows.mechanism: A flat annual licence is an operating cost small against profit; a per-device formula converts it into a variable cost indexed to the installed base, and a per-query formula into a variable cost indexed to usage. The classification (R&D versus services cost of sales) is not disclosed: the 10-Q attributes the R&D increase to AI infrastructure costs and headcount, which points to R&D, but the classification changes which margin is discussed, not EPS.
rows.benchmark: Two hundred basis points of gross margin are worth $0.52 of trailing EPS, eight times the reported licence cost per share; Microsoft's and Alphabet's AI spend is capitalised capex at 33.9-34.9% of revenue, Apple's is opex.
rows.weakens: At $2 per device the cost reaches $5bn and 3.2% of operating income, which would be visible; a per-query formula at 1bn queries a day costs $3.65bn a year for each cent, and Apple discloses neither query volume nor rate.
rows.implication: The licence is not a margin threat at flat or per-device pricing; the risk to underwrite is the renewal formula, not the current $1bn. An investor should ask for the pricing basis before treating the AI bill as immaterial.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic and the installed-base disclosure; medium on the $1bn input (press-reported, not company-confirmed) and low on the classification (not disclosed)
rows.follow_up: Is the licence priced flat, per device or per query, and will it be classified in R&D or services cost of sales when it renews?

rows.finding: Silicon stays the deepest in-house layer: A20 Pro in the iPhone 18 Pro on a 2nm process versus A19 on 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line. Products gross margin rose on mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by memory costs.
rows.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon converts into either margin or performance at fixed price; the modem insourcing removes a Qualcomm royalty and gives Apple control over cellular power and cost.
rows.benchmark: A19 (3nm) to A20 (2nm) is a full node step; the modem shift ends Apple's dependence on an external cellular supplier.
rows.weakens: Component costs are rising: the 10-Q warns of advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints expected to intensify. A node advantage does not protect gross margin when memory prices spike.
rows.implication: Silicon is the moat that is still widening; it supports the products margin line rather than revenue growth.
rows.confidence: medium — 2nm and C2 are press-reported; margins are from the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What is the C2 versus Qualcomm cost delta per unit, and how much of the FY2027 products margin assumption depends on tariff refunds that may not repeat?

rows.finding: U.S. patent grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024 (-12%), placing Apple seventh; the foldable Duo's hinge is made with AI-matched parts, confocal laser scanning and 3D-printed photopolymer micro-layers rather than protected by a single blocking patent.
rows.mechanism: The durable IP sits in process know-how and integration, which is harder to design around but also harder to assert; the portfolio is broad rather than deep in any one blocking area.
rows.benchmark: Apple's grant count is declining while U.S. patent activity overall declined; Huawei and TSMC rank ahead of Apple in the same 2025 table.
rows.weakens: A falling grant count is not proof of a weakening moat, but it removes the patent-count argument for one; the hinge know-how must be proven in field reliability.
rows.implication: Underwrite the moat on switching costs and manufacturing yield, not on patent breadth.
rows.confidence: medium — aggregate counts are third-party (IFI) data; individual patent families were not retrieved
rows.follow_up: What is the granted-versus-pending mix in the foldable and on-device-AI families, and are there blocking third-party hinge or display patents?

rows.finding: Health features are shipping and regulated: Apple Watch hypertension notifications were FDA-cleared, with peer-reviewed commentary in Hypertension treating the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening and questioning accuracy and utility; the feature notifies over a 30-day signal rather than measuring blood pressure.
rows.mechanism: Health adds a regulated, trust-based reason to upgrade a watch every few years and raises the cost of leaving the ecosystem, but it is sold inside a hardware product rather than as a therapy.
rows.benchmark: Apple Watch is described as the most widely adopted consumer health device; the clinical evidence level is a cleared screening notification, not a diagnostic claim.
rows.weakens: Contested clinical value limits pricing power and invites litigation and regulator scrutiny; it is a differentiator, not a new revenue pool.
rows.implication: Wearables and health support the installed base and ASP without changing the growth slope on their own.
rows.confidence: medium — clearance reported by a peer-reviewed journal; the FDA record itself returned no match in the openFDA device search
rows.follow_up: What is the attach and upgrade rate for watches with the hypertension feature, and what does the FDA clearance letter allow Apple to claim?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's silicon/OS/AI stack a durable moat, or is Apple falling behind in AI while the hardware cycle matures?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer that the next upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it.
plan.why_different: This section judges mechanism and replicability of the technology itself — how the silicon, OS and AI layers work and what can be copied — not market size, valuation or the industry's growth rate.
plan.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon and OS converts into margin or performance at a fixed price and into switching costs; buying frontier models and renting TPU compute converts a would-be fixed-cost AI moat into a variable cost paid to a competitor, which protects cash flow but leaves the differentiation in hardware, privacy and distribution. The licence's pricing basis (flat, per device, per query) determines whether that variable cost stays below 1% of operating income or becomes a visible margin line.
plan.comparison_set: Google (owns Gemini, TPUs and Android), Samsung (licenses Google's stack), Huawei (constrained by domestic process), Microsoft (cloud capex model), and Apple's own prior cycle (iPhone 17, A19 3nm, no foldable); on the licence, flat fee versus per-device versus per-query pricing, and two points of gross margin as an EPS benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: AI talent left for Meta through 2025; the Siri rebuild shipped as an English beta in September 2026, two years after Apple Intelligence launched; capex fell while R&D rose; patent grants fell 12%; the Duo's hinge durability is unproven; memory costs threaten products margin; a per-query renewal would turn the licence into a services-margin item.
plan.visual: The licence sensitivity table (per-device price against annual cost, services gross margin, EPS and share of operating income) plus the moat table with the replication test (funded team of 50), the performance-metrics table and the evidence component on the Google dependency.
plan.prohibited: AI leader, seamless ecosystem, strong team, huge market, well positioned, innovative company, best-in-class without a metric, 'many patents', 'about' before a figure, any sentence describing how the section is written.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, 8,922 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; at 8.5% it gives $277 and at 9.5% $133, so the whole band sits below the close. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth — assumptions that make the price exactly fair, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value here; the difference is arithmetic. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 33 times gives $323 (-6%) and 35 times — today's forward multiple — gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive. The operating case makes 29 times defensible: consensus capitalises a 50.1% June-quarter gross margin that included two points of tariff refunds. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 sets out the FY2027 build; $9.79 is our estimate, not a consensus figure, and a primary consensus feed is still missing. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean rather than a dated series [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights, the $291.5 weighted value and the entry price. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with conduct remedies: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the cloud, not the settlement, created the return. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007 and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record — 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not. At a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201) and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration, not extinction [S143, S145, S147].

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price. arguments.markdown:
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; at 8.5% it gives $277 and at 9.5% $133, so the whole band sits below the close. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth — assumptions that make the price exactly fair, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value here; the difference is arithmetic. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 33 times gives $323 (-6%) and 35 times — today's forward multiple — gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive. The operating case makes 29 times defensible: consensus capitalises a 50.1% June-quarter gross margin that included two points of tariff refunds. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 sets out the FY2027 build; $9.79 is our estimate, not a consensus figure, and a primary consensus feed is still missing. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean rather than a dated series [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights, the $292 weighted value and the entry price. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with the DCF at $212-277 below it. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF at a 9.5% cost of equity as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S146]. The discounted cash flow is $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; and the price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. On exit multiples the answer is a ladder: $284 at 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, $303 at 31 times, $323 at 33 times and $343 at 35 times, so the 18% discount to the base case is a de-rating call. It holds below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times; at 31 times the three-year return in section 12 is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, products earn 39.9% on a nine-month basis and 40.1% in the June quarter against 36.9% a year earlier, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. The score table below carries the figures and their sources.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter. At $344.63 the probability-weighted value of $292 is 15.3% below the price, so the position is zero. At the cap the loss on the 30% bear drawdown from $344.63 to $241 is 1.5% of the fund. arguments.markdown:
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. A discounted cash flow gives $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at the stock's own mean of 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence; the difference lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value of $292 is 15.3% below the price; at $270 a fractional Kelly of 39% of the fund still exceeds the 5% cap, which is why the cap is a risk-budget limit rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision [S6, S7].

arguments.markdown:
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares and $5,072bn on 14,715m diluted shares, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS; 39.0x on market value over $128,930M net income) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025 ($365.8bn to $416.2bn), and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung Electronics and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements and their multiples are not disclosed here, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story behind the multiple is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn year-on-year swing overstates it, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor treats the build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised nine-month FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025 [S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The weights and the $270 entry price come from the exit-multiple set, not the DCF cases. It applies 35x, 29x and 24.6x to FY2027 EPS — $10.20 in the bull case on a 34.4% operating margin, $9.79 in the base and bear — and weights them 25/50/25 to a $291.5 value, 15% below the price.

The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile [S97, S153]. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows.

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The counter-case deserves its weight. The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; $9.79 is the report's own build, and the only street target found is the low-confidence $338-355 range.

Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares and $5,072bn on 14,715m diluted shares, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS; 39.0x on market value over $128,930M net income) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025 ($365.8bn to $416.2bn), and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story behind the multiple is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn year-on-year swing overstates it, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor treats the build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised nine-month FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025 [S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

Revenue grows 9% to $519.9bn in FY2027 and 8% then 7% to $600.9bn in FY2029; gross margin normalises to 48.0% and then 47.5% as memory costs bite; the operating margin falls from 33.0% to 32.0%; tax is 17.5% (17.3% trailing); diluted shares fall from 14,550m to 13,940m on $82-90bn of annual buybacks; other income is $1.0-1.2bn.

The weights and the $270 entry price come from the exit-multiple set, not the DCF cases. It applies 35x, 29x and 24.6x to FY2027 EPS — $10.20 in the bull case on a 34.4% operating margin, $9.79 in the base and bear — and weights them 25/50/25 to a $291.5 value, 15% below the price.

| Weighted | | | $291.5 | 100% | S6, S7, S97 |

The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile [S97, S153]. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows.

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The counter-case deserves its weight. The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; $9.79 is the report's own build, and the only street target found is the low-confidence $338-355 range.

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story behind the multiple is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn year-on-year swing overstates it, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor treats the build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised nine-month FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025 [S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The weights and the $270 entry price come from the exit-multiple set, not the DCF cases. It applies 35x, 29x and 24.6x to FY2027 EPS — $10.20 in the bull case on a 34.4% operating margin, $9.79 in the base and bear — and weights them 25/50/25 to a $291.5 value, 15% below the price.

| Bull | 35x | $10.20 | $357 | 25% | S6, S7, S97 |
| Base | 29x | $9.79 | $284 | 50% | S6, S7, S97 |

| Weighted | | | $291.5 | 100% | S6, S7, S97 |

The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile [S97, S153]. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows.

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The counter-case deserves its weight. The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; $9.79 is the report's own build, and the only street target found is the low-confidence $338-355 range.

scenarios.evidence: The iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% year on year with memory 34% of it; the Ninth Circuit affirmed civil contempt on 2025-12-11; the DOJ cross-appeal seeks a payment ban; losing $20B is 12.9% of EPS [S99, S79, S76, S6].

assumptions.assumption: Gross margin normalises to 47-48%, not the 50.1% June-quarter print, as tariff refunds lapse and memory costs reset.
assumptions.disproof: A December 2026 quarter guided at or above 49% gross margin with FY2027 memory contracted at fixed prices.
assumptions.impact: -6.0% EPS per 200 basis points of gross margin, and multiple compression on a peak-earnings read [S6, S17].
assumptions.early_warning: The 2026-11-02 guidance and TrendForce bill-of-materials data, where the iPhone 18 Pro BOM is up 38% with memory at 34% of it [S99, S72].

assumptions.assumption: The Google default-search payment survives the D.C. Circuit appeal, renegotiated lower rather than banned.
assumptions.disproof: An appellate ruling banning payments or capping them below the current economics.
assumptions.impact: A ban is -12.9% of EPS and about 15% of operating income; a materially lower rate resets the services multiple [S6, S80].
assumptions.early_warning: D.C. Circuit briefing and decision expected in 2027; DOJ and state cross-appeal filed February 2026 [S76, S80].

assumptions.assumption: Services grows 12-14% without relying on hardware mix, and the EU take-rate cut does not accelerate.
assumptions.disproof: Two consecutive quarters of services growth below 10%, or faster migration to external distribution in the EU after 2026-10-01.
assumptions.impact: A 3-point cut in services growth removes roughly a tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value; each $1B of EU commission lost is $0.75B of gross profit [S78].
assumptions.early_warning: The quarterly services line and developer take-up of the 5% Core Technology Commission [S77, S6].

assumptions.assumption: The buyback continues at $80B a year or more with net cash positive, so EPS growth keeps its 2-3 point financial tailwind.
assumptions.disproof: A cut to the authorisation, or repurchases funded by new debt.
assumptions.impact: Buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% nine-month EPS growth; losing that cuts EPS growth to mid-single digits [S6, S17].
assumptions.early_warning: The May 2027 authorisation and the FY2026 10-K cash-flow statement [S5, S6].

assumptions.assumption: The Gemini licence stays an R&D expense and is not repriced per device or per query into services margin.
assumptions.disproof: Renewal terms disclosed that price the model per device or per query.
assumptions.impact: A $1B annual licence is 0.65% of TTM operating income; per-device pricing across a 2.5B installed base would be several times that [S111, S73].
assumptions.early_warning: Renewal commentary from Apple or Google, and any services margin step-down unexplained by mix [S111].

consensus.consensus: The market pays 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings, which implies a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual NOPAT growth, and consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4B in FY2026 (+20.4%) and $277.4B in FY2027 (+9.9%) with the 2026 gross margin as the base.
consensus.our_view: Non-consensus on price, not on franchise: the business is a genuine compounder, but the 2026 margin is a peak and even the DCF at an 8.5% cost of equity ($277) sits below $344.63. The evidence supports a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at the current multiple.
consensus.evidence: The DCF is $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, the sum of the parts $177-238 and the DCF at 8.5% is $277; the market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and the June-quarter margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds [S6, S10, S71, S72, S17].
consensus.proof_event: The December-quarter gross-margin guide on 2026-11-02, and the D.C. Circuit decision on the Google payments expected in 2027.

one_question.question: Will the Google default-search payment survive the D.C. Circuit appeal, and at what annual rate?
one_question.why: The payment, put at $20B in 2022 by the trial record, is 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and about 15% of operating income at near-pure margin. A ban or a materially lower rate resets the services multiple that carries most of the valuation, and it moves fair value from the base case toward the bear case regardless of how well the hardware cycle trades.

Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, with the DOJ's cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares and $5,072bn on 14,715m diluted shares, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS; 39.0x on market value over $128,930M net income) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025 ($365.8bn to $416.2bn), and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story behind the multiple is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn year-on-year swing overstates it, because the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor treats the build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months and capital expenditure sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised nine-month FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and total debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

| Weighted | | | $291.5 | 100% | S6, S7, S97 |

The weights and the $270 entry price come from this exit-multiple set, not the DCF cases: the bull row applies 35x to $10.20, a 34.4% operating margin, and the table weights 25/50/25 to $291.5, 15% below the price. The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows. The investor implication is a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at $344.63; at today's price the shares are a hold only for a holder with a lower basis [S6, S7, S97, S153].

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The counter-case deserves its weight. The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range in the table.
