Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn swing overstates it: the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor treats the build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in nine months and capex sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow suits a company whose value is almost all terminal, and is the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

| Base | 29x | $9.79 | $284 | 50% | S6, S7, S97 |

The weights and the $270 entry price come from this exit-multiple set, not the DCF: the bull row applies 35x to $10.20 on a 34.4% operating margin, and the weights give $291.5, 15% below the price. The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows. The investor implication is a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at $344.63; at today's price the shares are a hold only for a holder with a lower basis [S6, S7, S97, S153].

The sum of the parts shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range in the table.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares and $5,072bn on 14,715m diluted shares, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS; 39.0x on market value over $128,930M net income) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025 ($365.8bn to $416.2bn), and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn swing overstates it: the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor treats the build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles; on the $13.5bn non-current build alone the figure is $123.2bn and 41.2x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in nine months and capex sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow suits a company whose value is almost all terminal, and is the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The weights and the $270 entry price come from this exit-multiple set, not the DCF: the bull row applies 35x to $10.20 on a 34.4% operating margin, and the weights give $291.5, 15% below the price. The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows. The investor implication is a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at $344.63; at today's price the shares are a hold only for a holder with a lower basis [S6, S7, S97, S153].

The sum of the parts shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range in the table.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With a 1.9% dividend and gross buyback yield and earnings per share compounding at 8.2%, the arithmetic clears a 9% hurdle only while the 35.2x forward multiple holds; if it reverts to the four-year mean of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 at 2026-07-17; 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. As the table shows, Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so the exit is never closed and market impact is measured in basis points. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on the $5,029.6bn basic market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2027E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.2% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return at the current 35.2x forward multiple | 5.7% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return at the 31.0x four-year mean | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8.2% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is not a scandal; it is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. Measured on the forward basis used here, a reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x is -11.9% on the multiple, about -4.1% a year over three years, which the 8.2% EPS growth and 1.9% yield more than offset but leave only +1.3% a year. The 29x base case in the valuation is 18% below the market for the same reason: at the 31.0x mean the same earnings give $303, 12% below. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

| Precedent realisation | Year | Value | Multiple at the time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repurchases, FY2022 | 2022 | $89.4bn | 24.6x year-end P/E | S2, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2023 | 2023 | $77.6bn | 27.9x | S3, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2024 | 2024 | $94.9bn | 37.5x | S4, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2025 | 2025 | $90.7bn | 34.2x | S5, S7 |
| Observed drawdown, twelve months to 2026-10-30 | 2026 | $243.42 low | 29.4% below $344.63 | S7 |

The precedents are all capital returns, because that is the only exit a company of this size has ever offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-27% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 35.2x forward makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

The sell discipline follows from that table, which assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45 built in section 8, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. The band is a judgement around the 31.0x four-year mean, not a dated forward series; at 31x the return from $344.63 is 1.3% a year, and at the current 35.2x it is 5.7%. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12%. The conditions that would make me raise the entry price are specific and observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The conditions that force a sale are equally specific: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The drawdown case sets the risk, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241: 24.6x FY2027E earnings of $9.79 is $240.8, and the 2022 multiple is the low end of the four-year range; the $243.42 low printed within the past twelve months is a separate observed anchor. That is a 30% drawdown, and it is the realistic bad case for a fund holding the shares. The $133 DCF case at a 9.5% discount rate is a different animal — gross margin compression, 2-4% growth and a higher rate — and should be read as the permanent-loss scenario rather than the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded strongly while the technology sector fell in the last month, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That is a reason to size modestly and buy on weakness rather than to abandon the arithmetic: the exit route is liquid, the cash return is real and growing, and the only thing between today's price and the fund's required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is publicly disclosed in the sources here and both set the floor under the services multiple.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With a 1.9% dividend and gross buyback yield and earnings per share compounding at 8.2%, the arithmetic clears a 9% hurdle only while the 35.2x forward multiple holds; if it reverts to the four-year mean of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 at 2026-07-17; 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so market impact is measured in basis points. Price cannot: the buyers are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on the $5,029.6bn basic market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2027E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.2% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return at the current 35.2x forward multiple | 5.7% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return at the 31.0x four-year mean | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8.2% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. On the forward basis, a reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x is -11.9% on the multiple, about -4.1% a year over three years, which the 8.2% EPS growth and 1.9% yield more than offset but leave only +1.3% a year. The 29x base case is 18% below the market for the same reason; at 31.0x the same earnings give $303, 12% below. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS continuous auction | $13.8bn a day; exit complete in days | Any trading day | Near-certain, and the default route | S7 |
| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

| Precedent realisation | Year | Value | Multiple at the time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repurchases, FY2022 | 2022 | $89.4bn | 24.6x year-end P/E | S2, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2023 | 2023 | $77.6bn | 27.9x | S3, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2024 | 2024 | $94.9bn | 37.5x | S4, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2025 | 2025 | $90.7bn | 34.2x | S5, S7 |
| Observed drawdown, twelve months to 2026-10-30 | 2026 | $243.42 low | 29.4% below $344.63 | S7 |

The precedents are all capital returns: the only exit a company of this size has offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-27% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 35.2x forward makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

| Entry price | Exit at 27x | Exit at 31x | Exit at 34x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 (2026-10-30) | -3.2% | 1.3% | 4.5% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $300 | 1.4% | 6.1% | 9.4% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $240 | 9.2% | 14.3% | 17.9% | S6, S7, S97 |

The sell discipline follows from that table, which assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45 built in section 8, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. The band is a judgement around the 31.0x four-year mean, not a dated forward series; at 31x the return from $344.63 is 1.3% a year, and at the current 35.2x it is 5.7%. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12%. The conditions to raise the entry price are observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The sale triggers are: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The drawdown case sets the risk, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241: 24.6x FY2027E earnings of $9.79 is $240.8, and the 2022 multiple is the low end of the four-year range; the $243.42 low printed within the past twelve months is a separate observed anchor. That is the realistic 30% drawdown for a fund holding the shares. The $133 DCF case at 9.5% — margin compression, 2-4% growth and a higher rate — is the permanent-loss scenario, not the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded strongly while the technology sector fell, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That argues for modest sizing and buying weakness, not abandoning the arithmetic: the exit is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is publicly disclosed in the sources here and both set the floor under the services multiple.

**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, handset re-pricing is evidenced only at launch rather than through a cost cycle, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, with the DOJ's cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue, and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income. It matters as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at $1,199 is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in the second half of 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's, and Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.2x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.5-41.0x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,029.6bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: from the 35.2x forward base, reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 11.9%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 30.1%, and the bear exit value is $241. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the 9.5% DCF; free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn on the band, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; the deferred-consideration case at $123.2bn, 40.8x, changes neither; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO. The 2025-12-06 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency, with no disclosed successor or retention award. The 107% payout is a tax artefact: FY2024 carried a $10.2bn State Aid charge and FY2025 paid $15.8bn of Irish tax. Cash quality is a smaller risk than it looked: a $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities against $13,270M of gross intangibles added, with $1,780M of investing "other", reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M fall in other current liabilities the build is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M other-liabilities line; if the whole purchase is unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, $1.9bn below the $125.1bn central case and inside the $122.6-127.3bn band. The 10-K on 2026-11-02 must tie the intangibles to the liability. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence is narrow: the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts fourth-quarter DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to about $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount. The 40.1% product margin is not permanent: the only pricing evidence is two launch windows — CIRP's $1,077 US-WARP in the December-2025 quarter against $953 after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro rise, and iPhone 18 Pro sales 23.5% higher in three weeks after a further $100 — both mix-led and launch-bound, with full-cycle elasticity unproven. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel. [S17, S6, S99, S136, S150, S96, S84]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, handset pricing is evidenced only at launch rather than through a cost cycle, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, with the DOJ's cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue, and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income. It matters as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at $1,199 is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in the second half of 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's, and Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.2x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.5-41.0x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,029.6bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 11.9% and to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 30.1% from the 35.2x forward base, and the bear exit value is $241. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the 9.5% DCF; free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn on the band, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; the deferred-consideration case at $123.2bn, 40.8x, changes neither; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO. The 2025-12-06 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency, with no disclosed successor or retention award. The 107% payout is a tax artefact: FY2024 carried a $10.2bn State Aid charge and FY2025 paid $15.8bn of Irish tax. Cash quality is a smaller risk than it looked: a $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities against $13,270M of gross intangibles added, with $1,780M of investing "other", reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M fall in other current liabilities the build is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M other-liabilities line; if the whole purchase is unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, $1.9bn below the $125.1bn central case and inside the $122.6-127.3bn band. The 10-K on 2026-11-02 must tie the intangibles to the liability. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence is narrow: the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 4 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,912 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; at 8.5% it gives $277 and at 9.5% $133, so the whole band sits below the close. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth — assumptions that make the price exactly fair, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value here; the difference is arithmetic. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 33 times gives $323 (-6%) and 35 times — today's forward multiple — gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive. The operating case makes 29 times defensible: consensus capitalises a 50.1% June-quarter gross margin that included two points of tariff refunds. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 sets out the FY2027 build; $9.79 is our estimate, not a consensus figure, and a primary consensus feed is still missing. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean rather than a dated series [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights, the $292 weighted value and the entry price. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with the DCF at $212-277 below it. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF at a 9.5% cost of equity as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with conduct remedies: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the cloud, not the settlement, created the return. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007 and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record — 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not. At a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201) and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration, not extinction [S143, S145, S147].

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $241 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety. At $270 the scenarios return +32.2%, +5.2% and -10.7%, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; a fractional Kelly of 39% of the fund still exceeds what one name can carry, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision and caps the loss at 1.5% of the fund on the 30% drawdown from $344.63 to $241. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the year to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed. Sell above $380, 38.8 times the FY2027 build, or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

Apple is a quality compounder priced for a peak margin and a contested services annuity: the risks that matter destroy the multiple, not the balance sheet, and none is priced at $344.63. At that 2026-10-30 price the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median; the DCF is $212 at 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%. [S7, S97, S10]

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp off a 40.1% margin; -25% to -30% value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM/NAND prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -11.9% at 31.0x; -30.1% at 24.6x, from 35.2x forward | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield above 5%; forward P/E above 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Cash quality and inventory | Medium, 30-50% | FCF -$1.9bn to $123.2bn, 40.8x; inventory -$3.3bn | Low | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | Other-liabilities note; inventory $11.1bn | Underwrite the $123.2bn case | S6, S5, S17 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | No named successor; director exits | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S141, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts fourth-quarter DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to about $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount. The 40.1% product margin is not permanent: pricing evidence is two launch windows only — a record $1,077 US-WARP after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro rise, and iPhone 18 Pro sales +23.5% in three weeks after a further $100 — both mix-led, launch-bound and struck into a cost shock, so full-cycle elasticity is unproven. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel. [S17, S6, S99, S136, S150, S96, S84]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, handset pricing is evidenced only at launch, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal No. 26-5023, with the DOJ cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue, and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income. It matters as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini licence reported at $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capex fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books it in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across 2.5bn devices would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells $1,199 handsets is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% (Counterpoint) and 15.4% (IDC), with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in H2 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's; Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.2x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.5-41.0x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,029.6bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 11.9% and to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 30.1% from the 35.2x forward base, and the bear exit value is $241. Each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the debate. Stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the 9.5% DCF; free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn on the band, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; deferred consideration at $123.2bn, 40.8x, changes neither; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

The board waived its age guideline for two directors who stood in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO. The 2025-12-06 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, concentrating rather than removing the dependency, with no disclosed successor or retention award. The 107% payout is a tax artefact: FY2024's $10.2bn State Aid charge and FY2025's $15.8bn Irish tax payment. Cash quality is a smaller risk than it looked: a $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities against $13,270M of gross intangibles added, with $1,780M of investing "other", reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M fall in other current liabilities the build is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M other-liabilities line; if the whole purchase is unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, $1.9bn below the $125.1bn central case and inside the $122.6-127.3bn band. The 10-K on 2026-11-02 must tie the intangibles to the liability. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence: the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 6 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,974 characters)
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With a 1.9% dividend and gross buyback yield and earnings per share compounding at 8.2%, the arithmetic clears a 9% hurdle only while the 35.2x forward multiple holds; if it reverts to the four-year mean of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so market impact is measured in basis points. Price cannot: the buyers are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8.2% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. On the forward basis, a reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x is -11.9% on the multiple, about -4.1% a year over three years, which the 8.2% EPS growth and 1.9% yield more than offset but leave only +1.3% a year. The 29x base case is 18% below the market for the same reason; at 31.0x the same earnings give $303, 12% below. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12%. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

That argues for modest sizing and buying weakness, not abandoning the arithmetic: the exit is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. ### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Nine months reconcile exactly: products gross profit of $108,819M on $272,629M is 39.9%, services $69,963M on $91,728M is 76.3%, summing to the filed $178,782M; the quarter ran at 40.1% and 75.6%, so applying 40.1% to nine-month products would overstate gross profit by about $0.5B. Services earn 40.3% of the trailing $227,123M gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue at 76.0%. The 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S6, S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS (S17); products gross margin is 39.9% against 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% (S6, S68).
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M; working capital supplied $16,366M of the gap. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build reconciling within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision). The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.2x price to free cash flow on the $5,029.6bn market capitalisation; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B (39.5-41.0x), with $125.1B the midpoint; anything below $122.6B subtracts more than the line contains. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, making $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion at 3.2% of trailing revenue. [S5, S6]

arguments.markdown:
Apple is a quality compounder priced for a peak margin and a contested services annuity: the risks that matter destroy the multiple, not the balance sheet, and none is priced at $344.63. At that 2026-10-30 price the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median; the DCF is $212 at 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%. [S7, S97, S10]

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp off a 40.1% margin; -25% to -30% value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM/NAND prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -11.9% at 31.0x; -30.1% at 24.6x, from 35.2x forward | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield above 5%; forward P/E above 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Cash quality and inventory | Medium, 30-50% | FCF -$1.9bn to $123.2bn, 40.8x; inventory -$3.3bn | Low | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | Other-liabilities note; inventory $11.1bn | Underwrite the $123.2bn case | S6, S5, S17 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | No named successor; director exits | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S141, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts fourth-quarter DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to about $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount. The 40.1% product margin is not permanent: pricing evidence is two launch windows only — CIRP's record $1,077 US-WARP after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro rise, and iPhone 18 Pro sales +23.5% in three weeks after a further $100 — both mix-led, launch-bound and made during a cost shock, so full-cycle elasticity is unproven. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel. [S17, S6, S99, S136, S150, S96, S84]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, handset pricing is evidenced only at launch, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal No. 26-5023, with the DOJ cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue, and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income. It matters as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini licence reported at $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capex fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books it in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across 2.5bn devices would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells $1,199 handsets is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% (Counterpoint) and 15.4% (IDC), with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in H2 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's; Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.2x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.5-41.0x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,029.6bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 11.9% and to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 30.1% from the 35.2x forward base, and the bear exit value is $241. Each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the debate. Stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the 9.5% DCF; free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn on the band, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; deferred consideration at $123.2bn, 40.8x, changes neither; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

The board waived its age guideline for two directors who stood in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO. The 2025-12-06 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, concentrating rather than removing the dependency, with no disclosed successor or retention award. The 107% payout is a tax artefact: FY2024's $10.2bn State Aid charge and FY2025's $15.8bn Irish tax payment. Cash quality is a smaller risk than it looked: a $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities against $13,270M of gross intangibles added, with $1,780M of investing "other", reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M fall in other current liabilities the build is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M other-liabilities line; if the whole purchase is unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, $1.9bn below the $125.1bn central case and inside the $122.6-127.3bn band. The 10-K on 2026-11-02 must tie the intangibles to the liability. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence: the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 6 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,849 characters)
Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year; Omdia 1.25B | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7%, steepest fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP) | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |

Two independent methods agree the market grows in dollars while shrinking in units, and sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and full-cycle elasticity is not established. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every segment in double digits, but that is margin evidence, not elasticity evidence. Two launch windows point to low elasticity: CIRP's US weighted average retail price reached a record December-quarter $1,077 after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro increase, and iPhone 18 Pro sales rose 23.5% in three weeks after a further $100 rise; both are mix-led and launch-bound, so they are anecdotes, not proof. IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months [S17, S87, S84, S150, S96].

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one can change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth $45.7B. Services: $120.5B trailing twelve months to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a $1.34T advertising pool in 2026 and $149B of App Store digital goods in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030, with smartwatches down 3.7% in 2026 and glasses up 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. The non-phone pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
