| Europe | Not published | Apple +16.1% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 26.7% of revenue | DMA take-rate cuts from 2026-10-01; GDPR | Samsung, Xiaomi, Google | S77, S6 |
| Greater China | 66M units in Q2 2026; 134M in H1 2026 | Market -10% in Q3 2026 (Counterpoint), -15.4% (IDC); H2 2026 decline could reach 20%; Apple +30.0% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 19.5% share in Q3 2026 versus Huawei's 21.3%, up 4.8 points YoY | Market access; local champion; data rules | Huawei, OPPO, vivo, Xiaomi, Honor | S139, S140, S87, S6 |
| Japan | Not published | Apple +10.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 6.9% of revenue | Yen weakness; carrier-controlled channel | Samsung, Google, Sharp | S6 |
| Rest of Asia-Pacific | Not published; emerging markets forecast down more than 20% in 2026 | Apple +19.4% in 9M FY2026 | Entered; 8.1% of revenue; India manufacturing and retail expansion | Price sensitivity; tariffs | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, OPPO, Transsion | S84, S6 |

Geography splits the durability question, and policy is a live variable in every region [S6, S87, S77]. Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue but produced 30% growth in the first nine months of FY2026; Europe is 26.7% and grew 16%, the Americas 42.9% and 11%, Japan 6.9% and 10%, and Rest of Asia-Pacific 8.1% and 19%. The China number is the most fragile in size, not share: the market fell 10% in Q3 2026 to the lowest third-quarter level since 2012, yet Apple's share rose 4.8 points to 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, and the top six vendors hold 96%. The EU's DMA terms cut the commission on externally distributed digital transactions to 5% from 1 October 2026. US tariffs moved twice in 2026: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026 and Section 301 duties were imposed since, while the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs on Apple products on 14 January 2026. Demand is organic consumer replacement, not policy-created: China's subsidies faded in 2026 and India's incentives are supply-side manufacturing support. The budget owner is the consumer or carrier financing plan; the procurement cycle follows the annual September launch; willingness to pay is being tested by the 27.6% ASP increase. What would change the conclusion: services growth above 15% with user growth, a foldable cycle adding IDC's $45.7B category value, or China stabilising after H2 2026. Confidence is high on 2026 data and low on 2027-2030 regional sizing, because regional market values are paywalled and Apple does not disclose units; the open questions are what share of iPhone growth is units versus price, whether services growth is users or price, how much China demand was pulled forward, and how much memory cost Apple can pass through in FY2027.

::: evidence
**Apple's markets are growing in dollars while shrinking in units, so its growth is price- and share-led, not market-led.**

The global pool is $613B of smartphone value in 2026 against just over 1.0B units, with a 27.6% ASP increase doing the work volume used to do (IDC, S84). Premium concentration (29% of units) and Apple's 65% share of it explain why Apple captures 36-43% of value on 20-24% of units (Counterpoint, S94; Apple filings, S5, S6). Foldables ($45.7B of category value by 2027) and services ($120.5B TTM at 76.0% gross margin) are the only pools large enough to move group growth; wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030 (IDC, S85).

Apple is winning on profit and price and, since the September 2026 quarter, on share in a shrinking China market: a 65% share of premium phone units at a 40.1% product gross margin, Huawei ahead in China 21.3% to 19.5% but Apple up 4.8 points, and regulation capping the services take rate. | Lenovo, HP, Dell | PC lines | Windows on x86 | Unrestricted | Enterprise channel | $600-2,000 | 24.4%, 19.1%, 13.6% Q2 2026 | Price tiers | No OS-silicon integration | S95 |

Huawei is the most dangerous rival to Apple's profit pool, Samsung to its unit position. Huawei led China 21.3% to 19.5% in Q3 2026, after 22.6% to 18.1% in Q2, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026, funded by CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of 2025 revenue [S96, S139, S140, S86]. Samsung is broader, with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth. Huawei takes price and Samsung volume, at a loss.

Apple's global smartphone market share was 20% in 2025 to Samsung's 19%, and 22% in Q3 2026 to Samsung's 23%, so its position moves sideways even as value capture rises [S92, S120, S94, S84, S150]. The premium layer is where Apple improves: a 65% share of $600-plus units in H1 2026, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% in 2026. Pricing power is partially established, not proven, because part of the price rise is a memory shock, with NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier. The mechanism is mix: a $100 Pro increase lifts revenue per unit even if unit demand is flat. Elasticity evidence is two launch windows: after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro increase in September 2025, CIRP put the US weighted average retail price at a record December-quarter $1,077 against $953, and iPhone 18 Pro sales rose 23.5% in the first three weeks after a further $100 rise. Both are mix-led launch windows, therefore full-cycle elasticity is not established.

China is where risk has flipped from share loss to market contraction [S139, S140, S87, S6]. Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% to the lowest third-quarter level since 2012 (Counterpoint) and 15.4% (IDC); Apple took 19.5%, up 4.8 points, Huawei led at 21.3%, and the two were the only top brands to gain. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in nine months of FY2026. The vulnerability is the pool's size and price level: IDC expects component costs elevated through much of 2027, Apple raised iPhone 18 Pro prices by $100 and holds the standard iPhone 18 to spring 2027, so part of the gain is pull-forward. Apple has steadied China without regaining structural leadership; HarmonyOS still gives Huawei a localisation advantage.

Two competitors sit above the handset fight; neither needs a phone to reach Apple's services wallet [S148, S149, S151, S118]. ChatGPT reached 1.2 billion weekly users by 29 September 2026, and OpenAI told investors it had about $50B of annualised revenue at end-September, 77% run-rate growth in the quarter against Apple's 14.1% services growth in nine months. That is 41% of Apple's $120.5B services revenue. OpenAI is also a future hardware entrant, working with Jony Ive on a device shipping no earlier than February 2027. Microsoft attacks the layer beneath: $331.8B of FY2026 revenue at a 46.8% operating margin and 20% of Q2 2026 cloud spend to AWS's 28% and Google's 15%. Apple buys compute rather than owning it, including Google TPUs, so its AI cost curve depends on rivals.

Regulation transfers rent from Apple to rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. That lowers switching costs in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and gives Spotify and rival storefronts an iOS channel; Spotify has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. Its spread to other jurisdictions is the risk to monitor.

| Services and AI | Challenger | OpenAI in AI subscriptions; Alphabet in advertising | Apple in app distribution | Spotify in music; Microsoft in enterprise AI | DMA-enabled alternative stores | S149, S151, S93, S77 |

That supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated services ceiling, not a share-gain story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China, medium on services. Diligence questions: how much of the premium and China gain is price inflation, how much ChatGPT usage substitutes for Siri, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, and whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 6 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,900 characters)
Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a 2.5-billion-device installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer this cycle sells on is rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capex fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026; the standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was cut to $899. Selling the 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March turns one spike into two, and the A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm plus the in-house C2 modem are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed price a node advantage becomes margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing expects semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. Prices rose into that memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112, S6]

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |
| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Own TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| AI organisation | Under Software Engineering since 2025-12-01 | DeepMind | Own research | Own research | S127 |

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as an English beta, five more languages promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither confirmed the price. Apple contributes the interface, personal context, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Ownership moved first: on 2025-12-01 Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety passed to software chief Craig Federighi, with Amar Subramanya as VP of AI, as John Giannandrea stepped down ahead of retirement. Apple bought what it could not ship. [S111, S122, S127]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed on 2026-01-12 a multi-year deal to supply Gemini for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface; not the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The licence is small per device and dangerous per query

At the reported $1bn a year the Gemini licence is 0.65% of the $154,859M trailing operating income and $0.06 of EPS, below the $0.52 that 200 basis points of gross margin are worth. Across the 2.5 billion active devices Apple disclosed on 2026-01-29, $0.50, $1 and $2 per device a year cost $1.25bn, $2.5bn and $5.0bn, taking EPS to $0.07, $0.14 and $0.28; booked as a service they would cut services gross margin from 76.3% to 75.3%, 74.2% and 72.2%. The $1bn implies $0.40 a device. Apple does not disclose the classification; R&D up 33% on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence" while capex fell points to R&D, and the choice changes the margin narrative, not EPS. The tail is per-query pricing: at an assumed 1 billion queries a day each cent is $3.65bn a year; Apple discloses neither volume nor rate. [S6, S111, S152]

### Where the moat actually sits

| Silicon design and process access | 8 | Custom SoC, 2nm allocation, modem integration | 4-6 years | S113, S112 |

| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite moat** | **Strong hardware, weak AI** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | Years on hardware | S113, S6 |

The replication test favours hardware: a funded team of fifty with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge in a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which questions their accuracy; a monthly alert is not a measurement, so the claim is narrow. Vision Pro sits inside Wearables with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. Both add upgrade reasons and are sold as features, not platforms with their own economics. [S124, S5]

### The patent position is broad, thinning and hard to verify

The portfolio is broad rather than anchored in one blocking family, and it thinned in 2025, when Apple slipped down the U.S. ranking (table below). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 7,916 characters)
Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.1% trailing gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.0% trailing gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| Line item | Per unit — per active device, per year | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $186.7 | $466,823M TTM ÷ 2,500M devices | S6, S73 |
| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |
| Research and development | ($17.2) | $42,901M TTM | S6 |
| Operating profit | $61.9 | $154,859M TTM | S6 |
| Gross profit ÷ selling cost | 7.8x a year | $90.8 ÷ $11.7 | S6 |
| Cash payback on acquisition | immediate | cash conversion cycle −56.8 days | S5, S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

| Offer | Price or take rate | Margin or peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (upfront hardware) | implied ASP $941 ($245,540M TTM ÷ 261M estimated units) | 39.1% trailing; 39.9% 9M FY2026 | S6, S74 |
| App Store (commission, ex-EU) | 15-30%; the 27% link-out commission was ruled prohibitive | services gross margin 76.3% (9M FY2026) | S6, S69 |
| App Store (EU, from 2026-10-01) | 26% in-app purchase, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission | EU band 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere | S77, S78 |
| Safari default search | 36% of Safari search advertising; $20B in 2022 | 16.6% of TTM services revenue | S70 |
| Subscriptions and cloud | recurring, bundled at the device sale | services 76.3% vs Microsoft 67.9% in FY2026 | S6, S49 |
| Handset peer — Samsung devices (DX) | — | KRW 0.8tn operating loss in Q3 2026 | S75 |

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Nine-month products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% (the June quarter was 40.1%), and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 — 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield. The price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

::: evidence
**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).
:::"}],"isError":false}

Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares, 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025 ($365.8bn to $416.2bn), and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x on $9.79 against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn swing overstates it: the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (39.5-41.0x band; 40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor zeroes the line; reading the $13.5bn non-current build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles gives $123.2bn and 40.8x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in nine months and capex sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow suits a company whose value is almost all terminal, and is the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The weights and the $270 entry price come from this exit-multiple set, not the DCF: the bull row applies 35x to $10.20 on a 34.4% operating margin, and the weights give $291.5, 15% below the price. The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows. The investor implication is a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at $344.63; at today's price the shares are a hold only for a holder with a lower basis [S6, S7, S97, S153].

The sum of the parts shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range in the table.

This is working research, not a recommendation: the second version of the report is with the investment committee and its verdict is still pending, so nothing here is a call.

**What the note was, and what changed**

The Market Analyst had asked that the risk case stop treating Apple's 40.1% product gross margin as a permanent level. The section now says so explicitly, and the effect runs against the bull case rather than softening it.

- **Pricing evidence covers two launch windows only.** CIRP's US weighted-average retail price hit a record **$1,077** in the December-2025 quarter, against **$953** a year earlier, after the **$100** iPhone 17 Pro increase. The iPhone 18 Pro then sold **23.5%** more units in its first three weeks after a further **$100** rise [S96, S150].
- **Both windows are mix-led, launch-bound and struck during a cost shock.** The section now states that full-cycle elasticity is unproven — there is no evidence of Apple holding price through a full memory-cost cycle.
- **The risk matrix's impact line now reads "off a 40.1% margin"**, and the danger card says handset pricing is evidenced only at launch, not through a cost cycle.

**Why that matters to the thesis**

The 46% gross-margin stress case now sits on a weaker pricing base than the previous revision implied. With memory up **146%** in the first quarter of 2026 and TrendForce's **30 September 2026** forecast of DRAM contract prices **10–15%** higher and NAND **15–20%** higher in the fourth quarter, the **47–48%** margin the base case underwrites is now the **optimistic branch, not the central one**. arguments.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With a 0.31% dividend plus a 1.63% gross buyback yield and earnings per share compounding at 8.2%, the arithmetic clears a 9% hurdle only while the 35.2x forward multiple holds; if it reverts to the four-year mean of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 at 2026-07-17; 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so market impact is measured in basis points. Price cannot: the buyers are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on the $5,029.6bn basic market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2027E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.2% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return at the current 35.2x forward multiple | 5.7% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return at the 31.0x four-year mean | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8.2% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x on trailing EPS and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. On the forward basis, a reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x is -11.9% on the multiple, about -4.1% a year over three years, which the 8.2% EPS growth and 1.9% yield more than offset but leave only +1.3% a year. The 29x base case is 18% below the market for the same reason; at 31.0x the same earnings give $303, 12% below. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS continuous auction | $13.8bn a day; exit complete in days | Any trading day | Near-certain, and the default route | S7 |
| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

| Precedent realisation | Year | Value | Multiple at the time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repurchases, FY2022 | 2022 | $89.4bn | 24.6x year-end P/E | S2, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2023 | 2023 | $77.6bn | 27.9x | S3, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2024 | 2024 | $94.9bn | 37.5x | S4, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2025 | 2025 | $90.7bn | 34.2x | S5, S7 |
| Observed drawdown, twelve months to 2026-10-30 | 2026 | $243.42 low | 29.4% below $344.63 | S7 |

The precedents are all capital returns: the only exit a company of this size has offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-27% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 35.2x forward makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

| Entry price | Exit at 27x | Exit at 31x | Exit at 34x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 (2026-10-30) | -3.2% | 1.3% | 4.5% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $300 | 1.4% | 6.1% | 9.4% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $240 | 9.2% | 14.3% | 17.9% | S6, S7, S97 |

The sell discipline follows from that table, which assumes FY2029E EPS of $11.45 built in section 8, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. The band is a judgement around the 31.0x four-year mean, not a dated forward series; at 31x the return from $344.63 is 1.3% a year, and at the current 35.2x it is 5.7%. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270, not from $344; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12%. The conditions to raise the entry price are observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The sale triggers are: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale on valuation alone [S71, S72, S7].

The drawdown case sets the risk, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241: 24.6x FY2027E earnings of $9.79 is $240.8, and the 2022 multiple is the low end of the four-year range; the $243.42 low printed within the past twelve months is a separate observed anchor. That is the realistic 30% drawdown for a fund holding the shares. The $133 DCF case at 9.5% — margin compression, 2-4% growth and a higher rate — is the permanent-loss scenario, not the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded strongly while the technology sector fell, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield that most models said would compress them. That argues for modest sizing and buying weakness, not abandoning the arithmetic: the exit is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is publicly disclosed in the sources here and both set the floor under the services multiple.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 8 by Lead Analyst, 8,978 characters)
The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S146]. The discounted cash flow is $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; and the price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. On exit multiples the answer is a ladder: $284 at 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, $303 at 31 times, $323 at 33 times and $343 at 35 times, so the 18% discount to the base case is a de-rating call. It holds below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times; at 31 times the three-year return in section 12 is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, products earn 39.9% on a nine-month basis and 40.1% in the June quarter against 36.9% a year earlier, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 40.8 times on the basic market value.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. The score table below carries the figures and their sources.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter. At $344.63 the probability-weighted value of $292 is 15.3% below the price, so the position is zero. At the first tranche of $270 the three scenarios return +32.2% on the bull case, +5.2% on the base and -10.7% on the bear, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; a fractional Kelly of 39% of the fund still exceeds what one name can carry, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. At the cap the loss on the 30% bear drawdown from $344.63 to $241 is 1.5% of the fund. The market regime reinforces patience: an elevated volatility percentile, a ten-year yield at 4.93% and a month of technology underperformance against the index are the profile the regime playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10]. The open diligence is the FY2026 10-K detail on working capital and intangibles, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, and the appellate outcome on the search payment.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 10 by Lead Analyst, 6,551 characters)
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. A discounted cash flow gives $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at the stock's own mean of 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence; the difference lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value sits below the price, and even a fractional Kelly exceeds what one name can carry, which is why the cap is a risk-budget limit rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 4 by Lead Analyst, 8,912 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; at 8.5% it gives $277 and at 9.5% $133, so the whole band sits below the close. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth — assumptions that make the price exactly fair, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value here; the difference is arithmetic. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 33 times gives $323 (-6%) and 35 times — today's forward multiple — gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year, roughly fair rather than 18% expensive. The operating case makes 29 times defensible: consensus capitalises a 50.1% June-quarter gross margin that included two points of tariff refunds. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 sets out the FY2027 build; $9.79 is our estimate, not a consensus figure, and a primary consensus feed is still missing. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean rather than a dated series [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights, the $292 weighted value and the entry price. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with the DCF at $212-277 below it. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF at a 9.5% cost of equity as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with conduct remedies: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the cloud, not the settlement, created the return. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007 and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record — 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not. At a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201) and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration, not extinction [S143, S145, S147].

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $241 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety. At $270 the scenarios return +32.2%, +5.2% and -10.7%, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; a fractional Kelly of 39% of the fund still exceeds what one name can carry, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision and caps the loss at 1.5% of the fund on the 30% drawdown from $344.63 to $241. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the year to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed. Sell above $380, 38.8 times the FY2027 build, or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

arguments.markdown:
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares sit above every rate point in the report's valuation grid. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case the rate grid gives $229 at 8.5% and $193 at 9.5%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise — but the claim rests on our own forecast, not on a consensus estimate. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence, and no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register; the difference we claim lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base [S7].

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value sits below the price, and the full Kelly on those inputs is 337% of the fund — several times any single-name limit — which is why the cap is a risk-budget limit rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

The composite score describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. It holds below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times; at 31 times the three-year return in section 12 is +1.3% a year.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, products earn 39.9% on a nine-month basis and 40.1% in the June quarter against 36.9% a year earlier, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter. At $344.63 the probability-weighted value of $292 is 15.3% below the price, so the position is zero. arguments.markdown:
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares sit above every rate point in the report's valuation grid. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case the rate grid gives $229 at 8.5% and $193 at 9.5%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise — but the claim rests on our own forecast, not on a consensus estimate. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence, and no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register; the difference we claim lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value sits below the price, and the full Kelly on the scenario inputs runs to several times any single-name limit, which is why the cap is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

::: one-question

The payment is the largest single item in services and runs at near-pure margin. A ban or a materially lower rate resets the services multiple that carries most of the valuation and moves fair value from the base case toward the bear case, regardless of how well the hardware cycle trades.

::: takeaways
1. Watchlist, not ownership: at $344.63 the shares trade at 35.2 times forward earnings against 18.09 for the index, and the 18% discount in the base case depends on a 29 times exit, itself 18% below today's multiple [S7, S97, S146].
2. The franchise is not the problem: services earn 40.3% of gross profit, cash conversion is 0.97x, 0.95x at the band floor, and net cash is $62,173M, so a 30% revenue fall leaves the company solvent [S6].
3. The entry is a price, not a narrative: 0.75-1.0% at $270, a second tranche at $245 and the 5% cap below $225, with $270 above the $241 bear case and a 1.5% maximum loss at the cap [S6, S7].
:::

The composite score describes a good company at a poor price: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low, as the weighted table below shows. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; on the forward convention the multiple is 1.3% below Apple's own twelve-month forward average of 35.66 times and 13.5% above its four-year average of 31.0 times [S97, S146]. The discounted cash flow is $277 at 8.5% (35% operating margin, 14% initial growth), $212 at 9.0% (33%/9%) and $133 at 9.5% (30%/4%); the rate grid on the base operating case gives $229 at 8.5%/4.0% and $193 at 9.5%/4.0%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12%. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and no point in that set reaches the price. On exit multiples the answer is a ladder: $284 at 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, $303 at 31 times, $323 at 33 times and $343 at 35 times, so the 18% discount to the base case is a de-rating call. It holds below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times; at 31 times the three-year return in section 12 is +1.3% a year.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, products earn 39.9% on a nine-month basis and 40.1% in the June quarter against 36.9% a year earlier, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 40.8 times on the basic market value.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is event-dense and mostly adversarial.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter. At $344.63 the probability-weighted value of $292 is 15.3% below the price, so the position is zero. At the first tranche of $270 the three scenarios return +32.2% on the bull case, +5.2% on the base and -10.7% on the bear, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; the full Kelly on those inputs is 337% of the fund, so the 5% cap, 1.5% of full Kelly, is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. At the cap the loss on the 30% bear drawdown from $344.63 to $241 is 1.5% of the fund. The market regime reinforces patience: an elevated volatility percentile, a 4.93% ten-year yield and a month of technology underperformance are the profile the playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10]. The open diligence is the FY2026 10-K detail on working capital and intangibles, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS, and the appellate outcome on the search payment.

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Nine months reconcile exactly: products gross profit of $108,819M on $272,629M is 39.9%, services $69,963M on $91,728M is 76.3%, summing to the filed $178,782M; the quarter ran at 40.1% and 75.6%, so applying 40.1% to nine-month products would overstate gross profit by about $0.5B. Services earn 40.3% of the trailing $227,123M gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue at 76.0%. The 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S6, S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS (S17); products gross margin is 39.9% against 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% (S6, S68).
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M; working capital supplied $16,366M of the gap. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build reconciling within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision). The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.2x price to free cash flow on the $5,029.6bn market capitalisation; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B (39.5-41.0x), with $125.1B the midpoint; anything below $122.6B subtracts more than the line contains. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, making $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion at 3.2% of trailing revenue. [S5, S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B due within twelve months; leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need checking: $2,604M of unrealised securities losses and intangibles of $25,417M net, up from $13,301M, unexplained in the 10-Q. [S5, S6]

### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: normalised free cash flow of $125.1B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 65.2%, against 57.3% in FY2025. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, a 9-11% cost of equity is cleared several times; the price is the constraint: $5,029.6bn of market capitalisation on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 is 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield; the $5,072B figure uses the June quarter's 14,715M diluted weighted-average count, 39.3x. Capital allocation agrees: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M are 67.0% of reported free cash flow and 72.4% of the $102,057M normalised figure, net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. Not a debt-funded buyback story. [S6, S7, S10]

### What the next print has to clear

No audited fiscal 2026 exists: Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026. Guidance is 9-11% revenue growth for the quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B), iPhone mid-teens; the register's only consensus is iPhone revenue, $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on the $209,586M filed for FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%), with no group-revenue consensus held. On trailing figures at a 17.3% tax rate: 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of EPS (6.0%), 500 basis points is $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment is $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue at 39.9% is $0.55 (6.3%). Gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue while a unit miss applies only to hardware. For the investor, earnings quality is not the constraint; the price is. The open diligence: December-quarter gross margin guidance, FY2027 memory contracted at fixed prices, what the $12,116M of net intangibles bought, and what sits in the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 10 by Valuation Analyst, 8,963 characters)
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares, 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025 ($365.8bn to $416.2bn), and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x on $9.79 against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium to everyone else: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not on growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its cost base rises. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn swing overstates it: the prior-year line absorbed the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (39.5-41.0x band; 40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor zeroes the line; reading the $13.5bn non-current build as deferred consideration for $13.3bn of gross intangibles gives $123.2bn and 40.8x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in nine months and capex sits at 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow suits a company whose value is almost all terminal, and is the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus $112.7bn for the fourth quarter, the 10% midpoint of the 9-11% guide), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and at 4.0% terminal growth each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The weights and the $270 entry price come from this exit-multiple set, not the DCF: the bull row applies 35x to $10.20 on a 34.4% operating margin, and the weights give $291.5, 15% below the price. The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows. The investor implication is a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at $344.63; at today's price the shares are a hold only for a holder with a lower basis [S6, S7, S97, S153].

The sum of the parts shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The discount rate is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the central case approaches the market price, and quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range in the table."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 7 by Valuation Analyst, 8,991 characters)
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With a 0.31% dividend plus a 1.63% gross buyback yield and earnings per share compounding at 8.2%, the arithmetic clears a 9% hurdle only while the 35.2x forward multiple holds; if it reverts to the four-year mean of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].
