| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 at 2026-07-17; 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so market impact is measured in basis points. Price cannot: the buyers are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8.2% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x on trailing EPS and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. On the forward basis, a reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x is -11.9% on the multiple, about -4.1% a year over three years, which the 8.2% EPS growth and 1.9% yield more than offset but leave only +1.3% a year. The 29x base case is 18% below the market for the same reason; at 31.0x the same earnings give $303, 12% below. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

The precedents are all capital returns: the only exit a company of this size has offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying back stock at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-27% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 35.2x forward makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

consensus.consensus: The market pays 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings. one_question.question: Will the Google default-search payment survive the D.C. Circuit appeal, and at what annual rate?

A ban or a materially lower rate resets the services multiple that carries most of the valuation, and it moves fair value from the base case toward the bear case regardless of how well the hardware cycle trades.

arguments.position_sizing: Watchlist, zero position today. First tranche 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34x exits; second tranche to 2.5-3.0% at $245; cap the position at 5% below $225. Sell review above $380 (38.8x the FY2027 build); sell on valuation alone above 45x forward, about $440; sell outright on two quarters of sub-10% services growth, gross margin below 47%, or a structure that removes the search payment.

Apple's profit is unusually cash-true. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 operating cash flow was $146,724M, capital expenditure $10,041M and free cash flow $136,683M against net income of $128,930M — a headline conversion of 1.06x, or 0.97x on a normalised $125,084M, on capex of 2.2% of revenue, versus peer Microsoft's 0.50x and 34.9% and Alphabet's 0.08x and 33.9%. Revenue grew from $383,285M in FY2023 to $416,161M in FY2025 and $466,823M trailing, with operating margin of 29.8%, 32.0% and 33.2%. Nine months to 27 June 2026 produced a 43.0% incremental operating margin — $21,809M more operating income on $50,662M more revenue. The question is how much of that increment is repeatable. ### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Nine months reconcile exactly: products gross profit of $108,819M on $272,629M is 39.9%, services $69,963M on $91,728M is 76.3%, summing to the filed $178,782M; the quarter ran at 40.1% and 75.6%. Services earn 40.3% of the trailing $227,123M gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue at 76.0%. The 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S6, S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS (S17); products gross margin is 39.9% against 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% (S6, S68).
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M; working capital supplied $16,366M of the gap. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build reconciling within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision). The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.2x price to free cash flow on the $5,029.6bn market capitalisation; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B (39.5-41.0x), with $125.1B the midpoint. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, making $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion at 3.2% of trailing revenue. [S5, S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B due within twelve months; leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need checking: $2,604M of unrealised securities losses and intangibles of $25,417M net, up from $13,301M, unexplained in the 10-Q. [S5, S6]

### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: normalised free cash flow of $125.1B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 65.2%, compared with 57.3% in FY2025. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, a 9-11% cost of equity is cleared several times; the price is the constraint: $5,029.6bn of market capitalisation on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 is 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield; the $5,072B figure uses the June quarter's 14,715M diluted weighted-average count, 39.3x. Capital allocation agrees: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M equal 67.0% of reported nine-month free cash flow of $110,197M and 72.4% of the normalised $102,057M ($110,197M − $10,016M other-liabilities inflow + $1,876M, nine-twelfths of the $2,502M clean average); net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. Not a debt-funded buyback story. [S5, S6, S7, S10]

### What the next print has to clear

No audited fiscal 2026 exists: Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026. Guidance is 9-11% revenue growth for the quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B), iPhone mid-teens; the register's only consensus is iPhone revenue, $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on the $209,586M filed for FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%), with no group-revenue consensus held. On trailing figures at a 17.3% tax rate: 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of EPS (6.0%), 500 basis points is $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment is $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue at 39.9% is $0.55 (6.3%). Gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue while a unit miss applies only to hardware. For the investor, earnings quality is not the constraint; the price is. The open diligence: December-quarter gross margin guidance, FY2027 memory contracted at fixed prices, what the $12,116M of net intangibles bought, and what sits in the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities. [S71, S72]

arguments.markdown:
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares, 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025, and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x on $9.79 against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price and mix in a shrinking unit market while costs rise; price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle shows [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn swing overstates it: the prior-year line carried the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (39.5-41.0x band; 40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor zeroes the line; reading the $13.5bn non-current build as deferred consideration gives $123.2bn and 40.8x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in nine months; capex is 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow suits a company whose value is almost all terminal, and is the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months $364.4bn plus $112.7bn at the 10% guidance midpoint), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate; on the base operating case, at 4.0% terminal growth, each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The weights and the $270 entry price come from this exit-multiple set, not the DCF: the bull row applies 35x to $10.20 on a 34.4% operating margin, and the weights give $291.5, 15% below the price. The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A low-confidence market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x and, on the same basis, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows. The investor implication is a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at $344.63; at today's price the shares are a hold only for a holder with a lower basis [S6, S7, S97, S153].

The sum of the parts shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The discount rate is a judgement: a lower cost of equity brings the central case to the market price, and quality franchises have held premium multiples through high-rate periods. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range above.

arguments.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn all sit below Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. Earnings per share rise from $9.79 in FY2027E to $11.45 in FY2029E, 5.4% a year spread across the three-year hold; the 0.31% dividend and a 4.1% a year multiple drag to the 31.0x four-year mean leave about +1.5% a year, 1.3% on the table's compounding, against a 9% hurdle. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, review a re-rating above $380 (38.8x), and sell above $440.6 (45x) [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 at 2026-07-17; 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so market impact is measured in basis points. Price cannot: the buyers are the same index and active funds, and in a de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on the $5,029.6bn basic market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2027E to FY2029E over the three-year hold | 9.2% / 5.4% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return at the current 35.2x forward multiple | 5.7% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return at the 31.0x four-year mean | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: 5.4% a year of EPS growth spread over the three-year hold and a 0.3% dividend make a mid-single-digit compounding machine at a constant multiple, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x on trailing EPS and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. On the forward basis, a reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x is -11.9% on the multiple, about -4.1% a year over three years, which the 5.4% EPS growth spread over the hold and the 0.3% dividend more than offset but leave only about +1.5% a year, 1.3% on the table's compounding. The 29x base case is 18% below the market for the same reason; at 31.0x the same earnings give $303, 12% below. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-market sale | NasdaqGS continuous auction | $13.8bn a day; exit complete in days | Any trading day | Near-certain, and the default route | S7 |
| Issuer repurchase | Apple Inc., under its board authorisation | $82.2bn in the twelve months to June 2026; $100bn authorised in May 2025 | Continuous; next authorisation with the May 2027 results | High | S6, S5 |
| Dividend | Apple Inc. | $0.27 a quarter, raised annually | Quarterly, with an annual increase each May | High | S17 |
| Strategic acquisition | No buyer large enough: the four largest peers are all smaller than Apple | Antitrust review in the US, EU, China and UK would follow any bid | Not foreseeable | Negligible | S14, S15, S108, S110 |
| Break-up or activist | None identified | Sum of the parts is $177-238 a share against a $5,029.6bn market value | No campaign disclosed | Negligible | S6, S17 |
| Passive flows | S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds | Largest company in the peer set | Quarterly rebalancing | Structural, not a decision | S11 |

| Precedent realisation | Year | Value | Multiple at the time | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repurchases, FY2022 | 2022 | $89.4bn | 24.6x year-end P/E | S2, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2023 | 2023 | $77.6bn | 27.9x | S3, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2024 | 2024 | $94.9bn | 37.5x | S4, S7 |
| Repurchases, FY2025 | 2025 | $90.7bn | 34.2x | S5, S7 |
| Observed drawdown, twelve months to 2026-10-30 | 2026 | $243.42 low | 29.4% below $344.63 | S7 |

The precedents are all capital returns: the only exit a company of this size has offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-27% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying today at 35.2x forward makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

| Entry price | Exit at 27x | Exit at 31x | Exit at 34x | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $344.63 (2026-10-30) | -3.2% | 1.3% | 4.5% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $300 | 1.4% | 6.1% | 9.4% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% | S6, S7, S97 |
| $240 | 9.2% | 14.3% | 17.9% | S6, S7, S97 |

The sell discipline follows from that table: FY2029E EPS of $11.45 built in section 8, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. The band is a judgement around the 31.0x four-year mean, not a dated series; at 31x the return from $344.63 is 1.3% a year, and at the current 35.2x it is 5.7%. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12%. The conditions to raise the entry price are observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The sale triggers are: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward — $440.6, 45 x $9.79 — is a sale on valuation alone, with $380 (38.8x) the trigger for a sell review [S71, S72, S7].

The drawdown case sets the risk, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241: 24.6x FY2027E earnings of $9.79 is $240.8, and the 2022 multiple is the low end of the four-year range; the $243.42 low of the past twelve months is a separate observed anchor. That is the realistic 30% drawdown. The $133 DCF case at 9.5% — margin compression, 2-4% growth and a higher rate — is the permanent-loss scenario, not the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong before. Apple has compounded while the technology sector fell, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield. That argues for modest sizing and buying weakness, not abandoning the arithmetic: the exit is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is publicly disclosed and both set the floor under the services multiple.

The precedents are all capital returns: the only exit a company this size has offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-27% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying at 35.2x forward makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

| $270 | 5.0% | 9.9% | 13.3% | S6, S7, S97 |

The sell discipline follows from that table: FY2029E EPS of $11.45 built in section 8, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. The band is a judgement around the 31.0x four-year mean, not a dated series; at 31x the return from $344.63 is 1.3% a year, and at the current 35.2x it is 5.7%. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12%. The conditions to raise the entry price are observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The sale triggers are: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward — $440.6, 45 x $9.79 — is a sale on valuation alone, with $380 (38.8x) the trigger for a sell review [S71, S72, S7].

The drawdown case sets the risk, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241: 24.6x FY2027E earnings of $9.79 is $240.8, and the 2022 multiple is the low end of the four-year range; the $243.42 low of the past twelve months is a separate observed anchor. That is the realistic 30% drawdown. The $133 DCF case at 9.5% — margin compression, 2-4% growth and a higher rate — is the permanent-loss scenario, not the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong. Apple compounded while the technology sector fell, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield. That argues for modest sizing and buying weakness, not abandoning the arithmetic: the exit is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. The open diligence question is how much of services revenue the Google payment represents and when the appeal is decided, because neither figure is disclosed and both set the floor under the services multiple.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 8 by Valuation Analyst, 8,983 characters)
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn all sit below Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. Earnings per share rise from $9.79 in FY2027E to $11.45 in FY2029E, 5.4% a year spread across the three-year hold; the 0.31% dividend and a 4.1% a year multiple drag to the 31.0x four-year mean leave about +1.5% a year, 1.3% on the table's compounding, against a 9% hurdle. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, review a re-rating above $380 (38.8x), and sell above $440.6 (45x) [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 at 2026-07-17; 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so market impact is measured in basis points. Price cannot: the buyers are the same index and active funds, and in a de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on the $5,029.6bn basic market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2027E to FY2029E over the three-year hold | 9.2% / 5.4% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return at the current 35.2x forward multiple | 5.7% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return at the 31.0x four-year mean | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: 5.4% a year of EPS growth spread over the three-year hold and a 0.3% dividend make a mid-single-digit compounding machine at a constant multiple, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x on trailing EPS and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 5 by Lead Analyst, 8,999 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market value on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case section 8's rate grid gives $229 at 8.5%/4.0% and $193 at 9.5%/4.0%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. Nothing in that set reaches $344.63, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value here; the difference is arithmetic. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 35 times, today's multiple, gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year. The operating case makes 29 times defensible on our own reading: the market is capitalising the printed 50.1% June-quarter gross margin, two points of which were tariff refunds. That is an assumption about the price, not a consensus estimate: no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register, so the difference rests on our margin forecast alone. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 publishes the build; $9.79 is our estimate and no primary consensus feed exists. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean, not a dated series [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights and the $292 weighted value. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF at 9.5% on 30% margins as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with conduct remedies: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the cloud, not the settlement, created the return. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007 and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record — 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not: at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201) and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration, not extinction [S143, S145, S147].

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $241 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety. At $270 the scenarios return +32.2%, +5.2% and -10.7%, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; the full Kelly on those inputs is 337% of the fund, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision and caps the loss at 1.5% of the fund on the 30% drawdown from $344.63 to $241. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the year to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed. A re-rating above $380, 38.8 times the FY2027 build, triggers a sell review; above $440, 45 times, section 12 sells on valuation alone; sell outright if two quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 12 by Lead Analyst, 7,021 characters)
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares sit above every rate point in the report's valuation grid. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case the rate grid gives $229 at 8.5% and $193 at 9.5%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise — but the claim rests on our own forecast, not on a consensus estimate. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence, and no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register; the difference we claim lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value sits below the price, and the full Kelly on the scenario inputs runs to several times any single-name limit, which is why the cap is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

arguments.markdown:
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market value on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case section 8's rate grid gives $229 at 8.5%/4.0% and $193 at 9.5%/4.0%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. Nothing in that set reaches $344.63, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The gap to the price is arithmetic, not consensus. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 35 times, today's multiple, gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year. The operating case makes 29 times defensible on our own reading: the market is capitalising the printed 50.1% June-quarter gross margin, two points of which were tariff refunds. That is an assumption about the price, not a consensus estimate: no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register, so the difference rests on our margin forecast alone. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 publishes the build; $9.79 is our estimate and no primary consensus feed exists. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean, not a dated series. The only street target found, $338-355 from two low-confidence aggregators, is labelled and not used [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights and the $292 weighted value. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF at 9.5% on 30% margins as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with conduct remedies: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the cloud, not the settlement, created the return. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007 and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record — 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not: at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201) and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration, not extinction [S143, S145, S147].

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $241 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety. At $270 the scenarios return +32.2%, +5.2% and -10.7%, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; the full Kelly on those inputs is 337% of the fund, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision and caps the loss at 1.5% of the fund on the 30% drawdown from $344.63 to $241. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the year to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed. A re-rating above $380, 38.8 times the FY2027 build, triggers a sell review; above $440, 45 times, section 12 sells on valuation alone; sell outright if two quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 8 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,983 characters)
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn all sit below Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. Earnings per share rise from $9.79 in FY2027E to $11.45 in FY2029E, 5.4% a year spread across the three-year hold; the 0.31% dividend and a 4.1% a year multiple drag to the 31.0x four-year mean leave about +1.5% a year, 1.3% on the table's compounding, against a 9% hurdle. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, review a re-rating above $380 (38.8x), and sell above $440.6 (45x) [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,594,180,000 at 2026-07-17; 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S6, S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple's daily turnover dwarfs any position a long-only fund would take, so market impact is measured in basis points. Price cannot: the buyers are the same index and active funds, and in a de-rating they mark the same multiple down together.

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on the $5,029.6bn basic market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2027E to FY2029E over the three-year hold | 9.2% / 5.4% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return at the current 35.2x forward multiple | 5.7% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return at the 31.0x four-year mean | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: 5.4% a year of EPS growth spread over the three-year hold and a 0.3% dividend make a mid-single-digit compounding machine at a constant multiple, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does much of the work in that growth, and at 35.2x it buys a 2.8% forward earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value. That is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 35.2x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x on trailing EPS and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month forward average of 35.7x. On the forward basis, a reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x is -11.9% on the multiple, about -4.1% a year over three years, which the 5.4% EPS growth spread over the hold and the 0.3% dividend more than offset but leave only about +1.5% a year, 1.3% on the table's compounding. The 29x base case is 18% below the market for the same reason; at 31.0x the same earnings give $303, 12% below. That is how a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

The precedents are all capital returns: the only exit a company this size has offered its holders. They also show the cost of buying at the top: the FY2024 and FY2025 programmes together spent $185.6bn at 34-38x earnings, and those shares would have been retired 18-27% cheaper at the FY2023 multiple. An investor buying at 35.2x forward makes the same choice management made, at a higher price [S4, S5].

The sell discipline follows from that table: FY2029E EPS of $11.45 built in section 8, $3.55 of dividends and exit multiples of 27x to 34x. The band is a judgement around the 31.0x four-year mean, not a dated series; at 31x the return from $344.63 is 1.3% a year, and at the current 35.2x it is 5.7%. A long-only fund earns its 9% hurdle from $270; the shares are a hold only for a holder who owns them at a lower basis, and a buy only on a de-rating or on evidence that FY2027-28 earnings growth is running above 12%. The conditions to raise the entry price are observable: services growing above 10% with the Google payment intact, gross margin held above 48% through the memory cycle, and a buyback authorisation above $100bn. The sale triggers are: services growth below 8% for two quarters, gross margin below 46%, normalised free cash flow conversion below 0.9x net income, a buyback cut, or any remedy that removes the Google payment. A multiple above 45x forward — $440.6, 45 x $9.79 — is a sale on valuation alone, with $380 (38.8x) the trigger for a sell review [S71, S72, S7].

The drawdown case sets the risk, not just the return. Two independent methods converge on $241: 24.6x FY2027E earnings of $9.79 is $240.8, and the 2022 multiple is the low end of the four-year range; the $243.42 low of the past twelve months is a separate observed anchor. That is the realistic 30% drawdown. The $133 DCF case at 9.5% — margin compression, 2-4% growth and a higher rate — is the permanent-loss scenario, not the trading risk. The buyback limits both: the same $82-85bn a year retires 3.0% of the shares at $270 and 3.6% at $240, against 1.7% at today's price, so each leg down raises the forward earnings growth the buyer receives [S7, S6].

The strongest argument against this discipline is that it has been wrong. Apple compounded while the technology sector fell, and a fund that sold on valuation last year would have forgone most of that gain; multiples of this quality have held through a high long-bond yield. That argues for modest sizing and buying weakness, not abandoning the arithmetic: the exit is liquid, the cash return is real, and the only thing between today's price and the required return is the multiple paid on entry. Confidence is high on the liquidity and the cash-return mechanics, medium on the multiple reversion, which is a forecast rather than an observation. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 12 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 7,021 characters)
Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares sit above every rate point in the report's valuation grid. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case the rate grid gives $229 at 8.5% and $193 at 9.5%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise — but the claim rests on our own forecast, not on a consensus estimate. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence, and no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register; the difference we claim lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value sits below the price, and the full Kelly on the scenario inputs runs to several times any single-name limit, which is why the cap is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 6 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,984 characters)
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. The dispute is the price: at $344.63 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market value on 14,594m basic shares, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times. The question is whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three methods agree and none reaches the price. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case section 8's rate grid gives $229 at 8.5%/4.0% and $193 at 9.5%/4.0%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238, and the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303 [S6, S10, S97]. Nothing in that set reaches $344.63, against 3.3% revenue growth a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The gap to the price is arithmetic, not consensus. The base case of $284 is 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times, which gives $303 (-12%); 35 times, today's multiple, gives $343, the price. The 18% discount is a de-rating call, and it holds only if the exit multiple settles below 31 times; at 31 times the three-year return is +1.3% a year. The operating case makes 29 times defensible on our own reading: the market is capitalising the printed 50.1% June-quarter gross margin, two points of which were tariff refunds. That is an assumption about the price, not a consensus estimate: no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register, so the difference rests on our margin forecast alone. Memory has turned — the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% with memory 34% of it — and the base case underwrites 47-48%; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS to $9.3 and fair value at 29 times to $270, the first entry tranche. Section 8 publishes the build; $9.79 is our estimate and no primary consensus feed exists. The 29 and 35 times multiples are our judgement, anchored on the 31.0 times mean, not a dated series [S6, S17, S97, S142].

The scenarios below are the report's only bull/base/bear set: exit multiples over twelve to thirty-six months, owning the probability weights and the $292 weighted value. Bull ($357, 25%): AI and foldable extend iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF at 9.5% on 30% margins as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with conduct remedies: the asset survived, but the overhang ran three years and the cloud, not the settlement, created the return. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007 and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record — 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not: at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201) and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration, not extinction [S143, S145, S147].

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $241 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety. At $270 the scenarios return +32.2%, +5.2% and -10.7%, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; the full Kelly on those inputs is 337% of the fund, so the 5% cap is a risk-budget decision and caps the loss at 1.5% of the fund on the 30% drawdown from $344.63 to $241. The strongest counter-evidence is the stock's own record: it returned 27.5% in the year to 30 October 2026, and a sale at 35 times forward would have missed it. The open diligence is the appellate outcome on the search payment and a primary consensus feed. A re-rating above $380, 38.8 times the FY2027 build, triggers a sell review; above $440, 45 times, section 12 sells on valuation alone; sell outright if two quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a structure that removes the search payment [S6, S7].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 9 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,990 characters)
The composite score describes a good company at a poor price: the quality dimensions score high and the price-related ones low. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios.

The composite score is 6.0 out of 10. Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; on the forward convention the multiple is 1.3% below Apple's own twelve-month forward average of 35.66 times and 13.5% above its four-year average of 31.0 times [S97, S146]. The discounted cash flow is $277 at 8.5% (35% operating margin, 14% initial growth), $212 at 9.0% (33%/9%) and $133 at 9.5% (30%/4%); the rate grid on the base operating case gives $229 at 8.5%/4.0% and $193 at 9.5%/4.0%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12%. The sum of the parts is $177-238, none of which reaches the price. On exit multiples the answer is a ladder: $284 at 29 times FY2027 EPS of $9.79, $303 at 31 times, $323 at 33 times and $343 at 35 times, so the 18% discount to the base case is a de-rating call. It holds below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0 times; at 31 times the three-year return in section 12 is +1.3% a year.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, products earn 39.9% on a nine-month basis and 40.1% in the June quarter against 36.9% a year earlier, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $125.1bn, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3bn band, converts at 0.97 times net income and 0.95 times at the band floor, against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet; net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase, in which case free cash flow is $123.2bn and the multiple 40.8 times on the basic market value.

Growth and regulation both score low, and together they explain why the recommendation is not to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue growth has been price and mix rather than volume, so the growth dimension cannot carry the multiple. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple, through the search payment and the European fee schedule, and the catalyst calendar is adversarial.

The recommendation changes at identifiable points, and the sensitivity table below ranks them. A gross margin at the low end of the base range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it. An adverse appellate ruling on the search payment moves the bear case toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. Services growth in single digits removes one tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at the top end with FY2027 memory contracted would justify a higher base multiple that is still below the current price.

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter. At $344.63 the probability-weighted value of $292 is 15.3% below the price, so the position is zero. At the first tranche of $270 the three scenarios return +32.2% on the bull case, +5.2% on the base and -10.7% on the bear, an expected +8.0% against a 15.4% standard deviation; the full Kelly on those inputs is 337% of the fund, so the 5% cap, 1.5% of full Kelly, is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. At the cap the loss on the 30% bear drawdown from $344.63 to $241 is 1.5% of the fund. The market regime reinforces patience: an elevated volatility percentile, a 4.93% ten-year yield and technology underperformance are the profile the playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10]. Open diligence is the FY2026 10-K detail on working capital and intangibles, a primary consensus feed for FY2027 EPS and the appellate outcome on the search payment.

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Nine months reconcile exactly: products gross profit of $108,819M on $272,629M is 39.9%, services $69,963M on $91,728M is 76.3%, summing to the filed $178,782M; the quarter ran at 40.1% and 75.6%. Services earn 40.3% of the trailing $227,123M gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue at 76.0%. The 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S6, S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS (S17); products gross margin is 39.9% against 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% (S6, S68).
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M; working capital supplied $16,366M of the gap. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build reconciling within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision). The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.2x price to free cash flow on the $5,029.6bn market capitalisation; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B (39.5-41.0x), with $125.1B the midpoint. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, making $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion at 3.2% of trailing revenue. [S5, S6]

### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: normalised free cash flow of $125.1B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 65.2%, compared with 57.3% in FY2025. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, a 9-11% cost of equity is cleared several times; the price is the constraint: $5,029.6bn of market capitalisation on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 is 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield; the $5,072B figure uses the June quarter's 14,715M diluted weighted-average count, 39.3x. Capital allocation agrees: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M equal 67.0% of reported nine-month free cash flow of $110,197M and 72.4% of the normalised $102,057M ($110,197M − $10,016M other-liabilities inflow + $1,876M, nine-twelfths of the $2,502M clean average); net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. Not a debt-funded buyback story. [S5, S6, S7, S10]

### What the next print has to clear

No audited fiscal 2026 exists: Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026. Guidance is 9-11% revenue growth for the quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B), iPhone mid-teens; the register's only consensus is iPhone revenue, $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on the $209,586M filed for FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%), with no group-revenue consensus held. On trailing figures at a 17.3% tax rate: 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of EPS (6.0%), 500 basis points is $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment is $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue at 39.9% is $0.55 (6.3%). Gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue while a unit miss applies only to hardware. For the investor, earnings quality is not the constraint; the price is. The open diligence: December-quarter gross margin guidance, FY2027 memory contracted at fixed prices, what the $12,116M of net intangibles bought, and what sits in the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities. ### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The 50.1% gross margin carried 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; because that margin applies to $466.8bn of revenue, one point is $4.7bn of operating income. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts fourth-quarter DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter and NAND 15-20% higher; the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38%, memory at 34% against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to about $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount. The 40.1% product margin is not permanent: pricing evidence is two launch windows only — CIRP's record $1,077 US-WARP after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro rise, and iPhone 18 Pro sales +23.5% in three weeks after a further $100 — both mix-led, launch-bound and made during a cost shock, so full-cycle elasticity is unproven. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel. [S17, S6, S99, S136, S150, S96, S84]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, handset pricing is evidenced only at launch, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The Google trial record put the payment at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments; the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 brief asks the D.C. Circuit to strike it, and Google's appeal No. 26-5023, with the DOJ cross-appeal, keeps the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value. The EU fee schedule from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ: Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue, and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income. It matters as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### The growth swing factors are AI and China

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini licence reported at $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capex fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books it in operating expense; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation, and X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across 2.5bn devices would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells $1,199 handsets is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% (Counterpoint) and 15.4% (IDC), with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in H2 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's; Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.2x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.5-41.0x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,029.6bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 11.9% and to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 30.1% from the 35.2x forward base, and the bear exit value is $241. Each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the debate. Stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the 9.5% DCF; free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn on the band, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; deferred consideration at $123.2bn, 40.8x, changes neither; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

The board waived its age guideline for two directors who stood in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO. The 2025-12-06 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, concentrating rather than removing the dependency, with no disclosed successor or retention award. The 107% payout is a tax artefact: FY2024's $10.2bn State Aid charge and FY2025's $15.8bn Irish tax payment. Cash quality is a smaller risk than it looked: a $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities against $13,270M of gross intangibles added, with $1,780M of investing "other", reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M fall in other current liabilities the build is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M other-liabilities line; if the whole purchase is unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, $1.9bn below the $125.1bn central case and inside the $122.6-127.3bn band. The 10-K on 2026-11-02 must tie the intangibles to the liability. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence: the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]"}],"isError":false}

Then: services growth below 10% for two consecutive quarters (sell trigger), gross margin below 47% (sell trigger), EU developer take-up of the 5% Core Technology Commission, and the D.C. Circuit briefing through 2027.
