top_three: One scenario taxonomy across the briefing and sections 8, 11, 12 and 14: name the DCF outcomes by discount rate ($212 at 9.0%, $277 at 8.5%, $133 at 9.5%) and keep bull/base/bear for the exit-multiple set ($357/$284/$241), then rebuild the $292 weighted value, the 39% Kelly and the 1.5% maximum loss from the set that owns them.

Publish the FY2027 EPS $9.79 and FY2029E $11.45 build (or cite the consensus feed) and stop calling consensus a gap while quoting a forward multiple, since 35.2x is simply price divided by $9.79 and $284 is 29x it.

State the valuation conclusion as a multiple call: fair value is $284/$303/$323/$343 at 29x/31x/33x/35x FY2027 EPS and the price already implies 35.2x, so '18% overvalued' holds only below the stock's own 31x four-year mean, where section 12's three-year return is a positive 1.3% a year. Reconcile the headline figures to one filed basis while doing it (market cap $5,029.6bn, products gross margin 39.9% against 36.9%, FY2025 buybacks $90.7bn).

1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes: Completeness sweep against each section's standard and the lens checklist; the server's check of version 1 reports no rule findings (N1-N4, N6) and no depth or layout failures, so what follows is judgement, not a rule breach. Company Overview: single class, no VIE, float 99.94%, entity map, board map, timeline all dated (1976-04-01 to 2026-04-20); cap-table questions of liquidation preference and anti-dilution are correctly absent for a single-class public company; BlackRock 7.10% rests on a 2023-12-31 13G/A and is labelled. Team: degrees for six of seven executives recorded as not disclosed rather than inferred, pay and Section 16 gaps labelled, succession and retention open items listed. Technology: no verified patent number, labelled low confidence, and the freedom-to-operate gap is stated. Products: per-product inventory with stage, launch date, revenue, margin and next milestone; unit economics per active device. Market: bifurcated by region, bottom-up cross-check (1.0bn units x $581 = $581bn within 5% of IDC's $613bn), why-now mechanism (memory cost shock), and regional values declared unavailable with a data request filed. Competition: eight entries including the status quo and a second substitute (longer device life). Financials: margins by line, consensus, guidance, no burn rate required. Valuation: four methods, peer set justified and its limits stated (Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP accounts). ESG: dated regulator-by-regulator record. Scoring: weights sum to 100 and the weighted total recomputes to 6.05, rounding to the stated 6.0. Structural gap that is not an item: no section states the date of the next scheduled review after the 2026-11-02 results, which the stated discipline implies.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Claim verification by material claim. What checks out: the FY2023-TTM income statement, cash-flow and balance-sheet lines are internally consistent (gross margin 44.1/46.2/46.9/49.1/48.7%; FCF 99,584/108,807/98,767/110,197/136,683); the normalised-FCF bridge recomputes (136,683 - 14,101 + 2,502 = 125,084, 0.97x of $128,930M) and the $14,101M TTM build ties to FY2025 -11,076 minus 9M FY2025 -15,161 plus 9M FY2026 +10,016; the tariff refund at 2 points of margin and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS is attributed to the 2026-07-30 release with block maths (200bp = $0.52 = 6.0% of $8.72); memory +146% in 1Q26 is properly a TrendForce figure, not an Apple one, and the 10-Q's \"intensify\" language is quoted not paraphrased; the 4Q26 DRAM +10-15% and NAND +15-20% forecast is dated 2026-09-30 and independent; the $20bn search payment is correctly labelled a litigated 2022 estimate rather than a disclosure, with the period basis given (16.6% of TTM services, 12.9% of TTM operating income, 18.3% and 15.0% on FY2025); Judge Mehta's 2025-12-05 remedy and the D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 appeal are dated; the Ninth Circuit link-out ruling of 2025-12-11 and the 2026-06-30 cert grant are dated; the EU fee band is dated 2026-10-01 with a primary Commission source; China Q3 2026 shares carry two independent counts (Counterpoint 19.5%/21.3%, IDC 17.8%/21.1%) and the report states both; the 2.5bn active-device base is labelled an earnings-call figure and its use is flagged as an estimate. Company-only claims are labelled as such where they matter (Siri capability, Private Cloud Compute, the installed base, the App Store ecosystem figure, the reported $1bn Gemini price, which both companies decline to confirm). Stale but dated items I did not raise: the BlackRock 7.10% stake (2023-12-31 13G/A) is disclosed as such, and the S74 iPhone unit estimate of 261m is low confidence and labelled. No N1 or N2 breach found: every figure I could trace sits in the register at the cited ID.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Competitor challenge worked from the outside in. Geographic: the Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia-Pacific are covered with dated shares and two independent counts for China; India is the one blind spot — it is discussed as a manufacturing hedge (55m units, 25% of global assembly) but never as a competitive market, where Xiaomi, vivo and Samsung hold the volume tiers and Apple's own unit share is not stated. Adjacent giants: Alphabet and Google are present (search, Android, Pixel, Gemini); Microsoft, Amazon and Meta are not, except Meta glasses in one cell. Substitutes: the status quo is present and well argued (longer device life, IDC's 2028-29 China recovery); the cheaper-Android substitute is implied by the collapsing sub-$100 segment but never named as a switching option at the $600-800 tier. Open source: absent. Academic: not relevant to this company. Per-competitor detail is otherwise strong — Samsung, Huawei and Xiaomi each carry technology, price, share, strength and weakness, and the Samsung MX loss and Xiaomi's 8.5% handset margin give the profit-capture argument its teeth. The claim I would most want stress-tested is the premium-share one (65% of $600+ units, 29% of units in H1 2026): it is Counterpoint-sourced and dated, but it is the number that carries the whole value-capture thesis, and no second source is offered for it.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: Product/market-fit questions put to the report, with what it answers and what it does not. (1) Hardest thing about selling: not building the phone but re-pricing it into a shrinking unit pool while a competitor's model sits inside the flagship feature. The report names the mechanism (memory at 34% of a bill of materials up 38%) but tests demand with one three-week number. (2) Budget owner: consumer or carrier financing plan for hardware, developer and subscriber for services — answered in sections 1, 4 and 6, and the best part of the business-model section, because it identifies that the payer for the 76.3% margin line is someone else's commerce. (3) Sales cycle: annual September launch, validated by dated launch and guidance events; the enterprise and education cycles are absent. (4) Why adoption is not faster: the report's implicit answer is price and mix rather than volume, and it does not argue the AI case — Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14 with five more languages promised for October 2026, and no usage, engagement or attach data is offered for the feature the upgrade cycle is being sold on. That silence is itself evidence and the report should say so once, explicitly. (5) Lost deals: not applicable in the B2C sense, but the consumer analogue — churn, switching, trade-in capture, carrier promotions — is missing entirely, which is why the elasticity item above is Important rather than Minor. Sensible next checks: App Store and services attach per device, Apple Card/Apple Pay attach as a proxy for services depth, and the China weekly activation series, which would settle the pull-forward question within one quarter rather than at the 10-K.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress arithmetic, run on the report's own numbers, with the 30%-worse test for each key figure. Gross margin: 2 points = $0.52 of EPS (6.0% of $8.72) and, because it applies to $466.8bn of revenue, 1 point is about $4.7bn of operating income; 46% against a 47-48% base takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to $9.2-9.35, which at 29x is $267-271 — the $270 entry, not a discount to it, so the thesis survives only as \"buy at the level the downside implies\". Search payment: $20bn at a 17.3% tax rate is $1.12 of EPS (12.8%); if the 2026 run-rate is 25% higher ($25bn) the hit is about $1.40 (16%), and at near-pure margin it is 15-16% of operating income, so a ban takes the base case toward the $241-242 bear — the thesis survives the appeal only through the renegotiation assumption, which is stated. Memory: DRAM +10-15% and NAND +15-20% in 4Q26 applied to a bill of materials up 38% with memory at 34% implies a further 5-9% increase in the hardware cost base before any hedge, which is the same order as the 2-3 points of margin the base case gives up. Cash: free cash flow 30% lower ($85.8-89.1bn) is 56.4-58.6x and covers the $82.2bn buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends — survivable, not comfortable. Revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin is operating income of $95bn and EPS of $5.4. Discount rate: the grid implies 8-12% per 50bp at a 4.0% terminal growth (7.5%: $302, 8.5%: $229, 9.5%: $193), not the 15-18% the text claims. Exit multiple: 29x/31x/33x/35x on $9.79 gives $284/$303/$323/$343 against a $344.63 price, so the conclusion is a multiple call and should be stated as one. Probability-weighted $291.5 recomputes correctly from 0.25x357 + 0.5x284 + 0.25x241. Three-year exit table recomputes correctly (at $344.63: 27x -3.2%, 31x +1.3%, 34x +4.5% a year on FY2029E EPS of $11.45 and $3.55 of dividends). What survives a 30% shock: the franchise, the balance sheet ($62.2bn net cash, $146.5bn securities) and the rating of Watchlist with a fixed risk budget. What does not survive: the claim that $270 is a margin of safety, and the framing of an 18% overvaluation as a finding rather than a choice.

items.issue: Two different scenario sets carry the same bull/base/bear labels and the executive briefing stitches them into one sentence. Section 8's table gives bull $277 (an 8.5% discount rate, 35% margin DCF), base $212 (the 9.0% DCF) and bear $133, at -20%/-38%/-61%. Section 11's table gives bull $357 (35x FY2027 EPS $10.20), base $284 (29x FY2027 EPS $9.79) and bear $241 (24.6x the same EPS), at +4%/-18%/-30%, and calls $212-264 "intrinsic value". The executive briefing therefore reads: "the DCF at 9.0% is $212, the bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the base scenario is $284" — so the reader cannot tell whether the bull case is below the base case or above it, or whether fair value is $212 or $284. Everything downstream inherits the collision: the $292 probability-weighted value (0.25x357 + 0.5x284 + 0.25x241 = $291.5, so it is the multiple-based set that is weighted), the 39% full Kelly drawn from it, the 1.5% maximum loss at the cap, and the claim that $270 is "a 5% discount to the $284 base case and above the $242 bear".
items.action: Adopt one taxonomy across sections 11, 12, 14 and the briefing: name the DCF outcomes by method ("DCF, 9.0% cost of equity: $212; 8.5%: $277; 9.5%: $133") and reserve bull/base/bear for the twelve-to-thirty-six-month total-return scenarios that use an exit multiple ($357/$284/$241). Then state explicitly which set the probability weights, the Kelly fraction and the entry price are drawn from, and delete the duplicated labels from whichever table does not own them.
items.evidence_request: Confirm whether the 29x and 35x exit multiples in the scenario table are the report's own judgement or come from a dated multiple series; if judgement, say so in the table.

items.issue: The sell discipline has two thresholds for the same action: "sell above $380 or above 45 times forward earnings ($441)" in section 11, and "a multiple above 45x forward, $440, would be a sale" in section 12, while the executive briefing carries only the $380 review. The reader cannot tell whether $380 is a review and $441 a sale, or two competing sale triggers.
items.action: State one rule with its levels: a review at $380 and a mandatory trim or exit at 45x forward ($441), consistent in sections 11, 12 and the briefing.

items.issue: The lens asks for named reference-check targets and section 2 gives verification topics instead (Ternus's non-hardware operating scope, Srouji retention, 2026 awards to non-NEO SVPs, AI budget sign-off) without saying who would be asked or what a good answer looks like.

items.issue: Twelve of fourteen sections sit between 8,894 and 8,991 characters against a hard 9,000-character limit. There is no room for a single added figure, so any fix raises the section length error rather than the quality.

items.issue: The central valuation number has no visible origin and the register's own account contradicts its use. Section 11's base case is "29 times $9.79", section 8's own-history row says "implied FY2027 EPS of $9.79", and section 8's opening says "35.2x forward" — 344.63 / 35.2 = $9.79, so the forward multiple is the same FY2027 estimate. Yet section 8 closes by naming "consensus revenue, EPS and free cash flow for the next two fiscal years and a sell-side price target" as an open gap, and the valuation data request says the forward consensus is "not disclosed" because no free source carried it. $9.79 therefore drives the $284 base case, the -18% gap, the $270 entry (via 29x on $9.3) and the whole section 12 table (FY2029E $11.45, $3.55 of dividends), with no build, no source and no reconciliation. A prior-year comparison also fails: $9.79 on TTM $8.72 is +12.3%, while section 11 describes consensus as 9.9% growth.
items.action: Publish the EPS build in section 8 as a three-line table — TTM diluted $8.72, FY2026E (9M $6.88 plus the guided December quarter at 9-11% revenue growth), FY2027E $9.79 with the revenue and margin behind it, FY2029E $11.45 — or cite a dated consensus source; then make sections 11, 12, 14 and the briefing point at it. Either state that the forward multiple is FY2027E and the FY2026E multiple is X, or overlay forward-on-forward. Remove "implied" from every table row.
items.evidence_request: A dated consensus EPS and free-cash-flow export for FY2026-FY2029 (the subscription feed already requested), or the internal build with its revenue, margin, tax and share-count lines.

items.issue: The non-consensus framing rests on two low-confidence aggregator pages. The median target of $338-355 ("flat to +3% from the close") comes from S142 Tickernerd and S144 TickFlow, both recorded as low confidence, yet the executive briefing states "the sell side's median target sits at the spot price", section 11 says "the sell side sees fair value where this report sees an 18% overvaluation", and section 14 repeats it as evidence there is "no analyst catalyst". At the same time section 8 says the open gap is "consensus revenue, EPS and free cash flow for the next two fiscal years and a sell-side price target, none of which is publicly disclosed here" — a direct contradiction of the three sections that quote one. Either the target exists in the register or it does not.
items.action: Either keep the target but label it explicitly as low-confidence aggregator data in all three places, or drop the "sell side sees fair value where this report sees an 18% overvaluation" sentence and replace it with what the register can carry (a stated gap in consensus). Delete section 8's "none of which is publicly disclosed here" and state the position consistently: two aggregators at low confidence, a subscription feed outstanding. If the non-consensus framing is load-bearing, it needs a named, dated, medium-or-better source.
items.evidence_request: A dated sell-side target distribution or consensus price target from a licensed feed showing the median, the count and the dispersion.

items.issue: Section 7 reads: "guidance of 9-11% revenue growth for the quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B) ... against consensus of $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%)", which reads as group revenue and is arithmetically impossible: group FY2026 revenue is already $364.4bn after nine months and $416.2bn in FY2025, so $252.4bn would be a 40% collapse. The source (S71) carries iPhone revenue, and section 11 states it correctly. Section 8 then converts the same figure into an earnings claim — "the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027" applied to EPS growth — which conflates a revenue line with per-share earnings.
items.action: Label the units and the basis in the text and in the peer table: "consensus iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 (S&P Global Market Intelligence, 2026-10)", removed from the sentence that carries group revenue guidance; and rewrite "the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027" as iPhone revenue growth, not EPS growth. Add trailing and forward columns to the peer table so the premium is measured on one basis.

items.issue: The base rate for growth is stated two ways. Section 8: "revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021", used as the set-up for why the valuation is demanding. Section 4, section 11 and the section 14 growth row use 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8bn to $416.2bn), which is the correct arithmetic on those two points. The 5.0% figure appears nowhere else and is not derivable from the FY2021-FY2025 series.
items.action: Pick one revenue CAGR, define the window and the method (FY2021 $365.8bn to FY2025 $416.2bn is 3.3%), and use it in sections 8, 11 and 14. If 5.0% is meant to be a different window, give the years.

items.issue: The same headline figures differ across sections, and in several cases one side cannot be right. (1) Market capitalisation: $5,029.6bn in sections 0, 8, 12 and 14, but $5,072bn in section 7 ("$5,072B of market capitalisation on $128,930M of trailing net income is a 2.5% earnings yield") and section 6 ("$5,072B, or 39.3x trailing EPS of $8.72"), which is a $42bn gap and a 39.5x/39.3x/39.0x spread on the same EPS. (2) Products gross margin: 39.9% against 36.9% in sections 6 and 7, but 40.1% against 34.5% in sections 4 and 5 — a 2.4-point difference in the prior-year base that changes the pricing-power story. (3) FY2025 buybacks: $90.7bn in sections 8 and 12, $89.3bn in section 9. (4) Quarterly dividend: $0.27 in section 12 ($1.08 annualised), $0.26 in section 9. (5) Samsung's mobile result: KRW0.6tn operating loss in section 5, KRW0.8tn in section 6. (6) Sensitivities: sections 8 and 10 both say each 50bp on the cost of equity moves value 15-18%, but section 8's own grid moves $229 to $193 per 100bp at a 4.0% terminal growth, about 8% per 50bp.
items.action: Reconcile each pair to the filing and per-share count once, and carry that one figure everywhere: $5,029.6bn basic on 14,594m shares; $5,072bn diluted; then a single P/E convention. Products gross margin should be 39.9% against 36.9% — 40.1% with 76.3% services does not reconcile to the filed nine-month gross profit of $178,782M. Replace "each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%" with the grid's own number (8-12% per 50bp at a 4.0% terminal growth).
items.evidence_request: If the $5,072bn figure is not a diluted-share convention, say which share count it uses so the two market values can be traced to one filing.

items.issue: The competitor map has no AI-native device entrant and no Microsoft, although the report's own risk section treats their conduct as material: section 10 cites "X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI" over AI distribution, and section 5 lists only "AI agents that could move the assistant layer off the operating system" in prose. OpenAI therefore appears in the report as a litigant and as an abstraction, never as a competitor with a product, a price and a channel — which is the one adjacent entrant that could attack Apple's device layer rather than its take rate. Microsoft, the closest peer on AI and services, appears only in the valuation table and as an antitrust analog; Copilot and Windows on ARM appear only as "Snapdragon Windows PCs" in a threat cell. The lens question "has [a platform giant] shown interest in this space and could they enter with existing infrastructure?" has no answer for either.
items.action: Add two rows to section 5: OpenAI (a device programme and an assistant distributed through iOS and Android) and Microsoft (Copilot across Windows on ARM, Office and Azure, the only rival with both a model stake and a hardware channel), each with technology, price, share, strength and weakness against Apple. Add them to the positioning table under "iPhone (premium)" and "Services" as emerging threats, and say in one sentence what would turn each from a monitor into a competitor (a shipping device with carrier distribution; Copilot bundled below the price of an iPhone). Section 10 should then price the AI-distribution risk it already identifies rather than naming it as a lawsuit.
items.evidence_request: Any dated, sourced record of an OpenAI-branded consumer device programme (announcement, supply-chain reporting, regulatory filing, carrier partnership), and Copilot's attach rate on Windows OEM devices and any Windows-on-ARM share figures.

items.issue: Three smaller omissions. Epic Games and DMA-enabled alternative marketplaces reset the App Store take rate in the report's own sourcing (S79, S77) but sit only in the ESG section, never in the competitor or positioning table, so the services row has Spotify as its only rival. Honor, vivo, OPPO and Transsion appear in the regional table but not in the per-competitor table, so the Chinese mid-market and emerging-market threat has no price tier, share or weakness. Open-weight models are not considered at all: they would cut what Apple pays for the Gemini licence and at the same time shorten every rival's path to a competent assistant, which is exactly the tension the rented-intelligence argument turns on.
items.action: Add Epic Games and alternative storefronts as a distribution competitor with the DMA economics, promote Honor, vivo, OPPO and Transsion from the regional table into the global competitor table with share and price tier, and note in the moat table that open-weight models lower the price Apple pays for the licence as well as the barrier for its rivals.
items.evidence_request: Any dated measure of iOS external-distribution uptake since 2026-10-01 (developer migration, alternative marketplace downloads or billings).

items.issue: The single hardest thing in this case is selling a $1,199 handset into a market whose units are falling 16.7% and whose average selling price has just risen 27.6%, and the report answers it with one three-week datapoint: "iPhone 18 Pro sales up 23.5% in the first three weeks" (S139). No lost-deal, churn or switching evidence appears anywhere — no Android-to-iOS switching rate, no trade-in capture, no carrier promotional depth, no defection rate to Huawei in China. The launch split compounds the gap: holding the standard iPhone 18 to spring 2027 is presented purely as a supply tactic ("sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter"), but it also means FY2027's first half has no volume model at an $899 tier while memory costs are still rising. Section 4's own durability test concedes the point — "whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and the evidence is mixed" — and then attributes part of the China gain to pull-forward ahead of Apple's own price rises. If that is true, the December quarter is being flattered and the March quarter is exposed, and the base case's 9% FY2027 growth has no elasticity test behind it.
items.action: Replace the single datapoint with an elasticity paragraph: iPhone 18 Pro sell-through after the first three weeks against the iPhone 17 Pro at the same point, trade-in volume and average trade-in value, carrier promotional depth, and the Android-to-iOS switching rate; then state the revenue line that the spring-2027 split puts at risk (four to five months of the standard model's volume in FY2027) and price it as a downside sensitivity in section 11's base case. If no channel data is available, say so and grade the elasticity claim low confidence instead of medium.
items.evidence_request: Weekly or monthly sell-through and activation data for the iPhone 18 line after launch (Counterpoint or IDC tracking, carrier and retail channel checks), iPhone 17 versus 18 trade-in volumes, and Android-to-iOS switching estimates for the September-October 2026 window.

items.issue: The buyer is modelled for the consumer and the developer only. Apple's 40%-direct, 60%-indirect distribution is stated in section 1 but never turned into channel economics, and the enterprise, education and government segments that make up part of the direct channel have no buyer, cycle or attach rate anywhere in the report.
items.action: Add one short paragraph on the enterprise, education and government channel: the procurement cycle, who signs, and whether the services attach differs from consumer, plus the paid-subscription conversion inside the 2.5bn base if any disclosed figure exists.
items.evidence_request: Any disclosed or dated third-party estimate of Apple's enterprise and education revenue share and of paid-services attach per active device.

items.issue: The -18% gap is produced almost entirely by an assumed de-rating, not by the operating case, and the report states it as though it were a valuation finding. Base $284 is 29x FY2027 EPS of $9.79 — below the stock's own four-year mean of 31.0x and 18% below today's 35.2x forward. On the report's own numbers the choice of multiple decides the answer: 29x gives $284 (-18%); 31x gives $303 (-12%); 33x gives $323 (-6%); 35x gives $343, the price. Section 12 reaches the same place from the other direction: from $344.63 the three-year return at a 31x exit is +1.3% a year, which is a fair price, not an 18% premium. A partner will ask which it is. The sizing arithmetic inherits the ambiguity: full Kelly of 39% at $270 is presented with no win, loss or probability inputs, and it cannot be reproduced — the section 11 set at $270 (+32%/+5%/-11%) implies a Kelly well above 100%, while the section 8 bear ($133) would make the downside at $270 -51% and cut the fraction to single digits. A 39% figure that moves by an order of magnitude depending on which scenario table feeds it is a decision number with no derivation.
items.action: Add a row to section 8's valuation table that shows fair value at 29x, 31x, 33x and 35x FY2027 EPS and states what the market price implies (344.63 / 9.79 = 35.2x, i.e. no de-rating). Rewrite the "18% overvaluation" claim as conditional on an exit multiple below the stock's own four-year mean, and reconcile it with section 12's finding that at 31x the three-year return is +1.3% a year, which is roughly fair rather than 18% expensive. Then show the Kelly inputs in section 14 (win, loss and probability per scenario, and what 39% solves to) or drop the number and state the cap as a risk-budget decision.
items.evidence_request: Apple's forward P/E history over five and ten years with percentile bands, so the 29x base and the 31x mean are anchored to a distribution rather than to four year-end observations.

items.issue: The unit-economics table — the evidence behind the 9-of-10 profitability score — divides twelve-month flows by a denominator the company does not file. Every line moves one-for-one with the 2.5bn active-device figure (an earnings-call statement, S73, medium confidence): revenue per device $186.7, services $48.2 and operating profit $61.9 become $202.9/$52.4/$67.3 at 2.3bn devices and $172.9/$44.6/$57.4 at 2.7bn — a 9-13% swing on the number the section calls the most defensible unit. Mixing a point-in-time base with twelve-month flows is also a timing mismatch. The $941 ASP is weaker still: it is $245,540M divided by an estimated 261m units (S74, low confidence), so the "implied ASP" is an assumption restated as an output.
items.action: Sensitise the per-device table at 2.3bn and 2.7bn devices, label the 2.5bn base as a point-in-time earnings-call figure with its date, and replace the ASP line with either a filed revenue per unit or a stated range ($900-$960 on 255-275m units) rather than a single number derived from an estimate.
items.evidence_request: Apple's installed-base figure with its date and definition (active devices versus active iPhone), and any dated third-party unit estimate for FY2026 to bracket the 261m.

items.issue: Three arithmetic or basis slips in otherwise careful sections. (1) Section 11: "A $1bn licence is 0.9% of TTM operating income" — $1bn on $154,859M is 0.65%, and section 10 gets it right at 0.6%. (2) Section 10's risk matrix: "reversion to the 31.0x four-year mean -21.5%; -38% at 24.6x" — 24.6x on FY2027 EPS of $9.79 is $241, a 30% fall from $344.63, matching section 12's own -30%; -38% belongs to a different base or multiple. (3) Section 10's "40.8x" deferred-consideration multiple uses the $5,029.6bn value while section 8 quotes 41.2x on the diluted basis for the same $123.2bn, so one of the two is mislabelled.
items.action: Correct the licence share to 0.6-0.65% of operating income in section 11 to match section 10; restate the -38% as the multiple implied by the $242 drawdown on FY2027 EPS (35.2x to about 24.6x is -30%) and keep -38% only where it is computed from a different base; replace 40.8x with 40.2x where the basis is $5,029.6bn.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes:
No item raised: the product/market-fit questions are answered well enough in sections 4, 5, 6 and 9, and nothing found here overturns the thesis, which round 2 requires before a new item is added. The questions and where the evidence sits:
- Hardest thing about selling: re-pricing the handset while the input cost rises. ASP +27.6% to $581 (IDC, S84) into memory more than 300% higher, with the standard iPhone 18 held to spring 2027 (S113) — the report prices this as margin, not demand, risk, correctly, and the December 2026 guide is the test.
- Budget owner: the consumer or the carrier financing plan, stated in section 4. Enterprise and education procurement is not assessed; at 52.6% iPhone revenue that is a fair omission but it is the one channel where a 4-5 year replacement cycle could be shortened.
- Sales cycle: annual September launch plus carrier certification; the split launch (Pro/Duo in September 2026, standard models spring 2027) turns one spike into two, which is a real change to the cycle and is described as such in section 3.
- Why adoption is not faster: the assistant is an English beta from 2026-09-14 with five languages promised (S113); the installed base is 2.5bn devices on a multi-year replacement cycle; the intelligence layer is licensed, so a faster AI cycle does not accelerate the hardware cycle the way an owned platform would. The report says the AI case rests on distribution, not capability.
- Lost deals: none disclosed, and the observable is not lost deals but a shrinking pool — China -10% to -15.4% in Q3 2026 with Apple gaining 4.8 points (S139, S140), and the sub-$100 segment falling ~60% in Q2 2026, which is Apple exiting the low end rather than losing it. The services tolls are the closest thing to a lost-deal channel: the DMA 5% Core Technology Commission and the remanded 27% link-out commission (S69, S77) are customers routing around the toll, and the report prices both.
- One product/market question the report raises but does not answer: whether services growth is users or price (section 4 says so explicitly). Without it, 12-14% services growth in the base case cannot be decomposed into volume and take-rate, and a take-rate-led 12% is worth less than a user-led 12% at the multiple the report pays for it.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes:
Coverage on this version is eight rivals with dated figures: Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi, Alphabet, OpenAI, Microsoft, the three PC OEMs and Spotify, mapped by product in the positioning table and by layer (device, assistant, cloud, distribution) in the text. The four additions since R1 are sourced (S148-S151) and quantified against Apple's own base (OpenAI's ~$50bn annualised is 41% of $120.5bn services; Microsoft's 20% cloud share against AWS 28% and Google 15%).
No item raised, for one reason: none of the residual gaps changes the price conclusion, and round 2 admits new items only for a rule break or a thesis-overturning problem. Gaps recorded for the record rather than as findings:
- Samsung appears only as a handset rival. It is also the memory and display supplier whose cost shock carries the report's own margin case ($0.52 of EPS per 200bp), so the same counterparty sits on both sides of the P&L. Section 10 prices the memory risk without naming the supplier, which is defensible but understates the concentration: a supplier that is also a loss-making handset competitor (MX -KRW0.6T in Q3 2026) has both the means and the motive to allocate scarce memory away from a rival.
- Meta is absent although its glasses line is named in the wearables comparison, and Amazon's Alexa is absent from the assistant layer where OpenAI and Gemini are mapped.
- Qualcomm, the modem supplier Apple is displacing with the C2, is a competitor being removed rather than one to watch, but its licensing tail is a cost the silicon argument does not price.
- Transsion, Honor, OPPO and vivo appear in the market section's regional tables but not in the competitive map, so the emerging-market and China unit layer is thinner than the value layer.
On the substance, the competition section's judgement — profit capture and 2026 China share, not unit leadership, with a regulated services ceiling — is the right one and is supported by the 65% premium-unit share, the 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, and the OpenAI/Microsoft entries above.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes:
Stress test arithmetic.
Weighted value: 0.25x357 + 0.50x284 + 0.25x241 = 89.25 + 142.00 + 60.25 = $291.5, -15.4% from $344.63 (the briefing's $292 and 15.3% are the same number rounded).
EPS build: FY2027E 519.9 x 48.0% = 249.6 gross profit; 33.0% operating margin = 171.6; +1.0 other income = 172.6; x0.825 = 142.4; /14,550 = $9.79. FY2029E 600.9 x 47.5% = 285.4; 32.0% = 192.3; +1.2 = 193.5; x0.825 = 159.6; /13,940 = $11.45. Both reproduce.
Ladder: 29/31/33/35 x 9.79 = 283.9/303.5/323.1/342.7; price/9.79 = 35.2x; 344.63/8.72 = 39.5x; 5,029.6/128.93 = 39.0x.
30% worse: revenue -30% at the 43.0% incremental margin gives about $95bn of operating income and $5.4 of EPS; FCF -30% is $85.8-89.1bn, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; the deferred-consideration case at $123.2bn is 40.8x basic and changes nothing. With no position today the thesis survives a 30% worse operating case — it raises the required entry, it does not break the recommendation. What does not survive is a 30% worse exit multiple: 35.2x to 24.6x is -30.1%, and the first tranche at $270 sits only 10.7% above the $241 bear, which the report states openly.

final_memo:
# Apple Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Watchlist
Composite score: 6.0
Data as of: 2026-10-30

## Executive Briefing

Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares sit above every rate point in the report's valuation grid. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case the rate grid gives $229 at 8.5% and $193 at 9.5%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise — but the claim rests on our own forecast, not on a consensus estimate. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence, and no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register; the difference we claim lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value sits below the price, and the full Kelly on the scenario inputs runs to several times any single-name limit, which is why the cap is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

The payment is the largest single item in services and runs at near-pure margin. A ban or a materially lower rate resets the services multiple that carries most of the valuation and moves fair value from the base case toward the bear case, regardless of how well the hardware cycle trades.

## Company Overview

Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years — one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit — but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit at Apple's own age-75 ceiling, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality. Apple Inc. is a California corporation incorporated on 1977-01-03, listed on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars. At 2026-01-02 it had 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding against 50,400,000,000 authorised, all of a single class of $0.00001 par common stock with one vote per share. There is no dual-class structure, no VIE, no nominee shareholder and no contractual control chain — verified in the balance sheet and the 2026 proxy, not assumed. Float is effectively the whole company: directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares, or 0.06%, leaving 99.94%. Vanguard (9.63%) and BlackRock (7.10%) are the only disclosed 5% holders — and BlackRock's figure rests on a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the 2026 register is partly unknown. ### Business model: one platform, one rent, one budget owner

Apple sells integrated hardware to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, then monetises the installed base through Services. FY2025 net sales were $416,161m, split $307,003m products and $109,158m services, with 40% direct and 60% indirect distribution. The end user is usually the buyer, but the budget owner for the highest-margin line is the developer and the subscriber: Services earned a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products. Growth comes from installed-base expansion and price/mix, not unit share — Apple states it holds a minority share of global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 iPhone was 53.9% of revenue against 51.2% a year earlier and Services 25.2%, so concentration is rising again rather than falling. [S5, S17]

### Governance: senior, stable, slow to refresh

Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus the CEO. Independent tenure averages 12.0 years — Levinson 26 years and chair since 2000, Jung 18, Sugar 16, Wagner 12, Lozano and Gorsky 5, Austin 2 — and two of the seven (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75. Committees are conventional and fully independent: Audit under Sugar (nine meetings in 2025), People and Compensation under Jung, Nominating under Wagner; 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025. From 2026-09-01 the structure shifts in a way that matters: Ternus joins as CEO and Cook becomes Executive Chair, taking non-independent directors to two of nine (77.8%) and replacing an independent chair with a lead independent director. [S11, S56]

### A clean structure is not a clean earnings record

The forensic problem is optical, not legal. FY2025 returned $106.1bn — $90.7bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends — against free cash flow of $98.8bn, or 107% of it, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%. Diluted shares fell 6.9%, from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026, and $263.2bn of buybacks over three years bought the arithmetic. That is how a mature hardware company reports high-teens EPS growth; it is also what stops working the year the buyback slows. Counter-evidence is genuine: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% and gross margin reached 50.1%, so FY2026 is not an optical year; no audited FY2026 accounts had been filed on 2026-10-31. [S5, S17]

### Where the judgement breaks, and what to settle

Three events would change the call: a structural remedy in the DOJ monopolisation suit or the DMA Article 6(4) file that reaches commission economics would compress the 75.4% services margin; a board that keeps the executive-chair arrangement past 2027 would entrench a post-CEO chair; and a buyback slowdown would expose the underlying operating growth rate. Confidence is high on identity, ownership and capital-return facts and medium on the board's appetite for refresh, because its own age guideline is already being waived for two members. Diligence should settle whether that waiver was formal and who chairs the board after 2027; whether BlackRock's stake has moved since 2023; what share of Services revenue depends on US third-party payment rules; and the FY2026 buyback pace under the $100bn authorisation of 2025-05-01. ## Technology & Product

Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a 2.5-billion-device installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer this cycle sells on is rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capex fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026; the standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was cut to $899. Selling the 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March turns one spike into two, and the A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm plus the in-house C2 modem are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed price a node advantage becomes margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing expects semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. Prices rose into that memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112, S6]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as an English beta, five more languages promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither confirmed the price. Apple contributes the interface, personal context, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Ownership moved first: on 2025-12-01 Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety passed to software chief Craig Federighi, with Amar Subramanya as VP of AI, as John Giannandrea stepped down ahead of retirement. Apple bought what it could not ship. [S111, S122, S127]

**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed on 2026-01-12 a multi-year deal to supply Gemini for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface; not the model or the compute. [S111, S118]

### The licence is small per device and dangerous per query

At the reported $1bn a year the Gemini licence is 0.65% of the $154,859M trailing operating income and $0.06 of EPS, below the $0.52 that 200 basis points of gross margin are worth. Across the 2.5 billion active devices Apple disclosed on 2026-01-29, $0.50, $1 and $2 per device a year cost $1.25bn, $2.5bn and $5.0bn, taking EPS to $0.07, $0.14 and $0.28; booked as a service they would cut services gross margin from 76.3% to 75.3%, 74.2% and 72.2%. The $1bn implies $0.40 a device. Apple does not disclose the classification; R&D up 33% on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence" while capex fell points to R&D, and the choice changes the margin narrative, not EPS. The tail is per-query pricing: at an assumed 1 billion queries a day each cent is $3.65bn a year; Apple discloses neither volume nor rate. [S6, S111, S152]

## Market & Industry Analysis

Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

Two independent methods agree the market grows in dollars while shrinking in units, and sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and full-cycle elasticity is not established. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every segment in double digits, but that is margin evidence, not elasticity evidence. Two launch windows point to low elasticity: CIRP's US weighted average retail price reached a record December-quarter $1,077 after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro increase, and iPhone 18 Pro sales rose 23.5% in three weeks after a further $100 rise; both are mix-led and launch-bound, so they are anecdotes, not proof. IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months [S17, S87, S84, S150, S96].

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one can change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth $45.7B. Services: $120.5B trailing twelve months to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a $1.34T advertising pool in 2026 and $149B of App Store digital goods in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030, with smartwatches down 3.7% in 2026 and glasses up 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. The non-phone pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

The budget owner is the consumer or carrier financing plan; the procurement cycle follows the annual September launch; willingness to pay is being tested by the 27.6% ASP increase. What would change the conclusion: services growth above 15% with user growth, a foldable cycle adding IDC's $45.7B category value, or China stabilising after H2 2026. Confidence is high on 2026 data and low on 2027-2030 regional sizing, because regional market values are paywalled and Apple does not disclose units; the open questions are what share of iPhone growth is units versus price, whether services growth is users or price, how much China demand was pulled forward, and how much memory cost Apple can pass through in FY2027.

**Apple's markets are growing in dollars while shrinking in units, so its growth is price- and share-led, not market-led.**

The global pool is $613B of smartphone value in 2026 against just over 1.0B units, with a 27.6% ASP increase doing the work volume used to do (IDC, S84). Premium concentration (29% of units) and Apple's 65% share of it explain why Apple captures 36-43% of value on 20-24% of units (Counterpoint, S94; Apple filings, S5, S6). Foldables ($45.7B of category value by 2027) and services ($120.5B TTM at 76.0% gross margin) are the only pools large enough to move group growth; wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030 (IDC, S85).

Huawei is the most dangerous rival to Apple's profit pool, Samsung to its unit position. Samsung is broader, with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth. Huawei takes price and Samsung volume, at a loss.

Apple's global smartphone market share was 20% in 2025 to Samsung's 19%, and 22% in Q3 2026 to Samsung's 23%, so its position moves sideways even as value capture rises [S92, S120, S94, S84, S150]. The premium layer is where Apple improves: a 65% share of $600-plus units in H1 2026, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% in 2026. Pricing power is partially established, not proven, because part of the price rise is a memory shock, with NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier. The mechanism is mix: a $100 Pro increase lifts revenue per unit even if unit demand is flat. Elasticity evidence is two launch windows: after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro increase in September 2025, CIRP put the US weighted average retail price at a record December-quarter $1,077 against $953, and iPhone 18 Pro sales rose 23.5% in the first three weeks after a further $100 rise. Both are mix-led launch windows, therefore full-cycle elasticity is not established.

China is where risk has flipped from share loss to market contraction [S139, S140, S87, S6]. Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% to the lowest third-quarter level since 2012 (Counterpoint) and 15.4% (IDC); Apple took 19.5%, up 4.8 points, Huawei led at 21.3%, and the two were the only top brands to gain. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in nine months of FY2026. The vulnerability is the pool's size and price level: IDC expects component costs elevated through much of 2027, Apple raised iPhone 18 Pro prices by $100 and holds the standard iPhone 18 to spring 2027, so part of the gain is pull-forward. Apple has steadied China without regaining structural leadership; HarmonyOS still gives Huawei a localisation advantage.

Two competitors sit above the handset fight; neither needs a phone to reach Apple's services wallet [S148, S149, S151, S118]. ChatGPT reached 1.2 billion weekly users by 29 September 2026, and OpenAI told investors it had about $50B of annualised revenue at end-September, 77% run-rate growth in the quarter against Apple's 14.1% services growth in nine months. That is 41% of Apple's $120.5B services revenue. OpenAI is also a future hardware entrant, working with Jony Ive on a device shipping no earlier than February 2027. Microsoft attacks the layer beneath: $331.8B of FY2026 revenue at a 46.8% operating margin and 20% of Q2 2026 cloud spend to AWS's 28% and Google's 15%. Apple buys compute rather than owning it, including Google TPUs, so its AI cost curve depends on rivals.

Regulation transfers rent from Apple to rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. That lowers switching costs in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and gives Spotify and rival storefronts an iOS channel; Spotify has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. Its spread to other jurisdictions is the risk to monitor.

## Business Model

Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.1% trailing gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.0% trailing gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Nine-month products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% (the June quarter was 40.1%), and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 — 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield. The price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Nine months reconcile exactly: products gross profit of $108,819M on $272,629M is 39.9%, services $69,963M on $91,728M is 76.3%, summing to the filed $178,782M; the quarter ran at 40.1% and 75.6%. Services earn 40.3% of the trailing $227,123M gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue at 76.0%. The 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S6, S17, S68]

**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS (S17); products gross margin is 39.9% against 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% (S6, S68).

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M; working capital supplied $16,366M of the gap. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build reconciling within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision). The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.2x price to free cash flow on the $5,029.6bn market capitalisation; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B (39.5-41.0x), with $125.1B the midpoint. ### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: normalised free cash flow of $125.1B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 65.2%, compared with 57.3% in FY2025. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, a 9-11% cost of equity is cleared several times; the price is the constraint: $5,029.6bn of market capitalisation on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 is 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield; the $5,072B figure uses the June quarter's 14,715M diluted weighted-average count, 39.3x. Capital allocation agrees: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M equal 67.0% of reported nine-month free cash flow of $110,197M and 72.4% of the normalised $102,057M ($110,197M − $10,016M other-liabilities inflow + $1,876M, nine-twelfths of the $2,502M clean average); net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. Not a debt-funded buyback story. [S5, S6, S7, S10]

### What the next print has to clear

No audited fiscal 2026 exists: Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026. Guidance is 9-11% revenue growth for the quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B), iPhone mid-teens; the register's only consensus is iPhone revenue, $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on the $209,586M filed for FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%), with no group-revenue consensus held. On trailing figures at a 17.3% tax rate: 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of EPS (6.0%), 500 basis points is $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment is $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue at 39.9% is $0.55 (6.3%). Gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue while a unit miss applies only to hardware. For the investor, earnings quality is not the constraint; the price is. The open diligence: December-quarter gross margin guidance, FY2027 memory contracted at fixed prices, what the $12,116M of net intangibles bought, and what sits in the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities. ## Funding History & Valuation

Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares, 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025, and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x on $9.79 against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow suits a company whose value is almost all terminal, and is the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months $364.4bn plus $112.7bn at the 10% guidance midpoint), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate; on the base operating case, at 4.0% terminal growth, each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range above.

## Development Strategy

Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 and keeping 27 closures confidential, while challenging the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year, 0.65% of trailing operating income. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. The agreement was confirmed under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. ### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation.
